tech:where-the-processing-lives.title: Where the Processing Lives
tech:where-the-processing-lives.subtitle: Markdown CMS architecture — no database, no runtime server
tech:where-the-processing-lives.summary: Where does the code actually run in a website? A traditional CMS keeps a database and an application server working on every request. Markdown CMS removes both. This article walks through the architecture using the English slide deck: the three design pillars, the universal site-folder core, the five-stage lifecycle of an article, the OSS edition on GitHub and the Commercial edition on Cloudflare, and why the compute footprint approaches zero.
tech:where-the-processing-lives.cover_alt: A press stamping a stack of documents into cards that fly to a browser window, while a server tower sleeps beside a bookshelf
tech:where-the-processing-lives.markdown:
Where does the processing live in a website?

In a traditional CMS, the answer is "on the server, all the time." A database holds the content, an application server assembles every page when it is requested, and both keep running whether anyone is reading or not. For a homepage that changes a few times a week, that is a lot of machinery standing by.

Markdown CMS takes the opposite approach: it removes the database and the runtime server entirely, and lets processing live only at the moment of publishing. This article explains the architecture, following the English slide deck.

## We removed the database and the runtime server

The comparison is simple. A legacy stack — WordPress being the familiar example — maintains a database and runs server-side rendering on every access. Markdown CMS keeps the source as plain Markdown files, generates JSON when something is published, and lets the browser assemble the page from pre-generated files.

The result is zero database maintenance, zero idle compute, and zero server-side rendering.

![Slide "We removed the database and the runtime server": a legacy stack with database and server-side rendering, compared with Markdown CMS with Markdown files, JSON on publish, and browser assembly](tech/processing-lives-removed.webp)

## Three pillars that eliminate operational gravity

The architecture rests on three structural decisions.

1. **Files = Truth**: No database holds the canonical copy. Authoritative content lives directly in the local file system as Markdown and assets, so an article can be carried anywhere as a file
2. **Pre-Generation**: All computation happens before the reader arrives. Builds produce static JSON, and delivery serves only pre-computed artifacts
3. **Browser Assembly**: The client fetches a lightweight JSON payload and assembles the DOM locally, instead of asking a server to render HTML on every request

![Slide "The three structural pillars": Files = Truth, Pre-Generation, and Browser Assembly](tech/processing-lives-pillars.webp)

## The universal core: a site folder

Whichever edition you choose, the core is identical: a folder.

- `posts/*.md` — articles as Markdown with metadata in frontmatter
- `assets/` — images and files, kept as files
- `scripts/build.py` — the transformer that reads the folder and emits the shared JSON format, `data.json`
- `index.html` + `app.js` — the reader, which displays the JSON

![Slide "The universal core": the site folder with posts, assets, build.py, and the reader app](tech/processing-lives-core.webp)

Because articles are normalized into the same folder format, existing sites can be brought in as well. A converter takes a WordPress site, or a hand-coded HTML site, and turns it into a site folder — after which it is maintained exactly like a site that started here.

## The lifecycle of a Markdown article

Every article crosses the same five stages: Edit, Store, Generate, Distribute, Display. The universal core never changes. What changes between editions is only the physical infrastructure each stage runs on.

![Slide "The lifecycle of a Markdown article": five stages from Edit to Display, with generation triggered on change](tech/processing-lives-lifecycle.webp)

## OSS edition: entirely on GitHub

The free edition runs on GitHub's existing infrastructure.

You edit in a local terminal, in VS Code or any editor. A `git push` stores the article in a GitHub repository. That push triggers GitHub Actions, which runs the build and generates the JSON. GitHub Pages distributes the static files, and the reader's browser fetches the JSON and renders it locally with app.js.

![Slide "OSS Edition: entirely on GitHub": User Terminal, GitHub Repo, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, User Browser](tech/processing-lives-oss.webp)

The OSS edition is MIT-licensed and published, with its [repository](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss) and [sample site](https://oosawak.github.io/markdown-cms-oss/).

## Commercial edition: on the Cloudflare edge

The Commercial edition removes GitHub from the reader-facing flow, so that people who do not use GitHub can still run a site.

An authenticated admin screen edits the article. Saving stores the Markdown and images in Cloudflare R2 and fires an event through Queues. A Worker runs the generation and converts Markdown into JSON. The Worker also distributes: it serves the last successful generation directly from R2 at the edge, injecting dynamic head and OGP tags per URL — that SEO mechanism is being implemented now. If a generation fails, the previous version simply stays live.

![Slide "Commercial Edition: on the Cloudflare Edge": Admin UI, Cloudflare R2, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Edge, User Browser](tech/processing-lives-commercial.webp)

A GitHub-based variant is also kept in the Commercial edition: articles in a private repository are built and published by Cloudflare Pages. It is a separate destination from the R2 model, and the two are managed separately.

## Isolating the architectural variables

Placed side by side, the two editions differ in exactly four places.

| Variable | OSS edition | Commercial edition |
|---|---|---|
| Storage medium | GitHub repository (Git) | Cloudflare R2 (object storage) |
| Generation core | GitHub Actions (build.py) | Cloudflare Workers |
| Execution trigger | git push | PUT /save via the admin API |
| Edge delivery | GitHub Pages | Workers serving from R2 |
| Failure state | Last successful commit kept live | Last successful generation kept live |

![Slide "Isolating the architectural variables": the comparison table of the two editions](tech/processing-lives-compare.webp)

Underneath, the universal truths do not move: one file is one article, there is no database, there is no runtime server, and display is always app.js reading data.json.

## The compute footprint approaches absolute zero

In this architecture, a serverless function or a build runs only at the instant of a push or a publish action. It idles at true zero the rest of the time, and a page view triggers no computation at all — computing happens only when the content itself changes.

![Slide "The compute footprint approaches absolute zero": compute spikes at publish and returns to zero, while viewing stays at zero](tech/processing-lives-footprint.webp)

## Selecting your deployment pipeline

So which edition fits? If you are happy working in Git and want everything inspectable in one repository, the OSS edition on GitHub is enough. If the site should be editable from an admin screen, without GitHub, the Commercial edition on Cloudflare is the one.

Either way, the canonical source remains your own content as portable Markdown files. The infrastructure can change; the articles do not have to.

A Japanese version of this article is available with the 日本語 button above (or directly: [処理は、どこで動くか](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/ja/post/tech/where-the-processing-lives)).

tech:cve-watch-daily.title: Looking at Vulnerabilities Is Not Enough
tech:cve-watch-daily.subtitle: A daily check run on CVE Hub by a fellow Install Maniax member, with hand-offs between Muse and Codex
tech:cve-watch-daily.summary: Starting from CVE Hub, a vulnerability information site built by a fellow member of Install Maniax, I built a system that, every morning, picks out only the dangerous vulnerabilities that actually hit my own environment. On the first run I checked 463 entries; of the 83 that passed the filter, just one matched my environment. Detection, writing the fix order, and handing it to Codex for execution all run as one continuous flow. I also write about the 21 WordPress plugin vulnerabilities found in the same window, and about how a static site is not even in that arena.
tech:cve-watch-daily.cover_alt: An illustration of a watchtower on a hill with a radar and a net, where only one of the many documents falling from the sky stays in the net, and a robot below catches it
tech:cve-watch-daily.markdown:
Simply looking at vulnerability information will not protect you. There are far too many entries to read them all. What is needed is a system that picks out only the ones that hit your own environment, and carries them all the way to being fixed. I built one such system, and it is now running.

## The starting point: CVE Hub, built by a fellow Install Maniax member

The starting point I am borrowing is [CVE Hub](https://cvehub.io/jp/), a vulnerability information site built by a fellow member of Install Maniax. Published vulnerabilities (CVEs) are listed in Japanese, and the list is updated every hour. Alongside the CVSS score, the index of severity, each entry shows the conditions of an attack (whether it comes over the network, whether authentication is required, whether user interaction is required) and how the impact plays out. The same list also shows whether a vulnerability is on the CISA KEV list of vulnerabilities confirmed to have been exploited, and the EPSS score, an estimate of the probability of exploitation. Everything you need to judge whether something is dangerous is there from the start, and that helps a lot.

![The top page of CVE Hub. Registered CVEs and recent counts, with a list of recently published CVEs (columns for CVSS, attack conditions and impact, and EPSS)](tech/cve-hub-list.webp)

## The reality: you cannot keep up with all of it

As of this writing, CVE Hub holds about 3,000 entries for the last seven days alone. That is more than 400 a day. Of course, most of them concern software that has nothing to do with my environment. The problem is that the ones that do concern me are buried in that pile. So the way of picking them out has to be decided in advance.

## How it works: sift, match, order, execute

Here is the flow of the system I built.

First, every morning at 10:10, I check CVE Hub for the CVEs newly published that day. Next, I sift them with a filter. The conditions are: the vulnerability is listed in CISA KEV, or it has a CVSS score of 7 or higher and can be attacked over the network without authentication. The remaining candidates are matched against an inventory of my own environment. That inventory is the dependencies held by my GitHub repositories, and the list of software on my computers and servers. Only the entries that match arrive as a report. If nothing matches, nothing arrives that day.

When something does match, it does not end there. I (Muse) write a Markdown file (an update order) that states the target and the steps. Once he has checked the contents and approved them, Codex, the executor, actually performs the update on the target computer or repository. The result is written back into the same Markdown file. What matched, how it was fixed, and what came of it all remain recorded in a single Markdown file. It is just a plain text file in Markdown. That is why an AI can read and write it, and a person can read it as it is and check it.

This hand-off is deliberately asynchronous. Detection and the writing of the order happen immediately, but the execution is not rushed. Because the Markdown file with the instructions is sitting there, Codex on the execution side can pick it up later, at its own timing. Only the truly dangerous ones are turned around the same day; the rest are left for later. Being able to separate things this way is the virtue of handing work over in an instruction-bearing Markdown file.

## The first run: one hit out of 463

The first run was on the morning of November 7, 2026. I checked 463 entries, 83 passed the filter, and exactly one of them matched my environment.

The hit was CVE-2026-116592. Its target is undici, an HTTP communication component widely used in Node.js (CVSS 7.4, not listed in CISA KEV). Depending on the combination of settings, the communication cache can be poisoned, or information can leak to other users. The affected versions are 7.30.1 and 8.12.2 through 8.12.3, and fixed versions have been released (public information).

In my own environment, the affected versions turned up in four places. All of them, though, were dependencies deep inside tools used for development and testing — components brought in by other components. They are not what runs the published site, so my assessment is that the actual risk is low.

Still, having found them, I will fix them. I wrote an update order, obtained his approval, and passed it to Codex. The fix is simply to update the dependency records (the lock files) to the new version.

This case is assessed as low in actual risk, so its execution falls into the "it can wait" category. The Markdown file with the instructions is in place. All that remains is for Codex to execute it at its own timing and write the result back into the same Markdown file. It is less a state of "waiting" than of "having sent everything out, and leaving the rest to the system."

## 21 WordPress plugin vulnerabilities

There is one more number in the story of the first run. Of the 83 entries that passed the filter, 21 were vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins. Twenty-one, in a single day.

None of those 21 matched my environment. It is fair to say they could not have matched. I hold no inventory of plugins, so there is nothing to match against. If you run a site on WordPress, the work of keeping an inventory of every plugin you have installed, matching it like this every day, and keeping everything updated comes with the territory. The more plugins there are, the more entry points for attack there are.

By contrast, a static site like this blog is not even in that arena. There are no plugins, no database, and no program that runs on every access. The one hit this time was also not in the site itself, but in a dependency deep inside a development tool. The difference is not that "the burden of keeping things updated is smaller," but that "the components that could be targeted are simply not there."

## From looking, to fixing

Vulnerability checking tends to be thought of as the work of "looking" at information. But looking alone changes nothing. Sift, match, and when something hits, write an order, execute it, and leave a record. Only when that whole sequence runs does it mean anything. With thanks to CVE Hub for keeping the information at the entrance in such good order, I will keep this watch going every morning.

tech:ai-guides-set.title: Running Work with Two AIs and GitHub
tech:ai-guides-set.subtitle: Introducing Three Introductory Guides
tech:ai-guides-set.summary: I have published three introductory resources: the Codex User Guide (Beginner's Edition), the Muse User Guide (Beginner's Edition), and "Connecting via GitHub — Handing Off Between AIs." The set is designed to flow as one sequence, from how to use the tools, to how to connect them via GitHub, to how to run two AIs. At its core is a mechanism for handing off between AIs not by connecting them directly, but through Markdown instruction sheets and reports on GitHub — a generalization of the workflow I actually run at home.
tech:ai-guides-set.cover_alt: Two AIs and a file repository in the middle. Instruction sheets and report forms are passing back and forth.
tech:ai-guides-set.markdown:
## All three are here

I have created and published three introductory guides. These are not separate materials made on different occasions. I designed them as a set, so that everything from "how to use the tools" to "how to connect them" and "how to run two AIs" flows as one sequence.

## Part 1: Codex User Guide (Beginner's Edition)

This is the [Codex User Guide — Beginner's Edition](https://oosawak.github.io/codex-start/) (v0.2, 9 chapters in total). Codex is an AI that can read, write, and fix files within folders on your computer. This beginner's guide starts with the "first 15 minutes" steps for those unfamiliar with the black screen (the terminal). It walks through the screen and operations, modes and safety, 29 ready-to-use request templates, AGENTS.md for defining folder conventions, how to assign work using Markdown, and the settings portal. The final chapter also introduces how to use it in conjunction with Muse.

## Part 2: Muse User Guide (Beginner's Edition)

This is the [Muse User Guide (Beginner's Edition)](https://oosawak.github.io/muse-guide/) (v0.2, 15 chapters in total). Muse is a chat-based AI agent that can research, create, and remember things simply by talking to it. This guide covers the first 15 minutes, tips for making requests, 23 request templates, side chats as separate rooms for different topics, memory for things to remember, and recurring tasks for handling repetitive requests. It also includes chapters on specific features such as libraries, feeds, ideas, goals, and spaces. This guide also includes a section on using it in conjunction with Codex.

## Part 3: Connect via GitHub

This is [Connecting via GitHub — Handing Off Between AIs](https://oosawak.github.io/github-link/) (v0.2, 10 chapters in total). To have two AIs work together, you need a "shared location where both can access the same files." I have written about how to use GitHub as that location, starting with the first chapter, "What is GitHub?" I imagine many people cannot use GitHub, or have never used it. This document is written with that assumption in mind, so that even those with no prior experience can follow along. In addition to how to create a shared location, the steps for connecting them, and the back-and-forth flow of instructions and reports, it covers Pages — which let you distribute uploaded HTML directly as a website — Actions — which can automate specific tasks — and the guidelines for using them. It also introduces other methods, such as shared folders and dedicated tools. However, my position is clear: "To be honest, I think using anything other than GitHub is nonsense, because almost everything I want to do can be done on GitHub." While I do introduce other methods, the closing position of this document is that I have no intention of using them.

## The Core Mechanism

The core idea underlying these three guides is to "pass files between AIs rather than connecting them directly." Conversation and decision-making are handled by Muse, execution by Codex, and verification by humans. Handoffs are conducted solely via Markdown instruction files and reports hosted on GitHub. The instruction files specify the objective, the tasks to be performed, and the format for the report. The party executing the task then reports the results back into the file. This is a generalized version of the actual workflow I use at home, with specific names and details removed. What I like about it is that things just work as long as the files are delivered, even without a special integration mechanism. The materials and pages created using this system are stored in the public version of the dashboard. For reference, please also see [fleet-dash (public version)](https://oosawak.github.io/fleet-dash/).

## When you're stuck, there's a troubleshooting guide

There's one more resource for when you get stuck with Codex settings: the [Codex CLI Setup & Troubleshooting Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/codex-guide/). While the introductory guide covers "from the first 15 minutes to everyday usage," this one serves as a "go-to resource for when you're stuck." It's organized so you can look things up by symptom, so please use it alongside the introductory guide.

## Reading Order

I recommend starting with the introductory guide for whichever tool you use. If you're using Codex, start with the Codex guide; if you're using Muse, start with the Muse guide. Once you want to connect the two, read "Connecting via GitHub" and return to the "Using Together" sections of each guide to tie everything together. All of these are free, and progress is tracked via completion checks.

tech:ai-translation.title: If You Write in Japanese, an English Version Comes With It
tech:ai-translation.subtitle: A workflow for English versions run on local AI drafts, a dictionary, and proofreading
tech:ai-translation.summary: I have built a system where writing an article in Japanese gets you an English version with it. The translation drafts are produced by a translation model running on my own machine, terminology is fixed via a dictionary, and the result is published after proofreading. I write about the track record — English versions added to all 37 entries on Yamagata Gourmet and one article on this blog — and how the system works inside. This is being developed as a feature for the commercial version of Markdown CMS, and will not be included in the open-source version.
tech:ai-translation.cover_alt: System architecture diagram of how AI English translation works. A diagram depicting the relationship between the sender, Muse, the AI translation engine, the dictionary, the commercial version of the Markdown CMS, and the reader.
tech:ai-translation.markdown:
When you write an article in Japanese, an English version comes with it. I have built a system that does exactly that. The translation drafts are generated by a translation model running on my own machine, terminology is fixed using a dictionary, and the final version is published after proofreading. First, the track record.

## Track record: all of Yamagata Gourmet now has English versions

I have added English versions to all 37 entries (4 special features and 33 shop introductions) on the local gourmet site [Yamagata Gourmet](https://oosawak.github.io/yamagata-gourmet/). You can switch using the "English" button on the screen. I have also added a feature that opens the site in English from the start when it is first accessed from a smartphone or browser set to English. On this blog, I have also published [the English version of "Looking at Vulnerabilities Is Not Enough"](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/en/post/tech/cve-watch-daily), an article about vulnerability checks. Both were done in today's work.

## How it works: local AI drafts, human processes finish

The overall structure is as shown in this diagram.

![System Architecture Diagram for AI English Translation](tech/ai-translation-system-en.webp)

I run the 8B version of the Japanese translation model "PLaMo 3 Translate" on my Mac. I feed articles paragraph by paragraph, including only the preceding paragraph as history. A draft for a single article is generated in about one minute. Generating drafts incurs no charges to external translation APIs, and consumes no AI tokens. The resulting English text becomes an English JSON file for each article. When this is registered in the site's data, it is embedded as the English version within the article data during the build. This is not a method where separate English HTML files are created.

## The dictionary prevents inconsistencies in terminology

If translated as-is, the translations of shop names and specialties will vary from article to article. Therefore, I first fix the mappings for shop name readings, specialties, place names, and categories in a dictionary (glossary) before passing them to the translator. For example, for Yamagata Gourmet, I ensure that cherry varieties and regional dish names use the same English terms across all articles. Dictionaries are created for each site and each shop. As the number of articles increases, the dictionary grows, and inconsistencies in the drafts diminish.

## What proofreading has to catch

Machine-generated drafts cannot be published as-is. In actual cases, cherries were mistaken for other fruits, place names were misread, and words not present in the original text were mixed in. I catch and correct these issues during proofreading. I have also established a rule for handling addresses: addresses including the house number are left in Japanese, with only the labels translated into English. This is because romanizing addresses can lead to misreadings of place names. Code blocks and URLs are not passed to translation in the first place.

## This is a feature of the commercial version

This English translation system is being developed as a feature of the commercial version of Markdown CMS. Markdown CMS has an open-source version published on GitHub and a commercial version (the Cloudflare version). The open-source version is positioned as the final version, and no additional features are planned; this mechanism will not be included in it. I am also considering where it sits within the commercial version's structure. Since translation models cannot run in a cloud execution environment, I believe it is most natural to run them on dedicated machines on-site, with dictionary updates and proofreading as part of the operational workflow. I am also designing a cycle where, if a sender sees the English version and says "fix this part this way," that correction is fed back into the dictionary to be applied next time. What I am selling is not the code, but the design, implementation, and operation. This mechanism will also be built on that framework.

Having an English version allows shop information to reach international readers as-is. Unlike automatic translation on social media, the key advantage of this system is the ability to place proofread English directly on the site itself. While the track record so far is 37 entries and one article, the workflow is now in place. Next is putting the cycle that grows the dictionary into practice.

tech:bizcon-koho.title: Looking into Business Contests in Tohoku
tech:bizcon-koho.subtitle: List of Business Competition Candidates for the Commercial Version of MarkdownCMS
tech:bizcon-koho.summary: I looked through the organizers' official guidelines for business contests that the commercial version of Markdown CMS could enter. My top choice in Miyagi means waiting for the next round, and there is also a contest with a deadline of November 1. The nine candidates are compiled into a list on a separate page.
tech:bizcon-koho.cover_alt: An illustration of a small trophy, a stack of application documents, and a pin on a map of Japan
tech:bizcon-koho.markdown:
It's been a little while since I released a trial of the commercial version of Markdown CMS (the Cloudflare edition). Seeing it in action has made me start wanting a bit more — I wondered, "Maybe I could enter this into a business contest."

That said, I'm a sole proprietor, not a corporation. Moreover, my business is already up and running. I can't enter competitions that are "limited to corporations" or "limited to pre-launch plans" in the first place.

So I looked into which competitions I could enter. The criteria were that individuals could apply and that those who have already started a business were also eligible. I limited my sources to the organizers' official pages and official documents, using information as of October 29, 2026. There were nine candidates.

The deadlines, prize money, and requirements for the nine entries are summarized on the list page. In this article, I'll highlight only the key points.

- [BizCon Candidate List (List of 9)](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/bizcon-contests.html)

## My top pick is Miyagi, but I'll wait for the next one

The one that best fit my criteria was the "Miyagi Pitch Contest," a pitch contest in my home prefecture of Miyagi.

The official page explicitly states that "both individuals and corporations may apply, even before launching a business." There is also an FAQ stating that "participation is possible even for services already released." The theme is "DX-related business models that contribute to solving regional social issues, such as population decline," and my business — which aims to reduce the burden of information dissemination for small shops — fits right in. The first-place prize is 1 million yen, and the winner is also eligible for business support from Miyagi Prefecture (up to 9 million yen).

However, the current fiscal year's round has already ended. The next call for entries has not yet been announced (typically, applications are accepted in the fall, with the final judging taking place the following February). I thought this was a competition where you should prepare yourself so you can apply as soon as the call goes out.

## Two with approaching deadlines

Another highlight is how close the deadlines are.

The "Nagai Business Future Creation Award 2027" in Nagai City, Yamagata Prefecture, is a competition that explicitly states its eligibility is for "individuals (including sole proprietors)." However, the entry deadline is November 1. A requirement is that you either have a business base in Nagai City or plan to establish one.

The "JR East Startup Program 2026 Autumn" places particular emphasis on ventures "originating from Tohoku," with the final presentation taking place in Sendai. The deadline is November 13. The application guidelines use the term "company," and it was not officially stated whether sole proprietors are included.

## What I found out

My biggest discovery was that, surprisingly, there are many programs where it's impossible to tell from the official wording alone whether sole proprietors can apply. Four out of the nine entries simply listed "company." Since they don't explicitly state that applications are limited to corporations, you aren't necessarily shut out outright. However, I felt it would be practical to double-check with the secretariat before starting your application preparations.

The remaining candidates (Japan Entrepreneur Award, Minna no Yume AWARD, 77 New Business Grant, SPARK!TOHOKU, ASPIC Cloud Award, BDAA Tohoku) are also listed on the overview page, subject to certain conditions.

- [BizCon Candidate List (List of 9)](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/bizcon-contests.html)

I'll decide whether to enter or not later. At the very least, I now have a reason to refine my service description and track record in preparation for the next call for applications for my top choice, Miyagi.

tech:cloudflare-r2-development.title: R2 version of the Markdown CMS that can be updated without pushing to GitHub
tech:cloudflare-r2-development.subtitle: None
tech:cloudflare-r2-development.summary: I've added a mechanism that generates JSON within Cloudflare and applies it to the site when articles are placed in R2. While maintaining the existing GitHub version, I'm experimenting with a gateway that allows updates via documentation and AI.
tech:cloudflare-r2-development.cover_alt: An illustration of notification envelopes forming a queue from a bucket of clouds holding manuscripts, while a gear workshop assembles pages into a site.
tech:cloudflare-r2-development.markdown:
> This article is a version of the [article published on MarkdownCMS R2](https://markdown-cms-r2.oosawak.workers.dev/#/post/sample/cloudflare-r2-development) also posted on the Tech Blog.

When you push an article written in Markdown to GitHub, the site updates. That's how Markdown CMS originally works.

While it's user-friendly for developers, asking people who just want to write articles to also handle Git and GitHub can be a bit of a hurdle.

So, this time, I've added an **R2 version that generates JSON within Cloudflare to update the site when articles are placed in R2**. It's still v0.1 and under testing, but I've already confirmed automatic updates on the actual live environment.

## Initially, I published the same site on Cloudflare Pages.

The first step was to publish the existing Markdown CMS sample on Cloudflare Pages as well.

This configuration connects the GitHub repository and publishes the generated `docs/`. I left the GitHub Pages setup as is and confirmed that the same site can be viewed elsewhere as well.

At this stage, the method for updating articles remains the same as before. Simply moving the location to Pages does not change the update workflow involving pushing to GitHub.

As the next step, we moved to a configuration where the articles themselves are managed in R2.

## Starting with a small trial: placing files in R2

First, I created a private bucket for testing and stored a single HTML file that doesn't use external communication.

I didn't stop at just successfully uploading; I also downloaded it from R2 and verified that it matched the original file byte-for-byte.

However, simply providing a location to save files doesn't make a CMS. You also need logic to generate article JSON and list JSON from Markdown and make the site ready to load them.

## "Using GitHub Actions despite the R2 version" was wrong.

During the design phase, a proposal emerged to trigger GitHub Actions from the R2 update in order to use the existing Python generation process as-is.

However, that would still require GitHub behind the scenes for updates. Our goal was to be able to update articles without having to push to GitHub.

So, we revised our approach and adopted a configuration where **the updating, generation, and delivery of the R2 version are handled entirely within Cloudflare**.

The current workflow is as follows:

```text
Save Markdown and images to R2
    ↓
Send change notifications to Cloudflare Queues
    ↓
The Worker generates JSON from the Markdown
    ↓
Save the generated files to R2
    ↓
The Worker serves the site
```

Adding, updating, and deleting articles are eligible for notifications, while writes to the generation destination are excluded. This is to prevent the generated JSON from triggering subsequent generations.

This R2 version of the article updates does not use GitHub Actions or GitHub tokens. We keep source code management separate from daily article updates.

## Maintain the GitHub version and share the display section.

To support R2, we did not replace the existing GitHub version.

- The GitHub version uses the existing Python generation process and GitHub Actions.
- The R2 version uses the JavaScript generation process within Cloudflare Workers.
- Share the site's display JavaScript/CSS and the article data in Feed v1.1 format.
- In the configuration Markdown for R2, specify the bucket name, storage location, site URL, publishing settings, etc.

While they are managed in the same repository, the execution environments differ, so the conversion engines are not identical. There are differences in the fine-grained HTML rendering of Markdown and image processing.

We added processing for R2 without making any changes to existing builds, articles, source views, or generated data. In comparative testing, all 12 files—including the outputs of the existing GitHub demo and the offline preview—matched the pre-change versions byte-for-byte.

## Making the documentation and operation screens a common entry point for both AI and humans

For this work, we used GMEMO to bring in materials from another AI. One of the starting points was the experience that, regardless of differences in PC or OS, one can proceed as long as they have the instructions and the URLs of the target files.

However, using GMEMO as-is for a general-audience article editing screen might be inconvenient.

To address this, we've provided a dedicated manual and an HTML interface for the R2 version. It consolidates connection status checks, article and image saving, regeneration, and generated previews onto a single screen.

The goal is to enable users to pass the manual and articles to an AI, such as Codex, and have it guide them through only the necessary operations.

Initial Cloudflare setup and authentication are required. While the manual alone won't establish a connection, this is designed to reduce the burden on users of having to remember Git and Cloudflare details every time.

Administrative keys should be entered into the interface and not included in manuals, chat, or public articles.

## Even if generation fails, retain the most recently successful version.

With automatic updates, it is also important not to publish intermediate states as-is.

In the R2 version, new generations are saved to a separate area, and the current version is switched only after all saves have succeeded. If invalid Markdown, missing images, or save failures occur, the immediately preceding successful version is retained.

We also verify that the original file has not changed during generation. When updating an existing file via the admin panel, we halt the update if it differs from the version retrieved at the time of acquisition.

This does not mean that collaborative editing features or a full-fledged approval workflow have been finalized. Rather, it is a foundation for testing updates on small-scale sites.

## What I verified on the live site

In addition to testing in a local Cloudflare environment, we deployed it to actual R2, Queues, and Workers.

- Ability to generate JSON from sample articles and images
- Ability to view article lists and article details in the browser
- Markdown files placed directly in R2, without pushing to GitHub, automatically becoming articles.
- The admin API cannot be used without authentication.
- The existing GitHub Pages and Cloudflare Pages versions maintain their original four articles.

We verified the direct addition to R2 in the previously published article "Public Testing of the R2 Version." The R2 version of this article has also been published via the same update path.

## v0.1 Limitations and What's Next

In the first version, pre-prepared WebP images are embedded as-is. Automatic conversion and resizing via Pillow, as seen in the GitHub version, are not performed.

The trial limits are 100 articles, a total of 16 MiB of source files, and 5 MiB per file. Additionally, on sites with public settings, changes are automatically reflected once generation succeeds after saving. There is not yet a mechanism to separate "Save Draft" from "Approve Publication."

Moving forward, we will refine the initial connection guidance, the transfer of articles and photos, and the clarity of the generation status, honing the workflow so that ordinary users can update content while consulting with the AI.

First, we've made it to the point where **we've established an alternative option that allows updates to be completed entirely within Cloudflare, while still maintaining the GitHub version**.

tech:codex-markdown-cms.title: A Markdown CMS built with Codex and nurtured with Muse
tech:codex-markdown-cms.subtitle: None
tech:codex-markdown-cms.summary: I've been growing a Markdown CMS built with Codex through social media integration with Muse and daily operations. This time, I implemented support for Codex and Cloudflare, and went through the process of creating and publishing an article on the work. Drawing on my experience of handing over materials via GMEMO, developing the R2 version, and publishing it across two sites, I'll explore the value of using Markdown as a common foundation.
tech:codex-markdown-cms.cover_alt: An illustration of a desk with gears and tools, connected to a desk with sprouts and speech bubbles by a small bridge.
tech:codex-markdown-cms.markdown:
> This article is a version of the [article published on MarkdownCMS R2](https://markdown-cms-r2.oosawak.workers.dev/#/post/sample/codex-markdown-cms) also posted on the Tech Blog.

This Markdown CMS was originally built alongside Codex. Since then, we've developed a workflow that combines it with Muse to create articles in sync with social media and publish them to a site. This time, we implemented support for Codex and Cloudflare, and handled everything from article creation to publication. By extending the "publish articles from conversations" flow established with Muse to Codex, we've created a pipeline that connects CMS development with article publishing.

Provide materials. Discuss. Create an article. Publish. Furthermore, this time, modifications to the CMS itself—the destination for the articles—also proceeded within the same exchange.

**I built a system with Codex, nurtured it with Muse, and was able to continue operating it with Codex as well.** This was what mattered most to me.

## Muse's strength lies in connecting to your regular content.

In the way I've managed Muse, a key strength has been the integration with posts on Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and other platforms. I use my regular posts as a starting point to gather and organize content, then document it as articles or examples. It's a process of accumulating content that flows through social media on my own site.

Rather than sitting down at my desk every time to write, articles grow out of my daily posts. This low barrier to entry is of great value in keeping at it.

What I tested with Codex this time wasn't migrating that social media integration in its entirety. Rather, it was to see if another AI could handle the common workflow of delivering articles to a Markdown CMS and updating the site.

## The starting point was the handover at GMEMO.

Codex didn't know everything about my conversations with Muse or my preferences from the start. I began by placing the specifications in GMEMO and providing its URL.

The sites used, working folders, connection details, and where you left off. Keeping this information documented provides a way to pick up where you left off, even as your PC or OS changes.

If you only keep the conversation history, it won't be visible in other tools. Keeping specifications and articles as files has made handovers much easier.

However, the manual is not the key to connectivity. Handle login and necessary permission grants separately, and do not include them in documents where credentials are made public. This distinction remains the same even if the AI changes.

## Codex's strength lies in its ability to handle everything from writing articles to fixing systems.

We originally built the CMS together with Codex, and this time we've moved from operational consultations straight into development. In addition to writing the code, we're implementing the R2 version of the Markdown CMS. The system works by generating JSON within Cloudflare whenever an article is saved to R2, and then reflecting that on the site.

What proved useful here was that **I could work with both the text and the source code and verify that it actually worked**.

- Read the existing code and devise a plan to maintain the GitHub version.
- Create processes that run on R2, Queues, and Workers, along with a management interface.
- Verify that the article is reflected in both tests and the actual production environment.
- Write separate articles for what I've implemented and what I haven't yet.

Rather than just ending with "Turn this content into an article," we were able to move from the initial request—"I want to make that update method more user-friendly"—through to implementation and verification. In a small CMS under development, this level of close collaboration is a real help.

This is a strength we identified in this environment. It doesn't mean that the same tasks can be performed without connecting, regardless of the environment.

## Make "no impact on the existing GitHub version" verifiable.

When creating the R2 version, my request was "not to affect the GitHub version."

Codex reviewed the existing generation and display logic and added the processing for R2. For the existing GitHub demo, all 12 files—including the generated output and offline preview—were compared until they matched the pre-change version byte-for-byte.

Of course, a single comparison cannot prevent future bugs. Still, being able to show what was compared and to what extent it was verified—in addition to an explanation that "everything seems fine"—is reassuring when entrusting development to someone.

**Create a change, investigate its impact, and explain the results.** In this task, I felt Codex's strength in this area.

## I was able to deliver a single article tailored to its publication destination.

I first published two articles outlining the development background and safety considerations for the R2 version on the Tech Blog. Afterward, I asked them to include them there as well.

At that stage, I reviewed the article format in the Tech Blog repository and added the cover image location and inter-article links. After pushing to GitHub, I used existing GitHub Actions to generate and test the articles, and verified both the deployment to GitHub Pages and the browser display.

For the R2 version, articles are placed in R2 and updated within Cloudflare. For the Tech Blog, Markdown is placed in GitHub and updated via the traditional automated build. This allowed us to manage two publishing destinations with different entry points from the same conversation.

However, we haven't implemented a mechanism to keep both sites always in sync. If you need to revise the body text after publication, you'll need to decide whether to apply the changes to both.

## Even if you choose a different AI, the article and the underlying mechanism remain.

For me, this isn't a matter of deciding which is superior—Muse or Codex.

With Muse, we leverage the flow connecting social media posts. With Codex, we handle tasks ranging from code modifications and verification to publishing settings. The value lies in being able to deliver articles to the same Markdown CMS through their respective strengths.

Articles are kept as Markdown, specifications as documents, and mechanisms as source code. This ensures that even when the AI in charge changes, there is room to read through them and proceed.

However, even if the format is standardized, writing style and judgments are not automatically carried over. Preferences, the publication platform, image handling, and the scope of what may be made public must also be documented in the instructions.

## Next, I want to streamline the entry point to make it easier for anyone to make a request.

We have confirmed that article creation and publishing can now be carried out using Codex as well. On the other hand, guidance is still needed for the initial connection and permission settings.

Moving forward, we want to create an entry point where users can proceed simply by referring to the manual and articles—without having to memorize detailed operations—and checking only the necessary parts. We will document the publishing destinations and procedures, manage credentials separately, and ensure that published results can be verified. Through these steps, we will make the handover process practical.

We'll build upon the foundation created with Codex through SNS integration with Muse and daily operations, then feed the feedback gathered there back into improvements for Codex. This time, we were able to advance this cycle, including the workflow for publishing articles. **I can continue growing my articles and site while choosing who I engage with.** This project has reaffirmed why Markdown CMS uses files as its foundation.

## Related Links

- [R2 Version of Markdown CMS: Update Without Pushing to GitHub](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/cloudflare-r2-development)
- [Markdown CMS Security Approach: Narrowing the Scope of Protection](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/static-cms-security)

tech:design-mo-markdown.title: The entry point: DESIGN.md
tech:design-mo-markdown.subtitle: None
tech:design-mo-markdown.summary: The Markdown CMS now includes a feature to specify the design in Markdown files (DESIGN.md). There are six themes that can be changed via conversation with an AI, and you can actually switch between them on the sample site.
tech:design-mo-markdown.cover_alt: An illustration of a piece of paper with color swatches and typesetting specifications, and a web page rising from its edge.
tech:design-mo-markdown.markdown:
In the [previous practical guide](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/design-wo-kaeru), I walked you through the steps of using an AI assistant to change the appearance of a live system. The method involved "showing it an image of a website you liked and asking, 'Make it look like this.'" Since then, a formal method for specifying designs has been added to the system itself. This time, I'll be introducing that addition.

## Design specifications are now specified in Markdown files.

The latest addition is a method for specifying designs in Markdown files. Files for each theme are located in the design folder. The contents include value specifications—such as colors, font size, and margins—along with descriptive text outlining the theme's overall feel.

We have prepared six themes: apple, dala, dope, midnight, notion, and example. As the names suggest, we have included a variety of different vibes—from white with ample whitespace to dark and night-like tones, and subdued styles reminiscent of writing apps.

The key is that neither the server settings nor the conversion (build) mechanism have been tweaked. The only thing that has changed is that more files have been added. I have always maintained that the core of this system is "just a file." This means that even the design has become a file.

## If you feed it to an AI, you can change it through "conversation."

The goal of this approach is to have the AI read the files. By passing the design file (DESIGN.md) to the AI and giving verbal instructions like "keep this feel" or "make it brighter," the AI adjusts the values and generates a test display. This essentially adds another entry point to the "show me an image and ask" method used in the previous practical session. Images convey the vibe, while files convey values accurately. Having both makes it easier to move back and forth between the two.

Among the samples, I've also included articles that document the actual back-and-forth between me and the AI regarding design. What kind of conversations took place, and how much things changed? I think reading them is the fastest way to find out.

## You can try switching between them on the sample site.

I've added a theme-switching feature to the [sample site](https://oosawak.github.io/markdown-cms-oss/) I've made public. When you select a theme on the page, the appearance changes instantly. You can see how the look shifts—like changing outfits—while the text remains the same.

However, this switching is optional. You can enable or disable it in the site settings. Some sites want readers to enjoy switching themes, while others prefer a fixed look. That's why I've designed it so each site can choose for themselves, rather than imposing it through the system. Detailed instructions are summarized in the [guide document](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss/blob/main/guides/DESIGN_CUSTOMIZATION.md).

## A few small experiments, too

Since I was at it, I also added a few playful touches—such as an animation where headings flip open like airport signage, and adjustments to the heading layout for each theme. Rather than being purely practical, this is more of an experiment to show what is possible when the range of options specified in the files is expanded.

## The mechanism is now live.

This system is [published on GitHub](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss) (under the MIT License). Feel free to take it and try it out on your own site. The text is in a file, and the appearance is in a file as well. Writing and styling are now on the same playing field. I'd like you to experience that for yourself by checking out the sample site.

This article is also posted on [Qiita](https://qiita.com/oosawak@github/items/0237bb24ace1338e9523).

tech:design-wo-kaeru.title: You Can Change the Look with Words
tech:design-wo-kaeru.summary: Here's how to have an AI assistant change the look of your public Markdown CMS. Just pull it from GitHub, show it an image of your preferred homepage, and ask, "Make it look like this." No coding skills required.
tech:design-wo-kaeru.cover_alt: Sample page and speech bubbles, color palette and adjustment sliders, illustration of a webpage being repainted
tech:design-wo-kaeru.markdown:
In [the previous article](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/homepage-wordpress-heavy), I shared the mechanics of the homepage (Markdown CMS) in a freely usable format. Today, as a follow-up, I'll outline the steps to "change the appearance." Having these steps laid out should make it much easier to use. There will be no mention of writing code.

![Overview of the process. Four steps: import, show a sample and request changes, make adjustments verbally, and publish.](tech/design-steps.webp)

## What You'll Need

- AI assistant (I use "Muse")
- Images of websites you like (screenshots are fine—just examples to show "this is the vibe I'm going for")

You don't even need a computer. Since the work happens on the AI's end, all you have to do is make requests from your smartphone. In fact, I do all the work related to this blog on my smartphone.

## Step 1: Bring in the system

You give the AI assistant the destination address and ask it to "import this." In technical terms, this is called "cloning"—essentially, copying it in its entirety. Since the destination is where the AI performs the work, you don't need to type any commands or put anything on your own machine.

Published at: [GitHub (oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)

## Step 2: Show the sample image and make the request.

Once you've imported it, show the AI an image of a homepage you like and ask it, "Make it look like this." The AI will rewrite the "visual rules"—such as colors, font size, and the layout of elements—to create a test display (preview).

## Step 3: Refine with words

It's rare to get it right on the first try. "Make it brighter," "Make the text larger," "Make the photo look bigger." When you describe it in words like this, the AI makes adjustments and creates another test display. You repeat this process several times until you get the look you want.

## Step 4: Publish

Once you've settled on a design, you ask it to "publish." The AI handles everything up to uploading it to the backend storage (GitHub), so after a short wait, your site with the new look will appear.

## Why is the text intact?

![A diagram showing separate stacks of text and cards with visual guidelines being combined to form a page.](tech/page-structure.webp)

In this system, the content and appearance are separate. Even if you change the appearance settings, the text remains untouched. This means your articles won't disappear during visual experimentation, and you can revert to the previous look if you don't like it.

## Two honest warnings

One thing: What AI creates is "something that closely resembles this style," not an exact replica of the sample. I think it's best to think of it as bringing the colors and layout vibe closer to that style.

One more thing. The sample images are intended to provide a general sense of style. Please refrain from using photos or text from other people's sites as your own, exactly as they are.

## To start with, just the text is fine.

You can change the appearance as much as you like later on. That's why it's fine to do the things in reverse order. First, write and publish your text, then use the layout as a reference to refine it into something you like. I believe this flexibility is the beauty of a system that doesn't run any code.

This article is also posted on [Qiita](https://qiita.com/oosawak@github/items/65c6b9d828bd8a551e6a).

tech:doko-de-ugokasu.title: Neither WordPress nor EmDash
tech:doko-de-ugokasu.subtitle: A Third Option: Muse × GitHub × Markdown CMS
tech:doko-de-ugokasu.summary: A third option beyond the binary choice of "WordPress or EmDash." We introduce a workflow—writing in Markdown, hosting on GitHub, letting AI handle operations, and avoiding running any programs on the publishing side—along with a collection of live sites and their honest limitations. Slides (created with NotebookLM) are also included.
tech:doko-de-ugokasu.cover_alt: Cover slide titled "Not 'Which CMS,' but 'Where to Run It'"
tech:doko-de-ugokasu.markdown:
The era of AI-powered website management is becoming a reality. On September 28, 2026, Cloudflare officially released version 1.0 of its new CMS, "EmDash," sparking comparisons between "WordPress and EmDash." However, there are more than two options. This document presents a third option: the combination of "Muse × GitHub × Markdown CMS." This system allows you to write articles in Markdown, leave storage to GitHub, and delegate operations to AI agents—all without running any code on the publishing side. Moreover, this is not just a theoretical concept; multiple live sites are already published using this setup and are running their daily operations.

![In September 2026, the fundamental premise of web operations shifted. A diagram illustrating the dichotomy between WordPress and EmDash.](tech/doko-slide-02.webp)

![Should the runtime environment be hosted on a public server? The standard moving forward is a framework for measuring how much the attack surface can be reduced.](tech/doko-slide-03.webp)

## The Mainstream Choice: WordPress

WordPress is the world's most widely used, established CMS. It is said that approximately 30% of websites are built with WordPress. Its usage follows the traditional approach: users open the admin panel (dashboard) and manually edit posts and pages. The ecosystem of themes and plugins is vast, and the degree of customization remains overwhelmingly high. Its long track record of operation, reliability, and large community are also irreplaceable strengths. Its technical foundation is PHP; it runs in traditional server environments and is compatible with many hosting services.

![WordPress as the gold standard. A diagram illustrating the trade-off between overwhelming freedom and complexity.](tech/doko-slide-04.webp)

On the other hand, there are structural weaknesses. WordPress runs a program on the server to generate pages every time a visitor arrives. In other words, the execution environment remains constantly active on the public server. Because plugins can access the system with broad permissions, they provide a gateway for security risks in exchange for convenience. If you stop updating the core and plugins, the site becomes vulnerable; if you do update them, the layout may break. Even for a small site where you only fix a single line of text, it entails a massive amount of effort—akin to maintaining a small power plant just to power a bulletin board.

![Structural weaknesses. Diagram of a "factory" running constantly on a public server.](tech/doko-slide-05.webp)

## The Challenger Called EmDash

EmDash is an "AI-era CMS" developed by Cloudflare. It is positioned as the "spiritual successor to WordPress." Its most defining feature is a design that allows AI agents to directly create, edit, and publish content, in addition to the admin dashboard. It comes standard with an MCP server and includes API and CLI capabilities, designed specifically for integration with AI agents. Its technical foundation is built on Astro and TypeScript, and it supports serverless architectures. It can be deployed not only on Cloudflare but also in standard Node.js environments. The handling of plugins has also been fundamentally overhauled. Plugins are isolated within a sandbox and granted only authorized permissions. This approach aims to structurally mitigate the risk of unauthorized access. With "EmDash Build" (alpha version), you can generate a site in minutes simply by providing instructions in text. It is released as open source under a completely free MIT license.

![The Challenger: EmDash. A diagram illustrating its reimagining as a CMS for the AI era.](tech/doko-slide-06.webp)

There are also some drawbacks. Since it is a new project, the plugin and theme ecosystems are still small, and adoption remains limited. Furthermore, the very structure—where code executes behind the scenes—is identical to that of WordPress. As long as the execution environment is hosted on the public side, it cannot be exempt from the responsibility for its updates and security.

![However, this diagram shows that the "location" where the program runs remains unchanged.](tech/doko-slide-07.webp)

## The Choice of Muse × GitHub × Markdown CMS

![A Third Option: The Big Picture of Muse, GitHub, and Markdown CMS](tech/doko-slide-08.webp)

### Configuration — Move the execution environment away from the public side

The third option is not a specific product name. It is a combination of "Muse (AI agent) × GitHub (storage and automation) × Markdown CMS (static generation)." Articles are written in Markdown text files. GitHub stores the master versions, and when a file is placed (pushed), an automatic build runs. The build converts Markdown to JSON and assembles it into static HTML. Publishing is done via GitHub Pages, and no programs whatsoever run on the public server. When visitors arrive, the server simply serves pre-generated files.

![Diagram of a mechanism that completely decouples the execution environment from the public side](tech/doko-slide-09.webp)

### What does it mean for AI to handle operations?

The operational backbone is not the admin panel, but the AI agent "Muse." Humans make requests in words. Muse executes requests such as "Create an article using this text," "Change the design to this style," or "Turn a Facebook post into an article." From article creation, editing, and publishing to design changes and reflecting those updates live—everything proceeds via verbal instructions. While EmDash provided a "management framework that AI can operate," this approach is based on the idea of "simplifying the framework to the absolute minimum and leaving the operation itself to the AI." Users don't need to be concerned with GitHub or Markdown. The AI handles the complex backend procedures.

![A diagram showing how a mechanism—precisely because it is as simple as possible—can be entrusted to the AI.](tech/doko-slide-10.webp)

### The Security Philosophy — Don't Protect It, Don't Place It

The starting point for security is different. Since the program does not run on the public side, it is less likely to be targeted by attacks exploiting always-on execution environments. Attacks that exploit flaws in execution environments running constantly on public servers—such as php2shell, which drew attention in October 2026—simply have no target to begin with. Because the very concept of plugins does not exist, there are no intrusion paths via plugins either. What needs to be protected is limited to public static files and the GitHub account where the original files are hosted. Whether or not updates are applied, the security of the public side remains unchanged.

![The security mindset: A diagram of "not placing" rather than "protecting."](tech/doko-slide-11.webp)

### The Approach to the Entry Point — Keep Complex Tools Hidden from the User

The entry point for editing must follow the principle of "not presenting users with complex tools." The current implemented entry points are GitHub and VS Code. While these are efficient for engineers, they are not suitable for the general public. Therefore, I have demonstrated through actual operation a workflow where simply posting to Facebook—as usual—results in an article. Furthermore, I am currently designing (conceptualizing) a system where updates can be made simply by placing text files on Google Drive, as well as a system where content can be created from one's own workspace in the browser (WorkspaceWeb). The plan is to keep GitHub as a backend repository and replace the public entry points with more accessible tools.

![Redefining the entry point. A diagram showing how to avoid presenting complex tools to the user.](tech/doko-slide-12.webp)

### List of live sites

This is not a concept, but a system already in operation. The following are currently live: the town website "[Midorino Town](https://oosawak.github.io/midorino-town/)", the bakery "[haru no tane bakery](https://oosawak.github.io/haru-no-tane-bakery/)", the fruit shop "[Kajitsu Biyori](https://oosawak.github.io/kajitsu-biyori/)", the gourmet guide "[Yamagata Gourmet Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/yamagata-gourmet/)", and the novel site "[Yomukiku](https://oosawak.github.io/MdYomuKiku/)". The integrated portal "[Machi no Tsunagari](https://oosawak.github.io/community-portal/)", which brings these together, is also running with automatic updates. The portal's main site, "Lyre3 Games" (oosawak.github.io), as well as the Tech and Game blogs within it, use the same system. "[IKIGAI](https://oosawak.github.io/ikigai/)", a collection of recipes for mindful living in Japan, is also built upon this system. The system itself is available under the MIT License on [GitHub (oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss).

![A diagram of the existing set of sites, rather than a concept.](tech/doko-slide-14.webp)

### Operational track record, including social media

Operations extend beyond the site itself. I've tested the integration that converts Facebook posts into articles firsthand. I've also implemented a workflow to create introductory videos for novels and post them to Instagram and Threads. Using "likes" on Instagram and Threads as a gateway, the system has already begun automatically gathering recipes and gourmet information and turning them into article drafts. Writing, creating, publishing, and sharing on social media—my practical experience with this approach is that this entire cycle is handled through a division of labor between AI and humans.

![Diagram of an autonomous operational loop driven by social media](tech/doko-slide-13.webp)

## Comparison of the Three

![Architecture comparison. A diagram of who does what and where.](tech/doko-slide-15.webp)

| Comparison Criteria | WordPress | EmDash | Muse × GitHub × Markdown CMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operational Team | Manual updates via admin panel | Human + AI agents (integrated via MCP, API, CLI) | Verbal requests to AI agents |
| Content Source/Authoritative Version | Articles in the database | Content platform (via admin panel/AI) | Markdown files (authoritative version on GitHub) |
| Publishing Environment | PHP running continuously | Node.js (including serverless) executed | None (static file delivery only) |
| Security Approach | Continuous protection through updates and defense | Isolate plugins and restrict permissions | Avoid placing the attack target itself |
| Expansion Methods | Install plugins | Install plugins (sandboxed) | Leverage external services for only necessary functions (including conceptual planning) |
| Server | Rental server, etc., required | Cloudflare or Node.js environment | Not required (GitHub Pages) |
| Cost | Server fees + maintenance effort | Software is free under MIT, platform via Cloudflare, etc. | GitHub free tier + AI usage fees, no server costs |
| Ecosystem | Massive (themes, plugins, development companies) | Small during startup phase | Still small (mechanism itself published under MIT) |
| Ideal Use Cases | General-purpose sites capable of anything | New sites designed for AI integration | Sites focused on announcements and reading material, or sites where operations are delegated to AI |
| Strengths/Weaknesses | Heavy maintenance burden, large attack surface | Immature track record and ecosystem | No standalone functionality for user-generated content |

![Business Reality: Comparison Chart of Defense, Cost, and Suitability](tech/doko-slide-16.webp)

## What cannot be done / What needs to be rented

To be honest, there are things this system simply cannot do. As long as we adhere to the premise of "not running programs," there are three fundamental barriers that remain. The first is the shared writable state. To show what a visitor has written to other visitors, there must be a place to receive and save those writes. The second is the enforcement of confidentiality. Since anyone can retrieve static files if they know the URL, it is impossible to "protect the content itself" for members only. The third is arbitration requiring trust. To verify that payment has actually been made, allocate inventory, and prevent double bookings, a reliable arbitrator is necessary.

![Three fundamental barriers. A diagram of an honest understanding of "what cannot be done."](tech/doko-slide-17.webp)

Therefore, features such as comments, membership systems, genuine e-commerce, and reservation booking cannot be handled by this mechanism alone. However, that doesn't mean everything is impossible. The strategy for expansion is to "borrow only what is necessary" (Policy/Concept). For comments, one could consider using Google Forms to accept submissions and quietly displaying only those approved by management via a spreadsheet in the next build (Concept). For payments, the plan is to rely on Stripe and have the site focus solely on displaying products (Concept). For inquiries and applications, if these are handled via forms and sheets, the site only needs to place the links (Concept). Rather than constantly running a full-featured execution environment, it is an "additive" approach—borrowing other people's programs only for the functions you need.

![Additive architecture. A diagram illustrating the concept of "borrowing" only the necessary functions.](tech/doko-slide-18.webp) There are other weaknesses as well: dependence on GitHub as a storage repository, AI usage costs, the assumption that operators will become accustomed to how to ask AI, and the small size of the ecosystem. Since AI handles the behind-the-scenes work, the "ability to articulate" on the part of the person making the requests will be put to the test.

## Conclusion — Not "which CMS," but "where to run it"

![A diagram showing that AI changes "how things are built," while static architecture changes "how things are defended."](tech/doko-slide-19.webp)

In the AI era, the question of site management isn't just "which CMS to choose." It's "where to run the code." WordPress is the conventional approach, where everything runs on the public server. EmDash is a challenger that reimagines the setup for AI operation while maintaining the premise of running it on the public side. Muse × GitHub × Markdown CMS is a third approach that runs nothing on the public side, shifting the heavy lifting of creation, modification, and operation to AI. For a website centered on announcements and reading content, this agility is a powerful asset. Conversely, if posting content and payments are the core of your business, it's honestly better not to force the fit—instead, use external services in tandem or choose a different system. What matters is not the product name, but knowing what your site truly needs. The framework is released under the MIT License. Please try it out and see for yourself.

![What does your site truly need? A closing diagram showing that the framework is released under the MIT License.](tech/doko-slide-20.webp)
