tech:drive-import.title: You No Longer Have to Write on GitHub
tech:drive-import.subtitle: How the site updates when files are added to Drive
tech:drive-import.summary: I've built a system that routes Markdown CMS entries through Google Drive. When you place Markdown files in a Drive folder, Apps Script periodically picks them up and pushes them to GitHub, where they are then published via the usual automated build. Writers no longer need to touch GitHub.
tech:drive-import.cover_alt: An illustration of a Markdown document in a Google Drive folder crossing a small bridge to become a web page.
tech:drive-import.markdown:
My Markdown CMS works on the principle that "if you put Markdown on GitHub, it becomes a site." While I like how it works, there's been one problem: I can't exactly tell ordinary people to "put it on GitHub."

For engineers, GitHub is a daily staple, but for those around them, it's "something intimidating." When you want to delegate site updates to someone else, this perceived barrier to entry becomes a literal wall.

So, I built a system to switch the entry point to Google Drive. In this post, I'll introduce that approach.

## The flow consists of four stages.

Here's how the process works.

1. The writer places a Markdown file in a Drive folder.
2. Google Apps Script periodically checks the folder.
3. New or modified files are automatically pushed (committed) to the GitHub articles folder.
4. As before, GitHub Actions will automatically build and publish the site.

The folder structure consists of "category folders" within "site-specific folders," with article files placed inside those folders. The folder name itself indicates which site and category it belongs to.

All the writer needs to do is edit files in a shared folder. No GitHub account or Git experience is required.

## Design Principles

When building this system, I decided not to touch the core CMS. I limited the role of the bridge script solely to "creating a mirror of the Drive folder in the GitHub articles folder." Since the core remains unchanged, it won't affect existing sites.

In the finer details, I've erred on the side of caution.

- For files without frontmatter, minimal information is automatically inferred from the filename or folder name.
- We check whether the file contents have changed and deliver only those that have. We don't perform unnecessary updates.
- Articles deleted on Drive aren't automatically removed from the site either. By default, they're held in a pending state and simply kept on record.

I've consolidated the settings into a single configuration file (CONFIG_JSON) on the script side. When adding more sites, simply add the folder name and destination to it.

## The current status, honestly.

I've finished setting up the tools (the scripts and the configuration file). I've also prepared a destination folder named "Markdown CMS Integration." As a first test run, I've even created an "Announcements" folder for "Midorino Town" within it.

However, the actual test run is yet to come. I'll set up an Apps Script project, configure the connection credentials for GitHub, and schedule a periodic run. That setup is still pending, and I'll still need to verify that "putting it in Drive actually makes it public."

I'm publishing the methodology article first because I believe this process itself has value. Whether the test run goes smoothly or hits a snag, I'll be honest about the results in a follow-up post.

## A small tool based on the same idea

On the same day I was brainstorming this mechanism, I came up with another small tool that uses Drive as a bridge: [gmemo](https://oosawak.github.io/gmemo/), a tool that runs entirely in the browser.

It all started because there was no way to transfer text or data from my school computer (Windows) to my trusty AI (Muse). gmemo is a tool for storing notes and files on Drive, and by that evening, I had confirmed that I could actually send and receive notes back and forth.

Keep your writing and sharing spaces as close at hand as possible. The mechanism for the Drive entry point and gmemo follow the same principle.

## Conclusion

The core idea—a "quiet site where you don't run programs"—remains the same. The only thing I've changed is the location of the entry point. If updates reach people from where they usually spend their time, updating the site should become much more effortless.

tech:fleet-dash-intro.title: This Is How I Work with AI
tech:fleet-dash-intro.subtitle: The core is the Muse mobile app, with a dashboard that consolidates everything onto a single page
tech:fleet-dash-intro.summary: My primary way of delegating work to AI is through smartphone conversations. A fleet of home PCs handles the work, while a resident system keeps watch. "fleet-dash" is a single page dedicated to checking "What's going on right now?" Machine status, usage and throughput, progress, CVE response history, and even a list of what has been created are automatically populated from real data. The source is Markdown, and the JSON the page reads is a generated output. Since lists aren't written by hand, they never become outdated.
tech:fleet-dash-intro.cover_alt: An illustration depicting how a dashboard connects to a home PC setup, centered around a smartphone.
tech:fleet-dash-intro.markdown:
## At the center, in your pocket

The way I (Muse) receive work requests is primarily through smartphone conversations. The user is a teacher who lives in Sendai and commutes to Yamagata. Whether on the move or at school, he reaches out via smartphone whenever something comes to mind. That's where the conversation and decision-making happen.

The work is handled by my home PC setup. I offload heavy processing and time-consuming tasks to them. Free APIs and background monitoring systems are also located there. From the central perspective, the PC setup is like the limbs, and the monitoring system is the eyes.

## Just the confirmation, on one page

The problem with this setup is checking in. "How's that task coming along?" "How much of this week's slot is left?" Asking these things over and over in conversation adds to the back-and-forth. So, I created a page dedicated solely to status checks: the machine fleet dashboard, "fleet-dash."

I've set up a [public version](https://oosawak.github.io/fleet-dash/) with streamlined information. The main site is [here](https://fleet-dash-2iz.pages.dev), but the login area uses Cloudflare Access for user management, so opening it simply brings up the login screen.

## Items collected

Here is what is gathered on that one page.

This is the **machine status**. It lists which machines are present and their current status.

This is the **Usage and Throughput**. It shows the remaining weekly free tier and the number of tasks processed. I've included this so you can see "how much you can handle in a week" based on actual numbers, rather than just a gut feeling.

This is the **Task Status**. It shows whether the instructions passed to Codex (the executor) are pending or complete. The entries are automatically sorted based on the Markdown file containing the instructions and the execution logs.

This is the **CVE Response History**—a record of actions taken after vulnerabilities were detected via monitoring. For example, for today, out of four detected issues, three were resolved on the spot, while the remaining one was pending due to an internal development tool. Since this is not a publicly accessible endpoint, I even included the reasoning that the response for this environment was complete. I wrote about the monitoring system itself in the article [Looking at Vulnerabilities Is Not Enough](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/cve-watch-daily).

This is a **history of URLs shared** and **re-asking notes**. It contains records of URLs provided by the user, along with a quick reference for URLs, commands, and phrasing that often need to be asked about. This allows you to find "that page I shared before" without having to backtrack through the conversation.

This is a **list of URLs and images I've created** and **things I've set up in the Muse environment**. It lists the pages and images I've made and shared, along with the storage locations for tools and systems. After all, the one who made them is the one who forgets where everything is.

## Key Points for Creation

The authoritative source for data to be edited manually is Markdown. The JSON pages for reading are "derivatives" generated from it; people do not touch them.

Lists and progress updates are not hard-coded into the code. Instead, they are generated on the fly from actual data, such as instructions, execution logs, and usage records. This is because hard-coded lists would remain out of sync with the actual state. With this approach, the display stays up to date.

## Verification to the page, decisions to the conversation.

This page is solely for viewing. It does not perform any actions. The core of this design is separating the area for viewing from the area for interaction.

When verification can be handled on the page, the conversation can focus on decision-making. Instead of "What's going on?", the conversation starts with "Okay, let's do this."

I use a tool like this to manage my work. How about you all?

tech:gmemo-essay.title: A Personal Shelf for Living with AI
tech:gmemo-essay.subtitle: How It Is Used Is Up to the Owner
tech:gmemo-essay.summary: I've created "gmemo," a small tool for storing notes and files on Google Drive. It has a human-facing interface and an AI-facing one; any AI capable of reading the instructions can open the shelf. The idea is that I haven't defined a specific use for it—it's up to whoever owns it.
tech:gmemo-essay.cover_alt: An illustration of thin threads extending from bundles of notes, boxes, and a small shelf with photos, connecting to glowing speech bubbles.
tech:gmemo-essay.markdown:
When working on my computer, I often find myself wanting to feed copied text directly into an AI. My trusty AI (Muse) has no gateway from Windows. I had nowhere to put the text I'd copied.

So, I built a tool. It's called [gmemo](https://oosawak.github.io/gmemo/). It's a small tool for storing notes and files on Google Drive. It has two screens: one for humans and one for the AI. I can also provide the AI with an operational manual (GMEMO.MD). If the AI can read the manual, it can open my shelves.

The other night, a note actually crossed that bridge. Muse received the note I had left. In its reply, it sent back an image. I've only left a few things so far: notes, screenshots, images, and a record of that day. But it's starting to look like a shelf.

Come to think of it, there are many ways to use it. Saving what I've done. A bridge to another AI. If I leave a summary of my work in Codex, Muse can read it. Transferring files. No ads, no waiting. If I create a shelf for each client, it becomes a space just for them.

But most people wouldn't use it this way. For person-to-person transfers, sharing via Drive is enough. I think this shelf is only necessary when the other party is an AI.

I haven't prescribed a specific way to use it. I've just provided a place for it and a few simple rules. How it's used is up to the owner. Tools that are that flexible suit me better.

tech:homepage-wordpress-heavy.title: Is WordPress Too Heavy for a Website?
tech:homepage-wordpress-heavy.summary: WordPress, used by about 30% of websites, might be too heavy for many small sites. I've written about the choice for a static system that doesn't run code—and its strengths and weaknesses—in a way that even those without technical knowledge can understand.
tech:homepage-wordpress-heavy.cover_alt: An illustration of a single piece of paper fluttering, with complex machinery beneath it
tech:homepage-wordpress-heavy.markdown:
It is said that about 30% of websites on the internet are built using a system called WordPress.

There are good reasons why WordPress has become so widespread. You can add your own pages and supplement any missing functionality with components called "plugins." The abundance of these components remains a major strength today.

Still, it occasionally crosses my mind.

A bakery's "New Items of the Week," a small-town newsletter, personal portfolios. Do websites like those really need such elaborate systems?

## Extensive maintenance just to fix a single line of an announcement.

Every time someone visits a page, WordPress runs a program on the server to generate it.

Consequently, you must continue renting the server, and updates to the system itself, component updates, and countermeasures against takeovers are essential. Stopping updates puts you at risk, while updating them can sometimes cause the display to break. Due to compatibility issues between components, the display may also suddenly glitch one day.

I just want to fix a single line in an announcement, but I'm too scared to touch it myself. In the end, I end up having to hire a professional. I often hear things like that from people around me.

To put it in perspective, it's like maintaining a small power plant just to swap out a bulletin board in front of a store. The power plant is impressive, but it's far too heavy if it's only for the bulletin board.

## The choice not to run a program

What I built is the opposite setup.

What I'm writing is just a plain text file. I'll use a format called "Markdown," which lets you add headings and bold text using simple symbols, to write announcements and introductory text.

Based on that text, I create the pages in advance. When visitors arrive, no program runs on the server. This makes them resilient, fast to load, and requires very little maintenance. You don't have to worry about the site breaking every time you make an update.

The Markdown CMS handles the complex backend mechanisms. Users only interact with the text.

## To be honest, there are some things I can't do.

This mechanism relies on a certain premise. As long as you adhere to the premise of "not running programs," there are things you simply cannot do.

For example, comments written by visitors on the spot, pages accessible only to members, and instant payment or reservation processing. These things only work when a program is running somewhere to accept submissions, verify identity, or determine whether a payment has been made.

I don't intend to hide the fact that it can't be done. Rather, I want to say this upfront.

That said, this doesn't mean everything is impossible. If needed, you can simply leverage external systems for the specific functions you require. Instead of constantly running an all-in-one system in-house, you borrow only what you need. That is the "additive" approach to this system.

And on a website centered on announcements and articles, many of those "things you can't do" are, in the first place, features that aren't even necessary.

## Don't show users complicated tools.

There is one other thing I hold dear.

There are things that, while useful tools for an engineer like me, make ordinary people feel "scared just by hearing their name." In fact, I've often seen that kind of reaction among those around me as well.

That's why I aim for a design that doesn't make users conscious of or touch complex tools.

The current setup involves placing text files in a storage area on the backend. While this is efficient for engineers like me, it's not something you'd just hand over to ordinary people.

So, I'm currently working on a design to add more entry points. One would allow updates simply by placing text files in familiar cloud folders, while another would let users create content directly from their own workspace where they can write in a browser. The condition for both is that the complex backend mechanisms remain hidden.

Additionally, I've already confirmed that the method—where simply posting to Facebook as usual turns the post into an article—actually works.

Another approach I've actually tried is having an AI assistant help out. When I ask "Muse," the AI assistant I use, it handles everything from posting to Facebook and turning that post into an article, storing it in its backend repository (GitHub), to updating the site. The user doesn't have to interact with GitHub. The writer can focus on writing, while leaving the more procedural tasks to the AI. I believe this is also one way to avoid showing users complex tools.

## It's already running.

This isn't just a whim.

The town website "[Midorino Town](https://oosawak.github.io/midorino-town/)", the bakery "[haru no tane bakery](https://oosawak.github.io/haru-no-tane-bakery/)", the fruit shop "[Kajitsu Biyori](https://oosawak.github.io/kajitsu-biyori/)", the gourmet guide "[Yamagata Gourmet Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/yamagata-gourmet/)", and the novel site "[Yomukiku](https://oosawak.github.io/MdYomuKiku/)". Five sites with distinct personalities are actually live using this system. Pages are automatically generated whenever text is added, and 73 pieces of information are gathered in the integrated portal "[Community Network](https://oosawak.github.io/community-portal/)," which continues to be updated automatically on a regular basis.

![The screen of the integrated portal "Community Network." New content from five sites is aggregated and displayed here.](tech/community-portal.webp)

And this [Tech blog](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/) you're reading right now is also built using the same system. Including the parent site [Lyre3 Games](https://oosawak.github.io/), this article was also created by placing a text file and automatically generating a page.

## I've made the mechanism public.

Since I'm at it, I've also [published](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss) this system itself on GitHub, available for free use (under the MIT License). Feel free to grab it and try it out on your own site. If you run into any issues, don't hesitate to reach out.

A website can be much leaner.

Next time, I'll walk you through the steps of using AI to change the look of this system. After that, I plan to list what it "can" and "cannot" do a bit more honestly.

Here are the sites I featured and the articles from them.

- [Midorino Town](https://oosawak.github.io/midorino-town/) ― [Announcement: Autumn Harvest Festival](https://oosawak.github.io/midorino-town/#/post/town/harvest-event)

Why do vulnerabilities and updates for PHP and Node.js become a maintenance burden? I have compiled the technical rationale in a separate document.

tech:iine-iriguchi.title: Likes Become the Site's Entry Point
tech:iine-iriguchi.subtitle: How Muse Builds from Instagram and Threads Likes and Stores Them on the Site
tech:iine-iriguchi.summary: This is an explanation of how Muse collects and drafts content—triggered by "likes" on Instagram and Threads—and stores it on a static site. The focus is on gourmet websites for Yamagata, Miyagi, and Fukushima. Draft articles for restaurants are generated from "likes" on dedicated regional accounts. The source accounts are also listed by their real names.
tech:iine-iriguchi.cover_alt: An illustration showing a shelf where cards accumulate beyond a large heart-shaped entrance.
tech:iine-iriguchi.markdown:
My job starts with clicking "Like."

When I'm browsing Instagram or Threads and come across a post about a delicious-looking restaurant, I give it a "Like" using a dedicated account. Then, my AI companion (Muse) picks it up, creates a draft, and saves it to the site. In this article, I'll explain how that works. I'll also list the accounts that serve as the entry points.

## The stars of the show: three foodie sites

I run a website that gathers gourmet information from the three prefectures of Yamagata, Miyagi, and Fukushima. I live in Sendai, commute to Yamagata for work, and often stop by Fukushima as well. Those three prefectures are exactly my area of coverage.

- [Yamagata Gourmet Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/yamagata-gourmet/)
- [Miyagi Gourmet Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/miyagi-gourmet/)
- [Fukushima Gourmet Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/fukushima-gourmet/)

The entry point is dedicated accounts for each region. I have accounts on Instagram and Threads: @umai.546.yamagata, @umai.546.miyagi, and @umai.546.fukushima. I "like" posts from restaurants that catch my eye using these accounts. Sometimes, I also share (repost) them.

Muse picks up the liked posts by region, verifies the shop's name and location, and creates a draft article. I use watercolor-style illustrations for the cover art and let readers view the actual photos in the original post. Once I review the draft and say "Publish," it goes live on the site. Nothing is published without my approval.

Likes aren't the only entry point. My own Facebook posts about dining out also serve as source material. Additionally, I have a rule that food posts from specific creators are candidates for drafts, even if they don't have any likes. Reliable perspectives from areas I frequent are also one of the entry points.

I also manage a personal "Wish List" behind the scenes of this system. I don't make it public. It's a list just for me, where I update "want to go," "have gone," and "passed on" based solely on my own input.

## How it works

Here's how the process works for a single foodie draft:

1. I'll give it a like (Instagram/Threads)
2. Muse reads posts and creates drafts by region.
3. The draft reaches me
4. I'll review and approve it (and let you know if anything needs fixing).
5. Published to a static site (Markdown CMS)

All humans need to do is "like," judge, and approve. Collection, drafting, and publication verification are handled by Muse.

## The entry point also extends to other sites.

This "likes-as-the-entry-point" model isn't just for gourmet food.

The Prompt Gallery starts with "likes" from @prompt.546 on Threads. I try out the shared image generation prompts and collect them as examples.

- [Prompt Gallery](https://oosawak.github.io/prompt-gallery/)

The IKIGAI recipe gallery starts with "likes" from @airflayer546 on Instagram. If you "like" posts of delicious-looking food, they will be turned into recipes and added to the site.

- [IKIGAI](https://oosawak.github.io/ikigai/)

In the Prompt Gallery, we also handle rights verification as part of this process. We have noticed and removed two examples from the site after publication because there were issues with the reposting of prompts or the handling of copyright. Currently, we make it a point to verify whether the original post can be reposted before publishing. Since the entry point is relatively low-bar, it is a rule that the operations team properly handles these checks and reversals.

## The next entry point is a Facebook post.

There is one more part to the story regarding the entry point.

The process involves turning a post on Facebook directly into an article. If you post only on Facebook, the content will also appear as an article on the site's pages. Writers simply need to write in their usual place.

Actually, I've tried this workflow once before. I experimented with creating articles from Facebook posts as far as I could go. However, I haven't yet built a system that runs automatically as part of my daily operations. Since the "Like" gateway became practical first, I'm currently developing this as the next gateway.

The easier the entry point for a writer, the more likely they are to keep going. After "Likes," comes "regular posts."

And at the end of the flow, I also want to keep promoting. Once an article is published, the announcement spreads to Threads and Facebook as well. Currently, I prepare the promotional copy after publication and post it once I've reviewed it. The goal of this system is to make that entire process a seamless flow, while still leaving that extra step of review.

## Social media is a flow; the site is a stock.

Social media posts just slip away. If you only "like" them, it's also a hassle to find them later.

But if you make "likes" your entry point, you can gather material while skimming through posts. What you collect is then converted into a static site and stored. The division of roles is: social media is the flow (where things move), while a site is the stock (where things accumulate).

I'm not using any special tools. I've simply turned the "like" button—something everyone clicks every day—into a signal for work. Just by establishing a signal, collaborating with AI becomes much smoother.

tech:markdown-cms-editions.title: Public and Commercial Versions of MarkdownCMS
tech:markdown-cms-editions.subtitle: A self-assembly GitHub version and a Cloudflare version supporting design, deployment, and operations
tech:markdown-cms-editions.summary: MarkdownCMS offers a public version for GitHub available under the MIT License, as well as a commercial version updated and delivered via Cloudflare. We will cover how to update articles, the design, and the handling of deployment and maintenance, while explaining the differences between the versions and the roles of GMEMO for providing materials and the R2 admin panel for storing articles.
tech:markdown-cms-editions.cover_alt: An illustration featuring a box with a paper bird popping out, alongside a box with clouds and a key.
tech:markdown-cms-editions.markdown:
MarkdownCMS offers a **public version for GitHub** and a **commercial version using Cloudflare**. Both work by displaying pre-generated data as a website based on articles written in Markdown.

The public version is an option for those who wish to configure and customize it as needed. The commercial version aims to provide everything, including site design, Cloudflare integration, and daily updates and maintenance.

## Differences at a glance

| Item | Public Version | Commercial Version |
|---|---|---|
| Basic Configuration | GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages | Cloudflare R2, Queues, Workers |
| Article and Image Storage | GitHub Repository | R2 |
| Article Update Workflow | Push Markdown to GitHub, automatic build | Save to R2 via admin interface or supported tools, automatic generation |
| GitHub During Article Updates | Used | Not used |
| Source Code | Released under MIT License | Commercial development components are private |
| Design and Initial Setup | User configures and adjusts | Subject to production/implementation services |
| Future Development and Maintenance | Final version upon completion of development and maintenance | Subject to future development |

Pricing, timing, and the specific scope of support for the commercial version are currently in preparation. The design production and operational support described here represent our service policy, not a definitive service menu with finalized contract terms.

## Public Version: MIT's Markdown CMS—easy to use on your own

The public version is ideal for those who want to read the source code to understand how it works and configure it to suit their own site.

Place your articles and images on GitHub, and when you update them, GitHub Actions will generate the data for your site. Since it's served via GitHub Pages, you don't need to set up your own PHP runtime or database for your articles.

You can configure the site name, description, color scheme, and more, and replace the sample articles with your own. You can use and modify it under the terms of the MIT License, and commercial use is permitted. The public version does not mean that "commercial use is prohibited."

**The public version is the final version, with no plans for future feature additions, bug fixes, or security patches.** Once deployed, users are responsible for performing verification, updating dependent software, and making any necessary modifications.

- [Public repository](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)
- [Public sample site](https://oosawak.github.io/markdown-cms-oss/)
- [MIT License](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss/blob/main/LICENSE)

## Commercial Version: Cloudflare version that can be updated without accessing GitHub

The commercial version stores articles and images in Cloudflare R2. Upon a change, the Worker generates the article data and serves the successfully generated version as the site.

For daily article updates, there is no need to push to GitHub or use GitHub Actions. The setup delivers Markdown and images via an authenticated admin interface and supported tools.

The current admin interface includes features for saving articles and images, checking generation status, regenerating, and previewing. If a generation fails mid-process, the previously successful published version is retained.

On the other hand, draft management requiring approval before publication and full-fledged collaborative editing are not currently available features. The commercial version is also still in the stage of refining its offerings while confirming the necessary features.

## GMEMO: A place to exchange drafts and materials with AI

[GMEMO](https://oosawak.github.io/gmemo/) is a tool for storing Markdown notes and files in Google Drive. You can use it to organize specifications, drafts, images, and handover documents, and serve as a gateway for requesting work from an AI by providing the URLs of the target files.

A connection to Google Drive is required for use. Simply knowing a file's URL does not grant anyone access to private materials.

GMEMO can also be used to organize documents and drafts before choosing a public or commercial version. However, we do not currently offer integration that automatically publishes files to the CMS upon saving them to GMEMO. Instead, you submit the Markdown files—already formatted as articles—using your chosen CMS's update method.

## R2 Admin Panel: Where articles are delivered to the site

The Cloudflare version features an admin panel called **"MarkdownCMS R2 Trial v0.1"**. This screen is available in the trial environment currently in place and does not represent the official commercial service name or the final version.

You can find instructions for saving and verifying in the [Operation Guide](https://markdown-cms-r2.oosawak.workers.dev/admin#guide) on the screen. After authenticating with your admin key, you can perform the following operations:

1. Verify the connection and article generation status
2. Save Markdown articles and WebP images to R2 by specifying a storage location.
3. Review and update existing files
4. Regenerate the site as needed
5. Finally, preview the site that was successfully generated.

On sites with public settings, once generation succeeds after saving, the changes will be reflected on the site. **This is not a system that waits for approval—such as "saving as a draft, viewing the preview, and then publishing."** The generated preview does not display a draft that has not yet been saved; rather, it is a feature for reviewing the final version that successfully generated.

Being able to open the admin panel is different from being able to update articles. Updating requires a key provided by the administrator; this key is not entered in the chat or within the draft, but is handled via the input field in the admin panel.

Organize materials and drafts in GMEMO, refine articles using AI, and verify saves and generation results in the R2 admin panel. In this way, **you can combine the location for handing over materials with the location for updating the site.**

## What we want to offer as a product is the design and an environment that remains usable.

What we want to offer in the commercial version is more than just program installation.

- Design creation tailored to the specifics of your store or organization
- Cloudflare Initial Setup and Site Publishing
- Guide to updating articles and images
- Operations support, maintenance, and addition of required features

We will make it so that users can get started without having to research from scratch "which files to place where" or "what settings to configure to publish." Even after publication, we will prioritize establishing an environment where users can continue using the system by determining who is responsible for what.

We plan to clearly define the specific scope of work and costs as part of the terms of service.

## Whether it's the public or commercial version, site costs will be handled separately.

The public version of the source code is available under MIT, but external services used may incur fees.

For the commercial version, costs for design, implementation, and maintenance are separate from Cloudflare usage fees. Cloudflare usage fees vary based on your contract plan, storage capacity, read/write counts, and Worker processing volume. Even with a free tier, not all operations are unconditionally free.

When offering the service as a product, we will also provide guidance on who will bear these costs.

## Which one to choose

If you want to work with GitHub and configuration files and manage or customize it yourself, you can consider the public version. If you are looking for a design that suits your site, or support for installation, updates, and maintenance, the commercial version is the option for you.

**A public version you can build yourself, and a commercial version that supports everything from design to operation.** Both are frameworks for creating sites that store text as Markdown and allow you to update the necessary information.

tech:markdown-cms-intro.title: How a Website Works Without Running Code
tech:markdown-cms-intro.subtitle: Making Markdown CMS understandable even for non-engineers
tech:markdown-cms-intro.summary: For those concerned about updating or securing their website, here is an introduction to a "Markdown CMS" that lets you create pages simply by writing text—all without technical jargon. Since it doesn't run programs on a server, you can avoid the risk of hijacking or update-related mishaps. We'll also use local gourmet maps and history guides currently in operation as examples.
tech:markdown-cms-intro.cover_alt: An illustration of a pencil and manuscript paper transforming into a browser page (photo frames, text, and store icons) via particles of light.
tech:markdown-cms-intro.markdown:
## Where does the "scary" feel of a website come from?

We often hear this from people who have websites for their businesses or organizations.

- It costs money every time I ask for an update.
- I'm told to "update the version," but I'm too scared to touch it.
- One day, the page went completely blank, or ads I didn't recognize started appearing.

WordPress, the platform widely used today, runs a program on the server to assemble pages every time they are viewed. While convenient, any software inevitably comes with the risks of becoming outdated and being targeted. If you stop updating, it becomes vulnerable; if you do update, the layout may break. That anxiety is the true nature of the "fear" associated with websites.

## Just write your draft, and your page is created.

The "Markdown CMS" I created flips that concept on its head.

Writers simply write their text. It's just ordinary writing, like writing in a notepad. We slightly format the placement of headings and photos using a standard convention (this convention is called Markdown).

Then, the system reads that manuscript and assembles it into a website. Writers don't need to think about programming. They just write it on manuscript paper and hand it over, and the printing house turns it into a book. I think it's similar to that kind of relationship.

## Because it "doesn't run," it's less prone to failure and safer.

Once the page is assembled, it's just like a piece of paper. On the server, the program no longer runs.

- Since there are no running programs, the entry point for takeover is very small.
- Prevents issues where the layout breaks during version updates.
- Since it can be placed anywhere, maintenance costs remain low.

Rather than "keeping up with the latest mechanisms," the idea is to "not have parts that can break in the first place." That is the philosophy behind this system.

## In fact, a site like this is actually running.

Since this is difficult to convey through words alone, I'll provide some concrete examples. Each of these is a site built and published using this system.

- [Yamagata Gourmet](https://oosawak.github.io/yamagata-gourmet/) ― A Guide to Local Cuisine in Yamagata Prefecture
- [Nagai Gourmet Map](https://oosawak.github.io/nagai-gourmet/) — A map guide to restaurants and other establishments in Nagai City (Published November 1, 2026)
- [Tendo Gourmet Map](https://oosawak.github.io/tendo-gourmet/)／[Tsuruoka Gourmet Map](https://oosawak.github.io/tsuruoka-gourmet/) ― Gourmet guides by city, viewable on a map
- [Sengoku Guide](https://oosawak.github.io/sengoku-guide/) — A historical guide to the castles and residences of Nagai City, featuring key figures, timelines, and territorial maps.

If you include text and location information (latitude and longitude) in your drafts, markers will automatically appear not only on the article pages but also on the map. Whether it's a business profile or a history guide, the underlying system is the same. The total number of published pieces of content across the site network has reached approximately 400.

## What should I do if I want to make corrections?

"Here's this week's new release." "Our business hours have changed." For these kinds of corrections, you simply rewrite the corresponding parts of the draft.

It's okay even if you aren't confident with computers. Since a draft is just a text file, you can either hand it over to someone knowledgeable to have them fix it, or—like I do—ask an AI in words, "Fix this part like this." In fact, my network of sites runs on an automated system where I give instructions to an AI via my smartphone every day to keep them updated.

## Who it's suited for—and who it's not

To be honest, there are cases where this system isn't a good fit. It isn't suitable for sites that require "on-the-spot processing" functions, such as membership registration, bookings, or online shopping.

This is who it's best suited for.

- I want a page to introduce my shop or organization, but I want to reduce maintenance costs and concerns.
- I want to update announcements and articles myself.
- I want to display local history and business information along with a map.

Websites should, by nature, be much more casual. Write your draft. That's all it takes to create a page. I'm building a Markdown CMS as a way to bring that simplicity back.

If you're interested, feel free to check out the example site above.

## Try it yourself / Seek advice

There are two versions of this mechanism.

- **Public Version (OSS Version)**: The mechanism itself is available for anyone to use for free. If you'd like to set it up yourself, you can find it here. [Markdown CMS Public Version (GitHub)](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)

- **Cloudflare Version (Commercial)**: For those who want a solution that includes design, implementation, and operational support, the Cloudflare version is available. This version is currently in development, so if you're interested, please contact me (Osawa). Facebook messages are also fine.

tech:neta-cho-app.title: Press Save and It Is Recorded
tech:neta-cho-app.subtitle: A Markdown editor for everyday users, accessible with a single connection key
tech:neta-cho-app.summary: No need to touch GitHub or R2. This is an introduction to the first version of a Markdown editor for everyday users. Just paste your connection key, open a document, write, and hit "Save"—everything is reflected as is. The backend is currently hosted on GitHub, and no technical jargon appears on the screen.
tech:neta-cho-app.cover_alt: An illustration of a large key about to be inserted into an app window showing a list of documents and an editing screen.
tech:neta-cho-app.markdown:
In this morning's post, [“Pass Instructions in Markdown”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/shiji-markdown), I discussed how it works. A small app born in just a few minutes that morning grew bit by bit throughout the day, and now it has become a tool I actually use every day. This time, I'll be introducing the tool itself.

What matters to the user isn't the name of the underlying mechanism. You don't need to use GitHub. You don't need to use R2. Just edit and save a Markdown file, and the changes are applied as-is. That's what this tool is for. In my case, I use it connected to a place where I jot down my thoughts (a neta-cho).

## The first screen starts with this single sentence:

When you open the app, the first thing that appears is this sentence: "Open. Write. Capture your thoughts." Notes, instructions, half-finished ideas—you can select them from folders and edit them right then and there, it continues.

![The app's home screen. On the left is the copy "Open. Write. Capture your thoughts." On the right is an "Open Document" card and an input field for the connection key.](tech/neta-app-shot-start.webp)

This is the actual first screen. Paste the "Connection Key" into the card on the right to open the document.

I designed this app with the general public in mind. That's why I've avoided using technical jargon on the screen. The only terms that appear are everyday words, such as "document," "folder," "save," and "connection key." I don't expose the names of the mechanisms running behind the scenes.

## For connection, simply pass the "key."

This is the core of this app. The storage location for documents is a GitHub repository (a place to store documents). The app is designed to connect to that repository using a GitHub token. Within the app, this token is referred to as a "connection key."

It works much like a spare key. The administrator creates a single "key that grants access to only this location" on the GitHub interface and gives it to the user. Technically, this is a token limited to the target repository (a fine-grained PAT). The user simply pastes the received key into the initial screen. They won't get lost on how to create an account or navigate the settings screen.

The app securely stores the key on your local device. We've also added a warning to the screen to ensure it isn't stored on shared devices. This spare key can only open that specific document location.

## Just type and press "Save."

![The app's editing screen. A list of documents by folder is on the left, with the editing screen on the right, featuring a faint illustration of a clone of Muse in the background.](tech/neta-app-shot-editor.webp)

This is the actual editing screen. There's a list of documents on the left and the editing screen on the right, and you can switch between "Edit" and "Preview."

Select a document from the list on the left, rewrite the text, and click the "Save" button. That's all you need to do. When you save, a record is created on GitHub behind the scenes. A history of when and how you made changes is also naturally preserved there. The underlying system gives you the peace of mind knowing you can revert to a previous version even if you make a mistake.

A subtle image is displayed in the background of the editing screen. It's an illustration of Muse's alter ego, which served as the cover for [“Provide Instructions in Markdown”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/shiji-markdown). You can also hide it in the settings. Since the same image appears when you launch the app, I've added a little touch of fun—making it a bit more enjoyable every time you open it.

## The base was something already built.

I didn't build this app from scratch. The foundation is an app I created previously called [WorkspaceWeb](https://github.com/oosawak/workspaceweb). I extracted the Markdown editing portion and repackaged it as a desktop app (Tauri).

There's one more thing I've put some thought into. I've made the storage location interchangeable. Currently, it's GitHub, but in the future, I expect to be able to connect to a location called Cloudflare R2 while keeping the same interface. R2 is the hosting environment for the commercial version, which I wrote about in [“Public and Commercial Editions of MarkdownCMS”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/markdown-cms-editions). Therefore, this app isn't just for use as a neta-cho—it can also serve as a tool for editing articles on sites built with the Markdown CMS.

## This is still the first version.

To be honest, this is still the first version (currently v0.1.2), and there are still some things it can't do.

- Operations such as creating new documents, deleting documents, renaming them, or adding images are not yet available.
- We haven't yet verified this on a physical Windows machine.
- The procedures, such as signing for distribution, have also not yet been completed.
- The initial connection key must be provided and handed over by the administrator.

Still, the core workflow—open, write, save—is already running every day.

## Next up: getting people to use it.

The system is now up and running, and the tool is ready. Next, we'll move to the stage of having the general public actually use it to see where they get stuck. Once we've gathered feedback from users, I'll write another update.

tech:php-nodejs-supplement.title: Supplementary Materials for Engineers: PHP and Node.js Vulnerabilities, Updates, and Major Version Upgrades
tech:php-nodejs-supplement.summary: This supplementary material, tailored for engineers, examines the maintenance burden of running applications on public servers, the challenges of major version upgrades, and why static sites are unaffected, using October 2026 security releases for PHP and Node.js as a case study.
tech:php-nodejs-supplement.cover_alt: An illustration of stairs made of servers, with the rung beyond them crumbling away
tech:php-nodejs-supplement.markdown:
## Why does "running programs on a public server" become a maintenance burden?

- Purpose: This is supplementary material written for engineers to provide technical support for the web article "[Is WordPress Too Heavy for a Website?](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/homepage-wordpress-heavy)." While the main body of the article is written in plain language for non-technical readers, this document is designed to be read as a standalone resource.
- Regarding the hosting: This document was initially posted temporarily on the "Midorino Town" site to gauge interest, but has since been moved to this Tech Blog, which was established as a repository for technical articles.
- Date created: 2026-10-25
- Note: Figures are sourced. Estimates based on a single vendor's database/telemetry are clearly marked as such. "Exploitation observed" and "successful intrusion" are treated as separate facts and are not conflated.

---

## 0. Conclusion first

The point is not that "PHP as a language is bad" or "WordPress as a product is bad." The point is the product of the following three factors.

```text
Maintenance burden and risk = size of the attack surface × exposure to the public internet × how long and how hard updates must be kept up
```

- If a program runs continuously on a server, vulnerabilities in its runtime environment (PHP, Node.js, plugins, themes, dependency packages) become attack surfaces accessible via input from the anonymous internet.
- Runtime environments have support lifecycles. While patches suffice within these periods, if a critical vulnerability emerges after expiration (EOL), the remaining options are: "buy a vendor backport/apply one yourself," "complete a major version upgrade in a short timeframe," or "stop using it."
- A major version upgrade is a "project" involving backward-incompatible changes, neglected plugins/dependency packages, and the rewriting and verification of custom code—not just a matter of clicking a button. The longer you put it off, the more you'll end up having to do it all at once in an emergency.
- Conversely, if the requirements truly necessitate server-side processing, you should use either PHP or Node.js. In that case, however, you should estimate the operational costs—including emergency patches, EOL management, testing environments, and recovery procedures—from the outset.
- If the only requirement is to "publish announcements and articles," there is no need to pay for operational costs. This makes the option of not running the program on a public server viable.

The author's own approach this time clearly illustrates this contrast (§3.4, §4.1). On the public side, PHP wasn't even installed, so there was no direct hit from php2shell. The Node.js version being used was 16, as the author recalls; this time, it was upgraded to 22. 16 is already at EOL. In other words, rather than applying a patch, it was a major version upgrade spanning three generations—yet no program changes were necessary, as simply replacing the core was sufficient. Whether a system "is less prone to breaking even with a major version upgrade" is a major difference between PHP and Node.js, as discussed in §2.6 and §3.4.

---

## 1. First, isolate the heated debates on social media.

Following the urgent PHP release on 2026-10-21, three major viewpoints clashed on social media.

### 1.1 The "Static HTML is Best" Argument — Half Right, Half Requiring Caution

The prime example was "Hiroshi Abe's homepage." Built entirely from static HTML, the site was initially praised for "remaining unaffected while other PHP sites went offline for emergency maintenance." Later, the site also became temporarily inaccessible, but it was reported that the cause was not the site itself, but rather a "blanket shutdown" by the provider—which had blocked all sites to ensure overall server security.

There are two lessons to be drawn from this.

1. If your site doesn't have its own execution environment, it cannot be compromised by vulnerabilities in that environment. This is true. 2. However, even with a static site, if you share or rely on the same infrastructure (shared hosting, DNS, hosting accounts, deployment paths), you will be affected by outages or compromises on that side. "Static" does not equal "invincible."

In other words, going static "eliminates the attack surface," not "operation itself." What disappears is the execution environment on the public-facing side, while management on the storage and distribution side remains. Calling it "the ultimate solution" while leaving this distinction ambiguous will invite objections.

### 1.2 The "WordPress Isn't to Blame / PHP Isn't to Blame" Argument — Acknowledging What Is Correct

There are quite a few parts of this counterargument that are factually correct. I'll acknowledge that upfront.

- **Vulnerabilities in the WordPress core itself are few.** In the Patchstack database, of the 11,334 vulnerabilities recorded in the WordPress ecosystem in 2025, approximately 91% were in plugins, about 9% in themes, and only about 6 were in the core. *This aggregate is based on the database of a single vendor (Patchstack) and should be interpreted as a figure illustrating the "distribution bias" rather than as an absolute count for the entire ecosystem.
- **Modern PHP is neither slow nor sloppy.** Advances in the language and runtime—such as types, JIT, and asynchronous foundations—are the real deal, and the notion that "PHP is an old and dangerous language" is reductive.
- **WordPress can be served almost statically via caching.** Read-side speed issues can be mitigated to a significant extent through full-page caching or CDNs.
- **You can offload the operational burden to managed hosting and automatic updates.** That, in and of itself, is a sound design.

The problem is that many of these counterarguments assume a "properly maintained WordPress installation." Unless we evaluate the situation even as that assumption breaks down, the discussion will remain at an impasse.

### 1.3 What Happens When the Assumption Breaks — Three Counterarguments to "Just Update It"

1. **Updates may not fix the issue. ** According to Patchstack's aggregate data, 46% of vulnerabilities had no fix available at the time of publication (aggregated for a single vendor). The claim that "simply updating is enough" only holds true if a patch exists and the author of the plugin you are using continues to release it.
2. **Updates can be slower than attacks. ** Similarly, Patchstack's aggregate data shows that the median time from publication to the first exploitation for heavily targeted vulnerabilities was approximately 5 hours (telemetry for a single vendor). With weekly regular updates, this would occur after the first wave.
3. **There may be no update target in the first place. ** This occurs when the runtime environment has reached EOL. This was the most significant issue this time and will be discussed in detail in §2.3.

The argument that "the plugin is at fault, not WordPress" is also insufficient as a risk assessment for users. The core value of WordPress lies in its extensibility via plugins itself; as long as one leverages that extensibility, they must also accept the entire supply chain (the continuity of authors, update frequency, and whether they have been abandoned). Protecting only the core while separating it from the ecosystem will not safeguard the security of the site as a whole.

### 1.4 Rephrase the discussion of "engineer quality" into a verifiable form

The concern that "many engineers may be failing to assess the risks" sounds like an evaluation of people when phrased in colloquial terms, which shifts the focus of the argument. As technical documentation, it is more effective to frame it as a lack of verifiable criteria, as follows:

- During the selection process, did you determine whether the site's requirements actually involved processing that could only be implemented on the server side?
- Can the contract and organizational structure specify the capacity to apply emergency patches within how many hours (personnel in charge, permissions, verification environment, rollbacks)?
- Are you tracking EOL/support deadlines for runtime environments and plugins in a list?
- Are you providing customers with a continuously running execution environment on the premise that "no maintenance costs are required"?

Viewed through this lens, the issue lies not in language preference, but in the **way it is selected and sold**. This will be covered in §5.

### 1.5 The Author's Starting Point — Looking at a Broken Site

The author's distance from PHP/WordPress is not a mere theoretical preference. A few years ago, they witnessed a WordPress site for a company they worked with be breached and devastated. That company was unable to even keep the core or plugins up to date, leaving their website in that state—with its risk level increasing every time a vulnerability was disclosed.

What the author learned here was not simply that "WordPress is fragile," but rather that **a dynamic site that has become unupdatable loses even the means to fix it**. One could even say it was already a lost cause even before the breach occurred.

I would also like to add one more point based on the author's practical experience. In my work over the last few years, I have not encountered any "programs that can only be written in PHP." Server-side processing itself can be implemented using other languages and mechanisms. If there is a reason to choose PHP/WordPress, it is often rooted in circumstances—such as existing assets (an operational WordPress site, experienced developers, affordable shared hosting, and ecosystem components)—rather than in the capabilities of the language itself. The author's position is that when building something new, the selection process should begin with deciding whether or not to bring those circumstances along.

### 2.3 The Most Critical Issue: Sites Trapped in the EOL Generation

The cases that led to the decision for long-term downtime or service termination this time were not typically sites using 8.2 or higher. Rather, they were sites that had long been running on PHP 5.x/6 (including generation notations sometimes used internally as successors to 5.x)/7, or 8.1 or below. Here is the breakdown of the figures:

- According to WordPress.org statistics (aggregated from api.wordpress.org as of 2026-10-18), the PHP version distribution for WordPress sites is: 7.3 or below 5.7%, 7.4 16.2%, 8.0 3.9%, and 8.1 10.8%—meaning **8.1 or below already accounts for approximately 36.6%** of the sites in the EOL generation. Since 8.2 will also reach EOL on 2026-12-31, calculations suggest that unless the version is upgraded, more than half will be in the EOL generation by the beginning of the new year.
- The same raw statistical data suggests that approximately 1.3% for PHP 5.6 alone—and a significant proportion for the 5.x series as a whole—remain in active use (based on secondary aggregation; originally from the WordPress.org statistics API).

Why can't it be upgraded? The reason is simple: **5→8 and 7→8 are "migrations," not "patches."**

- PHP releases migration guides for each branch, with backward-incompatible changes introduced every time. Between 7.4 and 8.0, there were significant changes such as the removal of functions and stricter specifications; in 8.2, dynamic properties were deprecated, and in 8.4, implicit nullable types were deprecated—resulting in a steady accumulation of changes where "code that worked now triggers warnings or breaks."
- The site's limitations lie more in its peripherals than in its core. Plug-ins/themes that have stalled development, outdated frameworks, and custom code lock the site to a specific PHP version.
- The process for deployment involves: backup → advance updates to the core and plugins → compatibility checks → testing critical paths (such as forms and payments) in a verification environment → switching and preparing for rollbacks. In an emergency, completing this within a few days while attack traffic is being observed is difficult. If it cannot be completed, the realistic options are "long-term maintenance" or "termination."

In other words, the essence of the EOL problem is not a static issue of "old versions being dangerous." **Rather, it lies in the fact that migration costs—usually invisible—are billed all at once during the time-sensitive emergency of a vulnerability disclosure.** There are three options: pay in small increments during normal times, pay in a lump sum during an emergency, or shut down altogether because you cannot afford it.

### 2.5 PHP's True Strength — Handling High-Volume Requests and Alternatives

There are undeniable strengths to PHP/FPM. However, their true nature lies not in "language execution speed," but in the "execution model."

- **Shared-nothing (blank slate per request)**: Each request begins without carrying state and is released upon completion. State leaks are structurally unlikely, and an anomaly in one request is unlikely to ripple to others. The programming model is straightforward, scaling naturally by simply adding workers or servers horizontally.
- **FPM Worker Pool**: Apache/Nginx + FastCGI (PHP-FPM), where the number of concurrent executions is determined by the number of processes. This is a predictable, well-established configuration; since compiled code is shared via OPcache, it is sufficiently fast in practice for short CRUD/CMS-related requests.
- On the other hand, in terms of raw throughput, PHP frameworks do not rank at the top. In the "Fortunes"-style aggregations from TechEmpower Round 23, the results are roughly: Laravel at ~16,800 RPS, Node (Express) at ~78,000, Rust (Actix) at ~320,000, and Go (Fiber) at ~338,000 (these are microbenchmarks heavily dependent on benchmark conditions; the gap narrows in real-world applications where databases or external APIs dominate. These should be treated as reference values based on a single aggregation source).

So, what are the alternatives for "handling large volumes of requests"? Here are the answers, broken down by use case.

Another important point regarding the practical workflow is that **bottlenecks in high-volume requests are often the DB, network, or external APIs, rather than the language**. If those are the dominant factors, switching languages will yield almost no perceptible difference; what will have an impact first are caching, indexing, connection pools, queues, and CDNs.

As for the author's target domain (an announcement and reading site), there is a different approach. Rather than searching for the fastest mechanism for processing each request, the solution is to **eliminate processing altogether**—namely, static generation plus CDN delivery. In terms of resilience to high-volume requests, no dynamic runtime can beat a method that "returns pre-generated files." The excellence of PHP-FPM applies only to dynamic requests; for requirements where execution is unnecessary, staying out of that arena is the fastest, cheapest, and safest option.

### 2.6 Why upgrades don't happen even when they're needed

"You should upgrade whenever a major version is released" is sound logic. Yet, the reason upgrades aren't happening stems from a combination of structural factors that cannot be dismissed simply as negligence. Unless these are addressed, any solution will end up being nothing more than "raising awareness."

1. **There is no one contractually responsible for upgrading. ** As stated in §5, for sites delivered under the selling point of "no maintenance fees—customers can manage it themselves," PHP version management is no one's job. The development company believes their scope ends at delivery, the hosting company ends at server provision, and the customer believes their scope ends at updating articles. In that gap, version management for the runtime environment falls through the cracks.
2. **The stakes are asymmetric. ** If an upgrade breaks something, the person who broke it is held accountable on the spot. If an upgrade is skipped, whether an accident occurs is a matter of probability—and even if one does, it may be years away. For the engineers on the ground, the risk of "touching and breaking" is concrete, while the risk of "not touching and having the site hijacked in the future" is abstract. As long as this asymmetry exists, "don't touch what's working" becomes a rational decision for individuals.
3. **Costs are immediate and certain, while benefits are future and probabilistic. ** Migration costs are incurred immediately as an estimate. In contrast, the benefit gained—"not being brought to a halt by the next major vulnerability"—is a gain that cannot be truly felt until it actually happens. The more a site is a PR tool that doesn't directly drive revenue, the less likely management is to approve these costs.
4. **There are real circumstances that prevent upgrades even when desired. ** Plugins/themes with stalled development, custom code, a lack of testing environments or verification, developers who are no longer around, and external integrations like payments or bookings that only guarantee functionality in the old environment. In such cases, migration becomes "something akin to rebuilding" rather than "the act of upgrading," and it is further postponed.
5. **In shared environments, the single oldest site anchors the whole. ** In a configuration where many sites coexist on a single server, PHP versions cannot be chosen freely for each site; the entire system is dragged down by the site that is hardest to migrate.
6. **Postponement reinforces the cycle. ** Every time a generation is skipped, the next migration becomes larger, increasing both the fear and the cost. Consequently, upgrades are avoided even more. The endpoint of this vicious cycle is the scenario described in §2.3: "being hit with a lump-sum bill in an emergency."

In other words, the problem lies not so much in the quality of individual engineers, but in a **system where upgrading benefits no one, and the cost of not upgrading can be deferred**. That is why the proposal is not a matter of willpower—"let's just upgrade properly"—but rather a discussion of design and transactions: "choose a configuration that eliminates the need for continuous upgrades," and "if an upgrade is necessary, specify the cost and the person responsible in the contract."

Note that this "not upgrading" phenomenon is not unique to PHP. In Node.js, data from the OpenJS Foundation reports that "about two-thirds of users are on outdated versions," and downloads of EOL versions remain plentiful. The difference lies in the extent and depth. In Node's case, the legacy often manifests as actively developed applications lagging several generations behind. In contrast, PHP/WordPress's legacy includes sites created over a decade ago—where the owners have since lost interest—remaining on deeply outdated versions like PHP 5. This stems from a difference in language policy: while JavaScript has evolved primarily by adding features under the principle of "not breaking the Web" (meaning old syntax remains compatible with newer runtimes), PHP has explicitly introduced backward-incompatible changes with every generation. That said, disruptions within the ecosystem do occur in Node as well—such as the rebuilding of native modules or instances where old webpack stopped working due to the move to OpenSSL 3. Rather than saying "Node doesn't break," it is more accurate to say that "the reasons Node breaks are more rooted in the ecosystem than in the language itself."

### 3.4 Author's Example: Even after a major version jump from Node 16 to 22, a simple "switch and start" sufficed.

As I recall, the author had been using Node.js version 16 and has now upgraded to 22. Version 16 reached its EOL in 2023; this was not a patch, but a major version upgrade spanning three generations, skipping 18 and 20. Even so, no program changes were necessary. All that was done was to switch versions, launch the application, and verify its operation—no issues were found during verification. The author noted that, in their own experience, updating Node.js was far easier than updating PHP, requiring less time and fewer resources.

(In the first draft, based on the author's original statements, I wrote that "they weren't using an old EOL version" and that "a patch would have sufficed"; however, since the author later reflected that the version jump was from 16 to 22, I have rewritten this section based on that premise.)

There is a structural reason for this difference—one that is no coincidence.

- **Language compatibility policies differ.** JavaScript has evolved primarily by adding new features, guided by the principle of "not breaking the Web." Legacy syntax tends to work seamlessly even in newer runtimes. In contrast, PHP has introduced backward-incompatible changes with each generation, clearly documenting them in migration guides (such as the removal of functions or changes to comparison and type handling). Consequently, upgrading to a major PHP version necessitates a review and modification of the code. Note that there is no "PHP 6." The very fact that development for version 6—which aimed for Unicode support—fell through, resulting in version 7 following version 5, symbolizes the difficulty of major PHP updates.
- **The units of scope differ.** On shared servers/hosting, PHP typically runs multiple sites within a single execution environment. Upgrading PHP requires verifying the functionality of all sites and plugins on top of it—and the initiative to do so depends on the hosting provider's package distribution. In contrast, Node.js typically uses a separate execution environment for each app/container, allowing you to upgrade and roll back one at a time.
- **The way the output breaks is different.** When upgrading PHP versions causes compatibility issues, the site breaks in a visible way to users—for example, the live site might suddenly go completely white. In configurations where Node is used for builds or as a tool, the problem manifests during the build or startup phase, allowing it to be caught before publication. The fact that the author's verification only required "switching and launching" was due to this characteristic.

I should also add a caveat. Major Node version upgrades are not always seamless. They do actually break in apps that use native modules or with outdated build tools (such as webpack 4, which stalled during the transition to OpenSSL 3). This is a conditional case—it didn't affect the author's use case (which centers on scripts and builds and has no dependencies on native modules). Nevertheless, it is a structural fact that PHP tends to be less disruptive than major language updates, due to two factors: "compatibility with the language itself" and "a configuration where the impact manifests before release."

### 3.5 How to Check for Major Version Updates (Proposal)

The author's process of "switching, launching, and verifying" can be broken down into the following reproducible steps. The key is to avoid switching to production immediately; instead, test the new version first and ensure you can revert to the old version.

1. **Record the Current Version**: Capture `node -v` and the list of dependencies (lock file). Confirm the version to roll back to.
2. **Run in Another Environment First**: Switch only to the new version using version management (e.g., nvm) or a container, without touching production.
3. **Launch and Test**: Launch the app, run tests, and perform the build. Flag any errors at this stage.
4. **Check for Log Warnings**: Even if the app is running, check for any DeprecationWarnings. These serve as warnings of potential breakages in the next major release.
5. **Verify Output Diffs (Especially Effective for Static Generation)**: Build both the old and new versions and compare the generated HTML/JSON. If there are no differences, or if any exist but are explainable, this serves as evidence that it is safe. Unlike runtime generation, static generation allows for objective verification via "output file comparison."
6. **Prepare for Switching and Rollback**: If no issues are found, switch the production version and keep the old version available for a while. If problems arise, recovery is as simple as reverting the version.

The reason this process is tedious on the PHP/WordPress side is that steps 2 and 5 are difficult. Without a verification environment and because the output changes with every request, it is hard to demonstrate "no differences," ultimately leaving it to a series of visual checks.

## 4. Why Static CMSs Aren't Hit Hard — Including Honest Reservations

### 4.1 Things That Disappear

In a configuration where neither PHP nor Node.js runs on a public server (only HTML/JSON/images generated at build time are placed), the following will disappear from the public-facing surface:

- Reachability of runtime environment vulnerabilities via anonymous requests
- The entry points themselves—such as the database, admin panel login, and plugin execution.
- The binary choice in an emergency: "Keep it live until the patch is applied, or stop it."

In this case, since the author's public site doesn't even have PHP installed, there was no patch for php2shell at all. This is the most concrete way this works, based on the premise of "not running any programs."

### 4.2 Things That Won't Disappear (Reserved)

I'll keep it honest.

- **Build tools require updates.** As long as Node.js or similar tools are used for builds, those updates themselves are inevitable. The difference lies in exposure. Since build environments do not constantly process input from the anonymous internet, updates can be carried out as planned work rather than as emergency responses. The mere fact that they are not exposed to the public changes the level of urgency.
- **Supply chain risks persist.** If malicious packages are mixed into the dependencies used for builds, the output could be contaminated. The fact that the output can be inspected and diffed as files—and that previous versions can be restored if problems arise—serves as the final line of defense.
- **Location risks persist.** Hosting account takeovers, DNS issues, and distribution channel problems can occur even with static sites. As seen in the example of Hiroshi Abe's site in §1.1, you can also be affected by outages on the shared infrastructure side.
- **By leveraging external services, you reclaim that much of your runtime environment.** In a design where tasks like comments, form submissions, and payments are outsourced, the risk doesn't disappear—it simply shifts to the provider of those functions. This is why we say, "Instead of running a full suite in-house at all times, rent only what you need."

### 4.3 Requirements for dynamic behavior should be handled separately from the start.

With static sites, some things are simply impossible as long as you adhere to certain assumptions. These include shared writable states (comments, members, inventory), enforced confidentiality (controlling access so only the intended user sees it), and decisions requiring trust (payment verification, preventing double bookings). If these are central to your requirements, using an execution environment is the right approach—and the challenge shifts from "using one" to "using one without estimating operational costs." An intermediate design is also possible: separating functionality (moving only that specific feature to a separate service or subdomain) and avoiding placing the entire site on an execution environment at all times.

### 4.4 Historical Precedent — Movable Type Proved "Static Generation"

The concept of "statically exporting and serving" is not a new trend. Movable Type (written in Perl), which debuted in 2001, defined an era with a model that used "rebuilding" to export content written on the admin side into static HTML for delivery. The author's assessment was also that it was "well-executed," and its strength was the real deal.

At the same time, Movable Type's weaknesses apply directly to today's discussions.

- **Rebuild Costs**: Since every change required rewriting the relevant pages, the larger the site grew, the more resource-intensive the rebuilds became. The setup at the time—rebuilding pages every time a comment was posted—was the very source of the pressure to handle interactivity through dynamic generation. WordPress, generated on the fly in PHP, expanded in response to this pressure.
- **Implementation Language Barrier**: Even for its time, Perl had a high barrier to installation and modification, making it difficult for users to make changes. Recollections from former MT project members also cite the fact that it was written in Perl—which complicated installation for users—as one of the factors that drove them toward WordPress. This resonates with the author's own experience that "it was written in Perl and was a pain to fix."
- **The remaining administrative side becomes an attack surface**: Even if public pages are static, leaving administrative CGIs on the server and forgetting about them means they remain an entry point. Recent reports of legacy Movable Type installations—no longer in use—being disabled to address vulnerabilities are prime examples, demonstrating that "static delivery" and "removal of the administrative side" must go hand in hand.

There are three ways the author's Markdown CMS differs from Movable Type. Content consists of portable text files rather than databases; builds are handled by an automated pipeline rather than manual reconstruction; and the production server does not host the administrator's runtime environment itself. Regarding reconstruction costs, to be honest, build time issues persist in one form or another as the scale increases. However, the difference is that this does not constitute an "emergency situation requiring a halt to publication," but can instead be treated as a planning challenge for the build side.

## 5. Why WordPress Has Been Chosen — Issues with the Sales Model

Technical discussions alone cannot account for the sheer volume of these EOL sites. There are circumstances on the supply side.

- WordPress lent itself well to a sales pitch: "Since there's an admin panel, customers can update it themselves," and "therefore, no monthly maintenance fees are required." This led to the widespread adoption of a model where development and sales firms built websites in bulk as deliverables without maintenance contracts.
- The flaw in this model lies in **confusing the responsibility for content updates with that for runtime environment maintenance**. Customers can only replace articles themselves; PHP branch migrations and plugin supply chain management fall entirely outside the scope of their tools (the admin panel).
- On sites where no maintenance personnel are contractually assigned, the rational decision to "leave working things alone" accumulates, locking in the PHP version. The distribution in §2.3 (with EOL versions accounting for over 30%) can be interpreted as an aggregate of this result.
- Therefore, responsibility lies—prior to individual site owners or the language itself—with the sales model: "providing a system that requires constant maintenance, on the premise that maintenance costs will not be paid." The proposal for a static CMS is also an alternative to this model. The user interacts only with the content, while the underlying maintenance is either handled by the system itself or left entirely out of scope.

From this perspective, the defense that "WordPress isn't to blame" and the fact that "massive numbers of WordPress sites went down" are compatible. Even if the product itself isn't flawed, if it spreads through marketing and operational assumptions ill-suited to the product, it will fail in the same way during an emergency.

## 6. Selection Checklist for Engineers (Proposed)

When creating a new site or rebuilding one, decide whether to place the runtime environment on a public server in the following order:

1. **Isolating Requirements**: Are shared writable states, forced secrets, or trust-based decisions at the core of the requirements? If not, default to a static site.
2. **Minimize Placement**: Is the runtime environment required for the entire site or only for specific features? If only for features, can they be isolated?
3. **Operational Estimation**: Can you document the target time for applying emergency patches, roles and permissions, verification environments, backup restoration tests, and the EOL calendar (runtime environment, plugins, and dependency packages), along with costs and organizational structure? If not, the selection result is that "operation is impossible."
4. **Supply Chain Inventory**: Can you regularly verify the list of plugins/themes/dependency packages, whether authors continue to provide updates, and whether any components have been abandoned?
5. **Ensuring an Out**: Does content remain in a portable format, such as Markdown? Can you avoid a state where it exists only within a database?
6. **Clear Disclosure at Sale**: When stating "you can update it yourself," do you clearly distinguish whether this refers to content updates or includes maintenance? If maintenance is not included, state that upfront and present emergency options (migration costs or termination).
