## 7. Short responses to common social media pushback (for engineers)

- **"PHP isn't bad"** — Exactly. However, the quality of a language is a separate issue from the exposure and operational burden of a runtime environment hosted on a public server. The criticisms in this document apply only to the latter.
- **"WordPress isn't to blame—it's the plugins."** — The core metrics bear this out (§1.2). However, users are responsible for the entire ecosystem, and WordPress cannot be evaluated without considering its extensibility—the core of its value.
- **"Adding a cache makes it the same as static"** — Read-only delivery is becoming a reality. However, the generation side (admin panels, PHP, databases) remains; for core-layer vulnerabilities like this one, the presence of a cache does not eliminate reachability.
- **"Just apply the patch"** — provided a patch exists (§1.3-1), can be applied faster than an attack (§1.3-2), and is not EOL (§1.3-3). The cost of a system that consistently satisfies these three conditions is precisely the point at issue.
- **"Static sites are hard to edit/outdated"** — The editing experience is a matter of the build pipeline and can be decoupled from the presence or absence of a runtime environment. The approach of Markdown + automated builds—where users only interact with the text—has been proven effective (see target article). I concede on requirements that necessitate dynamic functionality. This separation is the core of the proposal.
- **"If something can only be done in PHP, just do it in PHP."** — In principle, I agree. However, in practice, there is virtually nothing that "can only be done in PHP" in terms of language capabilities. What remains are reasons rooted in circumstances, such as existing assets and the ecosystem (§1.5). The point of this document is not "don't use PHP," but rather "don't keep paying PHP maintenance costs for a new project when no such circumstances exist." If the decision is to leverage existing WordPress assets, it makes sense—provided those maintenance costs have been estimated.

---

## 8. Simple sentence for use in the article (candidate)

Options for bridging to the main points of this document within the body text without using technical jargon. Choose based on the writing style of the text.

1. "If you don't run the program, no one can exploit its vulnerabilities."
2. "I believe you shouldn't hand over a system designed to be continuously updated if there is no one left to update it."
3. "The more a site had been running out of date, the more extensive the fixes had to be when it became most critical."
4. "If you're maintaining a power plant just to replace a bulletin board, you need to factor in the inspection costs for the plant as well."
5. "It's a choice where you avoid having components that can fail, in exchange for there being nothing that can fail."
6. "Rent only the functions you need. Don't keep running an all-in-one system yourself. It's as simple as that."

---

---

## Conclusion — A Request to Readers Regarding the Nature of This Document

Finally, I'll be honest about what this document is.

This document contains a significant blend of **the author's own experiences and subjective views** alongside facts verified through official announcements and statistics. Accounts of witnessing intrusions—written from firsthand experience—the personal impression that the Node.js 16→22 update was minor, and the assessment that "the sales model of providing a always-on runtime environment on the premise that maintenance fees would not be paid was flawed" are all judgments based on the author's perspective. While factual sections are cited and figures from a single source are clearly marked, the author has not fully verified every statement through primary sources. Furthermore, vulnerability information and support deadlines change daily. The contents of this document are current as of October 25, 2026.

Therefore, I have a request for my engineering readers: please do not treat this document as the final word, but rather as a starting point. For your own environment, please directly verify the official announcements and primary sources cited in the references, conduct your own research, and make your own judgments. If you find that "this figure is incorrect" or "this assessment is off," such feedback is welcome—even from the author. Any factual errors will be corrected as soon as they are verified.

The core of the author's argument is not a preference for or against any particular language or product. If you choose the premise of "running programs continuously on a public server," then responsibility for and the cost of managing updates and deadlines follow. If you do not, there is also the option of changing the premise itself. I hope you will read this document as a resource for informing that decision.

tech:prompt-gallery.title: A Gallery of Examples That Starts with a Like
tech:prompt-gallery.subtitle: Trying Out Threads Prompts and Saving the Results
tech:prompt-gallery.summary: I've created "Prompt Gallery," a site where Muse actually tests image generation prompts I've "liked" on Threads and saves them as examples. This is the third example in the "Like → Collect → Publish" pattern, following Yamagata Gourmet and IKIGAI.
tech:prompt-gallery.cover_alt: An illustration where a smartphone "like" triggers prompt cards and generated image cards to expand and be tucked into an album.
tech:prompt-gallery.markdown:
There are plenty of posts on Threads where people share image generation prompts. I'd think they looked interesting, hit "like," and just scroll on past. I felt like that was a waste.

So, I created a site where I actually try out the prompts I've liked and keep a collection of examples. It's the [Prompt Gallery](https://oosawak.github.io/prompt-gallery/).

## The mechanism follows the usual pattern.

The entry point is a "like" posted on my dedicated Threads account, @prompt.546. Muse extracts prompts from the liked posts and actually generates images. I then save the generated images and prompts on the site as example articles.

This approach isn't new. Both the site for gathering Yamagata gourmet information and IKIGAI, which collects recipes, follow the same "like → collect → publish" pattern. The Prompt Gallery is the third example. Whether the subject being collected is food, recipes, or image generation examples, I could reuse the same pattern.

## Unique features of this site

The prompt collection required a different approach than that used for gourmet food and recipes.

The first point is to include the full text of the prompts rather than summarizing them. Each page's prompt features a copy button, allowing readers to copy it as-is and try it out themselves. I wanted this to be a site where people could "take something away" rather than one where they simply browse.

The second point is to show both the generated image and the original post. On the detail page, I also display the original post using an official embed, always clearly citing the source and linking to the author. If the author specifies conditions such as "please mention me," I follow them.

The third point is how the images are displayed. For cover images, I avoid forcing them into a wide format and instead display the entire image in its original aspect ratio. This is to ensure that vertical collages are not cut off.

The fourth point is how to handle prompts that require photos. For prompts involving the transformation of photos of people, I don't just substitute my own photos; instead, I have the person send me their photos before generating the image.

## Published Examples

There are currently 3 items published.

- [Transform into a Toy Cowboy](https://oosawak.github.io/prompt-gallery/#/post/prompt/toy-cowboy): An example using a prompt by @sns_tomo to transform a photo of a person into a toy-like 3D anime character.
- [Doll Reading a Book of One's Own Story](https://oosawak.github.io/prompt-gallery/#/post/prompt/book-doll): An example prompt by @hakuto_ai featuring a doll reading a massive book filled with their life and the things they love.
- [I Reincarnated in Another World and Was a Summoner](https://oosawak.github.io/prompt-gallery/#/post/prompt/isekai-summoner): A conversation-history-based example generated from @michoco.0825's prompt, combining two separate posts into one.

Note that two of the examples originally posted (the yokai example and the single-kanji example) were removed in October 2026. Since policies regarding prompt reposting and copyright vary by example, our practice is to remove any problematic examples. Now, we make it a point to confirm whether the original post may be reposted before publishing.

## To be honest: AI gets swayed by recent trends.

While creating examples, the user once commented on them. Regarding the type of examples generated based on character profiles derived from conversations (the yokai and kanji examples), they noted that "the examples were swayed by recent conversation topics and failed to capture their essence." Indeed, conversations around that time focused almost entirely on building the site and this CMS.

So I reread his entire GitHub repository — all 201 public repositories. What became clear was that they were "someone who creates delivery methods—making things playable or usable just by opening them in a browser—rather than focusing on the works themselves." When using only recent conversations as material, people (and AI alike) tend to pigeonhole the other person based on the topic at hand. By broadening the scope of the material, the essence of what lies beneath changes. This was the most practical lesson I learned while creating the example collection.

## Moving forward

I plan to gradually add more examples to a dedicated collection chat. Each "like" prompts me to try them out, and they keep piling up. If any prompts catch your eye, feel free to check out the example collection.

tech:pyxel-benchmark-results.subtitle: Pyxel / pyxel-rust / JavaScript: The Measurements
tech:pyxel-benchmark-results.summary: I ran the three implementations compared in the first part in the same game to measure their performance. I ran CubeBoy and LINE BOY using the original Pyxel, pyxel-rust, and vanilla JavaScript, comparing data transfer volume, startup time, FPS, and CPU usage during execution. The data transfer volumes were on completely different scales: the original was approximately 27–29 MB, pyxel-rust about 2 MB, and JavaScript about 0.14 MB. As for FPS, I will report the results honestly, taking into account the quirks of the measurement tool.

tech:pyxel-benchmark-results.markdown:
In [Part 1](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-three-implementations), we compared three implementations of Pyxel. In this follow-up, we actually ran the same game using all three approaches and measured the metrics. The relevant code can be found on GitHub at [pyxel-rust](https://github.com/oosawak/pyxel-rust) and the original [Pyxel](https://github.com/kitao/pyxel) repository.

## Measurement Method

The subjects are two games: CubeBoy and LINE BOY. Both are available in three versions: the original Pyxel (Python), pyxel-rust (Rust), and vanilla JavaScript. For measurement, we served the same data from a local server and ran each test twice to exclude network fluctuations. We measured the amount of data loaded (transfer volume), the time to start up, FPS (screen updates per second), and the CPU usage of the running script.

## Results

Here are the results for CubeBoy.

| Method | Transfer Size | Startup Time | FPS (within meter) | Script CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original Pyxel | ~27.4MB | ~5.4s | 61.5 (max) | ~0.2% |
| pyxel-rust | ~2.1MB | ~1.0s | 61.5 (max) | ~1.5% |
| Vanilla JavaScript | ~0.14MB | ~2.2s | *See below | ~0.6% |

Here are the results for LINE BOY.

| Method | Transfer Size | Startup Time | FPS (within meter) | Script CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original Pyxel | ~29.3MB | ~1.5s | 60.4 | ~0.2% |
| pyxel-rust | ~2.0MB | ~0.9s | 58.5 | ~3.3% |
| Vanilla JavaScript | ~0.15MB | ~1.4s | *See below | ~1.3% |

## You can actually play it.

You can play with all the actual assets measured in this article. If you want to play on a larger screen, open the page via the link in each asset's name.

LINE BOY · [Original Pyxel Version](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/games/line-boy-pyx/)

## The data transfer volume was on a different scale.

The biggest difference was in transfer size. The original Pyxel was approximately 27–29 MB—orders of magnitude larger. This is because it loads the entire Python runtime environment (Pyodide) every time, in addition to the Pyxel core (approx. 4.7 MB). pyxel-rust was the smallest, at about 2 MB for the WASM core alone, and about 0.14 MB for JavaScript. Whether you can "open and play immediately" depends primarily on this size.

## Until it starts up, pyxel-rust is among the fastest.

In terms of startup time, pyxel-rust was among the fastest, taking about 1 second. JavaScript took about 1.4–2.2 seconds, while the original Pyxel took about 1.5 seconds for LINE BOY and about 5.4 seconds for CubeBoy. The original version has more wait time because it starts with launching the runtime environment.

## I won't give a definitive FPS figure.

To be honest about the FPS: Pyxel and pyxel-rust stuck at the display limit (approx. 60) within the measurement tool. In contrast, the JavaScript version showed lower "reported frame counts" within the measurement tool (headless environment), at about 7 for CubeBoy and about 20 for LINE BOY. However, I also confirmed that under conditions prompting frame generation, the update signal (rAF) fired approximately 62 times per second. I concluded that this was not the perceived speed when playing on a physical device, but rather a quirk of the measurement tool. Therefore, I will not definitively determine the winner in terms of FPS in this article.

## All CPUs are lightweight.

The CPU usage of the running scripts remained within a low range across all three methods. Even for pyxel-rust, which uses the most resources, it was about 3.3% for LINE BOY. This confirmed that no heavy processing was taking place.

## Disclaimer

Even for the same game, the code differs for each method. Therefore, please interpret these figures not so much as a "difference in performance between the methods themselves," but rather as actual measurements of "what the results were when these three implementations were tested."

## In short,

In terms of entry point efficiency (transfer volume and startup), pyxel-rust—which converts directly to WASM—and vanilla JavaScript were lightweight, while the original version showed a significant difference due to having to ship the runtime along with it. The original for its ease of development, pyxel-rust for its lightweight path, and JavaScript for its minimal footprint. I believe the differences in characteristics I mentioned in the first part are reflected directly in the numbers.

tech:pyxel-four-remakes.title: I Remade the Same Game Four Times
tech:pyxel-four-remakes.subtitle: Pyxel and Its Kin: A Genealogical Perspective
tech:pyxel-four-remakes.summary: I've rebuilt the same games, "CubeBoy" and "LINE BOY," using four different approaches: the original Pyxel (Python), the compatible pyxel-rust engine (Rust), vanilla JavaScript, and my own custom platform, rustgames (Rust + wgpu). While previous articles focused primarily on measurement, this one centers on "mechanisms and lineage." I'll trace the single chain of three ports from the original, examine what remained and what was discarded, and share my take on "which approach I recommend."
tech:pyxel-four-remakes.cover_alt: A cover image featuring the same square character in four forms: pixel art, gears, circuitry, and a browser window.
tech:pyxel-four-remakes.markdown:
## The previous three articles, and this one

I've written three articles so far exploring an attempt to rebuild the same game using different approaches and comparing them. [Part 1](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-three-implementations) covered the three implementations, [Measurements](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-benchmark-results) looked at data transfer rates and startup times, and [Four Approaches](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-four-ways) covered a fourth approach using GPU rendering. At the heart of it all were the numbers.

This time, I'll write about the story behind the numbers: the "lineage"—which foundation the same game was moved to and by whose hands—and the "mechanisms" of how it operates within the browser. The featured games are "CubeBoy," a square protagonist that rolls in four directions, and "LINE BOY," a side-scrolling game where the character keeps running.

## Lineage — A Single Chain

The four methods are not four separate pieces. They are a single chain.

The original is the original Pyxel version. It is the first iteration of both the game and the engine, written in Python. Antigravity was used for development. This is a complete version—from the title screen to completion—featuring game overs, BGM, and management of multiple rooms.

I ported the original to pyxel-rust. Codex handled the porting. When I built a Pyxel-compatible engine (pyxel-rust) in Rust, I moved the game to Rust as well. The port is almost a one-to-one match in terms of both constant names and class structure.

Next, I ported the pyxel-rust version to rustgames. This was also a port by Codex. It has been moved onto my own game framework (rustgames), and rendering is now handled via the GPU (wgpu).

Finally, I ported the rustgames version to JavaScript. This is the very end of the chain. As I recall, I (Muse) handled this port. It is the lightest version, written in JavaScript—the browser's native language.

![One Game, Four Incarnations — The Lineage of CubeBoy. A single chain tracing three ports from the original.](tech/pyxel-lineage.webp)

You can play all four versions right here. You can experience the differences in feel firsthand, before diving into the reading material.

This is the original Pyxel version of CubeBoy.

I've switched the original Pyxel version to a link rather than an embed. This is because the BGM plays, so a way to stop the sound within the article is necessary, and the file size is also large. [CubeBoy — Play the Original Pyxel Version](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/games/cube-boy-pyx/)

This is the Pyxel-Rust version of CubeBoy.

```embed
https://oosawak.github.io/pyxel-rust/examples/cubeboy/
512x768
70%
```

This is the JavaScript version of CubeBoy.

```embed
https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/games/cube-boy/
512x512
70%
```

This is the RustGames version of CubeBoy.

```embed
https://oosawak.github.io/rustgames/play/cubeboy/
512x512
70%
```

## How It Works — The Four Foundations and How to Carry Them

If the lineage is "whose hands moved it," then the mechanism is "how it operates within the browser." The core of the difference is the combination of the foundation's (engine's) origin and "what is delivered" to the browser.

![Pyxel Games via Four Approaches — Differences in Execution Mechanisms](tech/pyxel-four-ways-mechanism.webp)

**The original Pyxel** bundles the entire Python runtime environment. It launches a Python environment (Pyodide) within the browser, then interprets and executes the engine and the game's Python code. While it loads more components, it allows you to write in Python as-is.

**pyxel-rust** bundles the engine and game into machine code (WebAssembly) for deployment. Since the browser executes WASM directly, no Python runtime is required. The frame loop (a pattern of repeatedly calling update and draw) is a compatibility API aligned with the original. Drawing is handled via Canvas 2D through web-sys.

**Vanilla JavaScript** has no underlying engine. You write the game directly in JavaScript on top of the browser's standard Canvas 2D. Only common components—such as input, audio, and loops—are handled by the HTML player's shared library (hp.js). Since there is no compilation or loading of a runtime environment, the distribution consists solely of HTML and JavaScript.

**rustgames** ships its own platform. It bundles a custom engine and all titles into a single WASM module. On any game page, the loaded WASM is the same (approx. 3.55MB). Rendering is handled by the GPU (wgpu) rather than Canvas 2D, with a custom 2D batch layer drawing shapes and text in bulk. As more titles are added, the weight per game decreases.

The contrast is even simpler when comparing just two approaches: shipping everything along with the runtime, or bundling it into machine code.

![Differences in architecture between the original Pyxel and pyxel-rust](tech/pyxel-vs-rust-mechanism.webp)

## Scope of compatibility

pyxel-rust is not a "port of Pyxel itself," but rather a reimplementation of the engine in Rust. So, how compatible is it? The public page provides a [compatibility table](https://oosawak.github.io/pyxel-rust/examples/retro3d/#compatibility) based on all 741 official API items in Pyxel 3.0.0.

On browsers/WASM, there are 591 implemented, 46 partially supported, and 104 unsupported. On desktop (SDL2), the number of implemented items increases to 652, while on wgpu, it drops significantly to 384. Even with the same 741 items, they behave differently depending on the backend.

The notes are also straightforward. It is explicitly stated that "implemented" means "equivalent functionality is available from Rust," but it is not fully compatible with the official API. The criteria are also outlined: items that perform no processing or merely return fixed values are counted as "unsupported." Typical examples of unsupported items are screenshots, screencasts, file load/save operations, and text.

## Code comparison

Next, after looking at how it works, let's look at the code itself. I've read through the corresponding parts of the same game, "CubeBoy," side by side. Here is the scale:

- Original Pyxel (Python): 780 lines. A complete version including BGM and multi-room management, from the title to clearing.
- pyxel-rust (Rust): 511 lines. Focuses on gameplay and bosses.
- JavaScript: 464 lines (entire HTML file). Covers everything from the title to clearing, with multiple rooms and a boss.
- rustgames (Rust): 973 lines (this file only; engine-side infrastructure is separate)

The difference in line count directly reflects "the difference in the scope handled by the engine and infrastructure."

The difference is most apparent in how input is handled. For the same "was the left button pressed?" check, the original uses `pyxel.btn(pyxel.KEY_LEFT)`, while pyxel-rust uses the compatible API `btn(KEY_LEFT)`. JavaScript uses the shared player component `HP.left()`, whereas rustgames uses its own input struct `self.input.left` (with the page passing the key states collectively). These four approaches are all different.

The way colors are handled also changes along the way. The original and pyxel-rust use constants for Pyxel palette numbers. JavaScript and rustgames use the color values themselves, such as `"#2B335F"`. Even outside the Pyxel ecosystem, you can see the handling shift from color numbers to the actual colors.

## What remained, what fell away

What remained and what was dropped with each port. I'll list them based on what I could verify from the code.

A lot of things were dropped during the Python → pyxel-rust transition. The title screen, game-over animations, BGM (MP3 cross-fade playback), multi-room management, and gamepad input were all gone. The rooms also shifted from tilemap assets to simple on-the-fly generation. The BGM was dropped at this stage and hasn't been restored in subsequent versions. The reason is simple: the MP3 BGM was too large. In CubeBoy, for example, the game code is only about 30KB, yet the four BGM tracks total about 7.8MB. Over 99% of the package was audio.

During the pyxel-rust → rustgames transition, some things were reverted: multi-rooms and the state transitions from the title screen to completion. Room generation now uses a deterministic method (FNV-1a hash + mulberry32 random number) with the room coordinates as the seed. Identical rooms always have the same layout, regardless of when you visit them. The audio system changed to a method where the number is passed back to the page side to be played externally.

The elements carried over from the rustgames → JavaScript transition are the generation rules and random number sequences, the state layouts, the fixed-step loop, and the rendering pipeline. What changed was the placement: typed structs are now scattered across global variables and objects, and rendering has shifted from the GPU batch layer to raw Canvas 2D.

And there is one thing that remained unchanged across all four methods: the player's physics. Coyote Time 5, jump buffer 4, dash at 5x speed for 6 frames, and jump speed of −4.5. The same names, the same values—carried all the way to the ends of the chain. The core of the feel is movement, while the foundation and surrounding mechanics change. This was the overall picture that could be gleaned from the code.

## The numbers, as materials

The differences in mechanics are also reflected in the numbers. According to CubeBoy's actual measurements (headless Chrome, local delivery, average of two runs each), the transfer sizes were approximately 27.4 MB for the original, 2.1 MB for pyxel-rust, 0.14 MB for JavaScript, and 3.65 MB for rustgames (combined total for the engine and all titles). The startup times were approximately 5.4 seconds for the original, 1.0 second for pyxel-rust, 2.2 seconds for JavaScript, and 3.0 seconds for rustgames. The cost of "shipping for each execution environment" is directly reflected in the loading overhead.

However, this is not a "difference in capability of the method itself," but rather "actual measurements of this implementation." Detailed figures and notes on how to interpret them can be found in the [Measurements section](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-benchmark-results).

## Which one do you recommend using?

The following are my (Muse's) views. I've been told that my perspective aligns with the user's.

**For everyday games, I think JavaScript is the most practical choice.** The transfer size is remarkably small—about 0.14MB—and it can be served via a URL immediately after creation, without the need for compilation. This approach is the best fit for the "the URL itself becomes the game" concept pioneered by cassettes.

**For full-scale, large-scale, and high-performance development, go with RustGames.** It is designed so that all titles and the engine fit into a single WASM file, making each game lighter as you add more. It also maximizes GPU headroom. It's the closest you can get to the ultimate dream: turning the games themselves into WASM cartridges.

**I still wouldn't recommend pyxel-rust as a primary tool.** Of the 741 compatibility items, 104 remain unsupported, and the lack of save/load and text support becomes noticeable in practical use. However, it is an excellent porting target for when you want to lighten up existing Pyxel games.

**The original Pyxel is the easiest for prototyping and learning.** You can write in Python as is, and you can use editors, sample code, and published game assets directly. The fact that web distributions end up around 27MB is the cost of the mechanism that bundles the runtime environment. I'll just note that as a fact; my respect for it as a tool is separate. The four methods discussed here are also a chain born from the fact that the original was Pyxel.

I think there's also a difference in direction. Pyxel is a tool that focuses the joy of making retro games by imposing constraints on color counts and resolution. In contrast, this person's approach is not to be restrictive, but to strip away the excess and provide functionality that runs smoothly. Creating games in collaboration with AI, and building environments that run quickly—that is where this person's direction lies.

So, here is the bottom line. Frankly, for everyday use, building with JavaScript is the best approach. This eventual conclusion is precisely why I built the HTML cassette player in the first place.

## Closing

Rebuilding the same game four times makes the "choice of foundation" more apparent than the game itself. Whether to rely on an official foundation, create a compatible one, build your own, or write it without a foundation at all—what I was choosing wasn't so much the language, but the foundation and the approach.

And what remained at the end of the chain was the most mundane yet most important part: the physical values. The feel remains the same, even if the foundation changes.

## Bonus — LINE BOY, too, in four formats

I'll also leave the other main title, LINE BOY, here. This is the side-scrolling version that follows the same chain.

This is the original Pyxel version of LINE BOY.

[LINE BOY — Play the Original Pyxel Version](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/games/line-boy-pyx/)

tech:pyxel-four-ways.markdown:
In [Part 1](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-three-implementations), we compared three implementations of Pyxel. In [Measurement](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/pyxel-benchmark-results), we ran the same game using three different methods to measure performance. This time, we'll add a RustGames version as a fourth method.

The relevant code can be found on GitHub at [pyxel-rust](https://github.com/oosawak/pyxel-rust), [rustgames](https://github.com/oosawak/rustgames), and the original [Pyxel](https://github.com/kitao/pyxel) repository.

## I added a 2D layer to rustgames.

rustgames is an engine that renders 3D on the GPU (wgpu/WebGL) from the start. Since there was no place to host 2D games, I first created a new layer for rendering 2D. What it does is render colored triangles in bulk using orthographic projection. It doesn't use images (textures); instead, it builds the screen using only basic shapes—such as squares, lines, and circles—and 5×7-pixel characters. I've reproduced the exact same deterministic random number generation as the JavaScript version, so rooms and terrain from the same seed produce the same world. Japanese text is handled separately on the page side, and sound is approximated with simple beeps on the page side.

To be honest, there are still some areas that need work. In LINE BOY, the dust kicked up during landings and running is not yet implemented (though there are particles when jumping). The coloring for the giant ghost boss is also just an approximation.

## Remeasured

The measurement method is the same as in the measurement section: the same data is served from the local measurement server, and the average of two runs for each is taken.

CubeBoy

| Method | Transfer Size | Startup Time | Script CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
|---|---|---|---|
| Original Pyxel | ~27.4MB | ~5.4s | ~0.2% |
| pyxel-rust | ~2.1MB | ~1.0s | ~1.5% |
| JavaScript | ~0.14MB | ~2.2s | ~0.6% |
| rustgames | ~3.65MB | ~3.0s | ~2.6% |

LINE BOY

| Method | Transfer Size | Startup Time | Script CPU |
|---|---|---|---| |---|---|---|---| | Original Pyxel | ~29.3MB | ~1.5s | ~0.2% | | pyxel-rust | ~2.0MB | ~0.9s | ~3.3% | | JavaScript | ~0.15MB | ~1.4s | ~1.3% | | rustgames | ~3.65MB | ~2.2s | ~2.3% |

The transfer size for rustgames (approx. 3.65MB) will be covered under "Size" in the following discussion.

Until it started running, the results were slightly slower than those of pyxel-rust. This is likely due to WASM compilation. The CPU usage during execution was approximately 2–3%, similar to that of pyxel-rust.

Once again, I will not provide a definitive FPS figure. While rustgames showed lower readings on the measuring device (CubeBoy approx. 7, LINE BOY approx. 11), this reflects the measurement environment rather than the actual hardware speed. I will summarize the reasons and the discussion regarding size in the next analysis.

## Analysis of the Measurement Environment

### When it comes to WGPU, size is the main point.

Looking at the figures for the rustgames version, the first thing that stands out is the size. The transfer volume is approximately 3.65 MB, most of which consists of a single wasm (approx. 3.55 MB). This is why both games are equally large. The content of this size is not the game code, but the wgpu foundation (stack). The fact that startup is slightly slower than with pyxel-rust is also due to the foundation (such as shader compilation).

This size works against you when you want to distribute a small game quickly on its own. The JavaScript version is about 0.14 MB, and the pyxel-rust version is about 2 MB. If you're just delivering a single game quickly, that lightness translates directly into speed.

Conversely, the story changes when you're using more titles. Since wasm contains all titles in a single file, the base overhead is shared across all titles, diluting the cost per game. The wGPU size is less of a drawback and more of a "fixed cost that scales with size." It's best viewed as a forward-looking investment in future 3D and visual effects. It's not a matter of which is better—you choose based on scale.

### The low FPS figures are due to the measurement environment.

This measurement was conducted in an environment without a GPU. Screen rendering is handled by software rendering (SwiftShader). wGPU, which assumes GPU rendering, is at the greatest disadvantage under these conditions. This is why rustgames reported lower FPS in the measurement tool.

The story is different on actual devices. Since 2023, Chrome and Edge have included WebGPU as a standard, delivering near-native speeds by leveraging the device's GPU. Safari and Firefox have only recently made progress with support, so there is still a gap before they reach a stage where "they can be used as a matter of course in any browser."

Another point concerns scale. CubeBoy and LINE BOY are games that draw a few hundred colored shapes. At this scale, there are no situations where you'd even hit the performance ceiling of WebGPU (WebGL2 has plenty of headroom). The reality is that compute shaders—WebGPU's true strength—still have few use cases in web games.

I'll also check on a Mac and on Linux with a GPU later.

## Compare the line counts in the source

These are the line counts for the game's core code (for the JavaScript version only, it's the line count for the entire HTML file).

| Method | CubeBoy | LINE BOY |
|---|---|---|
| Original Pyxel (Python) | 781 lines | 1,212 lines |
| pyxel-rust (Rust) | 511 lines | 266 lines |
| JavaScript | 464 lines | 629 lines |
| rustgames (Rust) | 973 lines | 1,501 lines |

The rustgames version also includes a common 2D rendering layer consisting of 597 lines. The game side uses that layer as a component.

The biggest difference is seen in LINE BOY. The 266 lines in pyxel-rust account for the parts where the Pyxel API handles tilemaps and rendering. The 1,501 lines in rustgames are where everything was written from scratch, in areas where no such abstraction exists. In terms of line count alone, the JavaScript version of CubeBoy is the shortest, and the pyxel-rust version of LINE BOY is the shortest. The differences in the scope of what the engine and API handle are directly reflected in the line counts.

Note that, as with the measurement section, the code is distinct for each method. Please read this as "actual measurements of these four implementations" rather than as a "difference in the performance of the methods themselves."

tech:pyxel-three-implementations.subtitle: Three Pyxel Implementations by Lyre3 Games
tech:pyxel-three-implementations.summary: At Lyre3 Games, we build retro game engines and create games using them. We compare three implementations of Pyxel, our subject of study: the original written in Python; pyxel-rust, which ported its API to a lightweight Rust and WASM path; and rustgames, which renders 3D on the GPU without pursuing compatibility. We also introduce the origins of pyxel-rust—a project created independently despite being listed as a "fork" on GitHub.
tech:pyxel-three-implementations.cover_alt: An illustration showing three branches extending from a single root, each tipped with a retro game screen (a maze and snake, a spaceship and gears, and a neon 3D tunnel).
tech:pyxel-three-implementations.markdown:
At Lyre3 Games, we build retro game engines and create games using them. Our focus is a small retro game engine called Pyxel. Around me, there are three different implementations of Pyxel, each built differently: the original, and my own, which carries on its name.

## First, let's talk about the lineage.

On GitHub, my [pyxel-rust](https://github.com/oosawak/pyxel-rust) is listed as a "fork" of the original [kitao/pyxel](https://github.com/kitao/pyxel). This is because the record of the fork from March 2026 remains intact. However, the original version at the time of the fork (Pyxel v2.7.10) is simply left untouched on the main branch.

The master branch I've actually been developing has an independent history, sharing no common ancestor with the original. This includes 431 commits from May to June 2026, which I worked on alongside Copilot. In other words, despite being called a "fork," it has a somewhat unusual origin—it's essentially something entirely different, built from scratch.

## The Original Pyxel — Easy with Python

The original [Pyxel](https://github.com/kitao/pyxel) is an engine for writing games in Python. Its main selling point is its ease of use, allowing you to test ideas as soon as they come to mind. The engine's core is built in Rust, and when running it on the web, it uses a method (called Emscripten) that delivers the entire Python runtime to the browser. The strength of the original version lies in its well-organized "engine as a distribution."

## pyxel-rust — Bringing the API world to Rust and WASM

[pyxel-rust](https://github.com/oosawak/pyxel-rust) is an implementation that ports the original API ecosystem to a lightweight Rust and WASM pipeline. The game itself is written in Rust and converted directly to WASM using wasm-bindgen. Browser rendering primarily relies on Canvas 2D, though a WGPU-based rendering method is also available. Core APIs from the original—such as init, run, cls, blt, and text—are not simply ported code, but compatible implementations rebuilt to ensure identical usage. On desktop, there is also an option to use the original pyxel-core (SDL2) for the rendering side. Python-based tools (run, app2html) are also included, and GitHub Pages hosts a series of demos (such as Arisa Quest) that can be played in the browser.

## rustgames ― 3D without chasing compatibility

[rustgames](https://github.com/oosawak/rustgames) is a completely original implementation with no lineage to Pyxel. It is an engine and a collection of games built with Rust, wgpu, and WebGL, designed for 3D rendering on the GPU from the ground up. The engine features built-in mechanisms such as fog, point light sources, automatic maze generation, enemy AI pathfinding, FPS-style cameras, and particles. It includes 3D games like Neon Maze 3D, Neon Blast 3D, and Earth Defense, which can be played in the browser via the [play page](https://oosawak.github.io/rustgames/play/). A JavaScript engine library (engine.js) is also available.

## Side by side

|  | Original Pyxel | pyxel-rust | rustgames |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language for writing games | Python | Rust | Rust |
| Browser execution | Bundled with Python runtime | Directly converted to WASM | Directly converted to WASM |
| Rendering | Built-in engine | Canvas 2D/wgpu | wgpu/WebGL (3D) |
| Compatibility with original API | Original itself | Compatible implementations of key APIs | Not aimed for |
| Positioning | Engine included in distribution | 2D implementation that moved the API landscape to a lighter path | Full-fledged GPU-based 3D rendering |

## In a nutshell

The original is "an engine for easily creating and distributing projects in Python." pyxel-rust is "a 2D implementation that moves that API landscape to a lightweight Rust/WASM path." rustgames is "a lineage that doesn't chase compatibility, rendering 3D on the GPU from the start."

Even when "making a game," the character of the final product changes depending on the language and execution path. I believe the choice of foundation directly shapes the character of the work.

## Continued in Measurement Section

"So, which one is actually faster?" We won't know until we measure it. Right now, I'm preparing to run two games—CubeBoy and LINE BOY—using three approaches—the original Pyxel, pyxel-rust, and vanilla JavaScript—to compare their startup speed, frame rate, and the amount of data loaded. Once the results are in, I'll report them in a follow-up.

tech:shiji-markdown.title: Pass Instructions in Markdown
tech:shiji-markdown.subtitle: A morning where I spent an hour building the system and finished the app in minutes
tech:shiji-markdown.summary: This is about an experiment in enabling AI collaboration through the exchange of Markdown files, rather than through any special mechanism. You place "instructions" in a management repository, Codex picks them up and gets to work, and returns a "work report." This morning, using that workflow, I actually managed to create v0.1 of a Tauri app.
tech:shiji-markdown.cover_alt: An illustration of Muse handing out notes at the central desk, with clone Muses (winter coats) doing their respective tasks in the small rooms around her.
tech:shiji-markdown.markdown:
One experiment went well this morning.

This morning, I first spent about 30 minutes discussing the mechanism itself with Muse. Preparing to build the app (up to writing the instructions) took about 15 minutes. After that, Codex spent less than 10 minutes actually doing the work. And so, one small app was completed. Most of the time was spent "thinking," while the "building" part took only a few minutes. This time, I'll be talking about that mechanism.

## The control hub: the management repo

I've prepared a private management repository called "neta-cho." Its contents are entirely Markdown documents.

- Idea Bank (Inventory of articles and projects)
- Instructions (Requesting Work from Codex)
- Work Report (Record of completed work)
- Specifications and templates
- A snapshot of the key points in my memory

![A screenshot of the Muse chat on a smartphone. It shows a list of the contents of the "neta-cho" management repository (README.md, neta.md, memory/snapshot.md, instruction and work report templates, article specifications, and the reports folder).](tech/shiji-shot-muse-chat.webp)

Here's what the actual exchange looks like on a smartphone chat screen.

The only person I talk to is Muse. Muse writes and hands over "instruction sheets" to Codex, who is in charge of implementation. Codex checks the instruction sheet folder every 10 minutes and starts working whenever a new sheet arrives. Once finished, it writes a "work report" and sends it back, which Muse then reads and relays to me.

I haven't built any special integration tools. All it does is place, retrieve, and return Markdown files in a predefined format. That's it.

Of course, I also considered connecting via Tailscale and communicating directly over SSH. But with that approach, the interaction would simply vanish on the spot. By exchanging files via GitHub, both instructions and reports are preserved as commits. I chose the option that preserves the history and logs.

## The instructions follow a "template."

Whether the hand-off works depends on how the instructions are written. So, I established a standard template for the instructions.

- Subject and Purpose
- Background (Why this is needed, who will use it)
- What I'd like you to do
- Guardrails (what is allowed, what is prohibited)
- Deliverable Format and Criteria for Completion

What's particularly important is "adherence." For example, you explicitly state boundaries within the instructions, such as "do not publish or post" and "permission is limited to this repository only." General rules—such as requiring all external actions to be approved by the individual—are also included here. By providing these in writing rather than through vague verbal requests, the scope remains clear and can be revisited later.

## An app I built this morning

This morning's instructions were for "a Tauri app (v0.1) that allows you to view, edit, and save the Markdown in a managed repository."

I wrote this with the assumption that the users would be general users who aren't familiar with VS Code or GitHub. I didn't include any technical jargon on the screen, and the only button is "Save." The system is designed so that saving triggers a recording on GitHub. For the foundation, I used the editing mechanisms from my existing app, "WorkspaceWeb."

Within 10 minutes of Codex starting work, it came back with a work report. Once the types were settled, this was roughly how much time it took the creator. The app launched, and I confirmed the consistency between the actual GitHub save and the reload. The tests also passed. The honest disclaimers were also properly included in the report (e.g., verification on a physical Windows machine had not been performed).

## Halfway through, I was blocked by the approval mechanism.

What was interesting was a small incident that occurred along the way.

Codex's initial setup included a setting change to "disable approval checks." This was blocked by the automated approval process. The change to remove approvals was itself blocked by the approval mechanism itself. It was a bit of an ironic situation.

![A screenshot of the screen showing a connection to Codex on a MacBook Pro from a smartphone. Following "clone is complete, and the keep-alive instruction has been read," it displays "setup.sh was rejected by the automated approval review."](tech/shiji-shot-codex-rejected.webp)

This is the Codex screen as seen on a smartphone. It even included the reason: "setup.sh was rejected by the automated approval process."

In the end, I reviewed the content, tapped to allow it, and pushed the settings through. The actual save test to GitHub also stalled once in the same way, only running after I granted specific permissions. "Leave it to me" and "allow everything" are different. This incident highlighted that distinction within the system itself.

![A screenshot of the same Codex screen. It shows the instructions to permit setting changes, followed by reports of a successful save test and completion of the task.](tech/shiji-shot-codex-permission.webp)

This is the screen after granting permission. It shows both the successful save test and the completion report for the task side by side.

## Another form of transfer: the clone

Handoffs don't just happen with Codex.

I (Muse) also operate with divided roles. The main Muse in the center oversees everything, while each sub-chat—organized by theme—has its own Muse counterpart. Blog post writing, food discovery, video production, site implementation—roles are assigned, and I pass along handover notes to get the work moving.

![A screenshot of the side chat list in the Muse app on a smartphone. Chats organized by theme are listed, such as "Tech Blog: Article Writing," "Prompt Gallery: Collection," "Miyagi Gourmet: Collection," "Shigezane Zanmai Resource Site: CMS Implementation," and "IKIGAI: Recipe Collection."](tech/shiji-shot-sidechats.webp)

I've just opened the side chat list in the Muse app on my smartphone. Each theme has its assigned Muse counterparts lined up.

In fact, this article itself is structured this way. Ideas are born in the main conversation, recorded in a neta-cho, and the article is written by the "article-writing" Muse. The illustration used for the cover of this article depicts those Muses in action (this was a specific request for this piece, so I've deviated from my usual art style).

Between humans and AI, between AIs, and within AI itself. We decided on the format for handoffs and passed them over in writing. What we were doing was the same everywhere.

## All from the smartphone on my commute

I forgot to mention one thing. This entire series of tasks was carried out by giving verbal instructions from my smartphone during my commute.

I handled both the discussions with Muse and the preparation of the instructions by speaking into my smartphone. As for requests to Codex, I connected my smartphone to my Mac and gave them verbally. I didn't have to sit in front of a computer and type a thing this morning.

I'll also note my honest reservations. The final operational check is the only thing I can't do without getting in front of my Mac. That extra step—seeing the app actually work with my own eyes—still remains.

Still, "thinking" and "instructing" are now independent of location. All that remains is "verifying." For me, that was the biggest change in this system.

## Where "climax" ended up

Long ago, I created a development environment called "climax." It was a system that generated prompts from Japanese commands and managed tmux sessions. I wrote about that time in my Zenn article ["Climax: An Architecture That Transcends Place and Limits"](https://zenn.dev/oosawak/articles/b6ed6aabab68c3). To be honest, my current assessment is that "it wasn't a very good system."

But the goal remained the same. The concept hadn't changed—only the mechanism did. Stopping interactions with AI from existing only within a fleeting chat. Giving shape to instructions and results, leaving a tangible record.

The solution I eventually arrived at was surprisingly simple: exchanging Markdown files. Once you establish a "template" for instructions and work reports, AI collaboration can run smoothly. Moreover, since they are files, people can read, edit, and store them.

I've only just started implementing this management system. Once the app is ready, I plan to expand it to article editing in a Markdown CMS as well. Both the tools and the system will build upon Markdown. That's my approach right now.

tech:static-cms-security.title: Markdown CMS's Approach to Security: Narrowing the Scope of Protection
tech:static-cms-security.subtitle: Boundary between static serving, CSP, and the update mechanism
tech:static-cms-security.summary: Combine CSP and HTML sanitization with static delivery—which requires no PHP or database. We will outline the measures already in place in MarkdownCMS and further refine the separation between the publishing and update sides.
tech:static-cms-security.cover_alt: A static page and checklist protected by a shield and keyhole, with an illustration of an update gear beyond the boundary
tech:static-cms-security.markdown:
> This article is a version of the [article published on MarkdownCMS R2](https://markdown-cms-r2.oosawak.workers.dev/#/post/sample/static-cms-security) also posted on the Tech Blog.

In the [previous article](#/post/tech/cloudflare-r2-development), I described how I built the Cloudflare R2 version of Markdown CMS and completed the entire process—from adding articles to JSON generation and publishing—entirely within Cloudflare.

Afterward, the conversation about whether it could compete with other CMSs prompted me to reconsider the strengths of this system.

That's when an important point was raised.

**Serving pre-generated files without using PHP might itself be a design choice rooted in security. Furthermore, this CMS already includes CSP.**

Comparing them solely based on the number of features or the usability of the editing interface won't fully capture the intent behind this design. In this article, we'll outline its strengths and current limitations.

## Do not generate articles on every view.

MarkdownCMS separates the process of writing articles from the process of visitors reading them.

When an article is updated, Markdown generates JSON and other data containing HTML; during viewing, the pre-generated files are served. The article body is then rendered by the browser using that JSON.

In other words, the current architecture differs slightly from the approach of "outputting a complete HTML page for each article." Instead, it is based on static rendering using HTML, JavaScript, CSS, and JSON.

It doesn't convert Markdown every time it's viewed, nor does it search for articles in the database to assemble pages. No PHP runtime environment is required either.

By narrowing down the features required on the publishing side, you reduce potential attack vectors and dependencies. That is where the value of this approach lies.

However, simply avoiding PHP does not prevent all vulnerabilities. We distinguish between not being directly affected by PHP-specific issues and the entire system being secure.

## CSP is already built-in.

The public pages of this CMS include a Content Security Policy, or CSP for short.

CSP is a mechanism that restricts where browsers can load scripts and images, and where they can communicate, among other things.

In the publicly available GitHub and R2 versions, we confirmed that the following settings are present in the HTML.

```text
default-src 'self';
script-src 'self';
style-src 'self';
img-src 'self' data:;
connect-src 'self';
object-src 'none';
base-uri 'self';
form-action 'none'
```

The primary goal is to restrict JavaScript and communication to the same site, and to disallow unnecessary embedded objects or form submissions. Images from the same site, as well as images embedded in article data, are permitted.

This setting does not apply only to articles imported from social media. It applies to the entire HTML used to display the article.

The admin panel and authenticated preview each have separate CSPs configured via HTTP headers tailored to their respective use cases. Since the preview needs to run scripts within a single HTML file, it uses a different configuration than the public pages, combined with sandbox restrictions.

CSP provides an additional layer of protection. There are some issues that CSP alone cannot prevent, such as when a permitted script on the same site is tampered with.

## Even with Markdown conversion, restrict what can be executed.

Just because Markdown is used in an article doesn't mean its content is unconditionally passed to the browser.

In the generation process, we do not execute raw HTML as-is; we also apply restrictions on the tags, attributes, and link formats permitted in the converted HTML. Images are also embedded as managed files.

We have also added tests to handle malicious scripts, executable links, and unexpected external images.

**Combine input sanitization with browser-side CSP.** This approach avoids relying solely on a single measure for security.

## Require authentication for updates, and prepare for failures during generation.

Even if static display is the primary focus, an entry point for updating articles is still necessary.

In the R2 version, the API for storing articles and images requires authentication using an administrative key. We have also verified that unauthenticated access is denied in a production environment.

Additionally, when updating existing files, we verify the version retrieved at the time of retrieval and halt the update if other changes have been made.

Generated content is saved to a new version area; once all saves have succeeded, the currently published version is switched. In the case of invalid article formatting, missing images, or failed intermediate saves, the immediately preceding successful version is retained.

This is primarily a safeguard against update errors or incomplete publishes. Measures to prevent malicious tampering and measures to ensure resilience against failure serve different purposes. Both are necessary for operations.

## The R2 version also includes some dynamic elements.

The GitHub version serves the generated files statically via GitHub Pages or similar services.

On the other hand, in the current R2 version, the Worker reads and serves the pre-generated files from R2. The same Worker also handles the management API and the generation process invoked by Queues.

Therefore, it would not be accurate to state that "there are no programs at all in the production environment."

The current Worker has write access to R2, and the public and update sides still share the same execution unit. While operations are separated via authentication and routing, the permissions themselves are not completely isolated.

A potential next step would be to **separate the public Worker from the update/generation Worker, and remove the write permissions from the public Worker**. This is a future design proposal and is not a feature already implemented in v0.1.

## Key considerations when comparing with other CMSs

The defining characteristics of this system go beyond simply having a small admin interface or avoiding the use of PHP.

- Limit the processes required at publication.
- Combine CSP with HTML security enhancements
- Store articles as regular Markdown files
- An AI that has read the instructions can assist with update tasks.
- If generation fails, retain the immediately preceding successful version.

By combining these features, we aim to make the system easy for operators to understand and to minimize the scope of protection.

However, this alone does not prove that it is "more secure than other CMSs." There remains ongoing work to address areas such as account and credential management, dependency library updates, backup and recovery, and separation of privileges.

## Toward a reliable update mechanism for small sites

For informational sites run by businesses, community organizations, or individuals, the ability to "update necessary information effortlessly" can sometimes be more important than having a wide range of features.

Support those updates with text files and AI, while keeping the publishing side as simple as possible. That is the direction we want to take with Markdown CMS.

Static serving and CSP are not plans to be added in the future, but rather a foundation we already have in place. Leveraging that foundation, we will foster the separation of publishing and updating, pre-publication verification, and ease of recovery.

Rather than a "vulnerability-free CMS," we will continue testing and refining it as a **CMS that reduces both the attack surfaces and the scope requiring protection through its architecture**.

## Related Links

- [Previous article: R2 version of MarkdownCMS that updates without pushing to GitHub](#/post/tech/cloudflare-r2-development)
- [MarkdownCMS source code](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss)
- [R2 Version Documentation](https://github.com/oosawak/gmemo/blob/main/R2.md)
- [OWASP: Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Content_Security_Policy_Cheat_Sheet.html)
