tech:update-flow.title: How Articles Get Published
tech:update-flow.subtitle: 5 Stages to Publishing Using a Smartphone and Muse
tech:update-flow.summary: I've outlined the process for publishing articles on this tech blog. It consists of five stages—from gathering materials to drafting, approval, publishing, and promotion—along with the division of roles between humans and Muse. The workflow is handled entirely via smartphone and chat.
tech:update-flow.cover_alt: An illustration depicting the journey from a smartphone to the flag across five stages, along with the checkpoints along the way.
tech:update-flow.markdown:
How are these Tech Blog articles published? This time, we'll walk you through the update process itself.

The general workflow consists of five stages: the "Entry Point" where materials are gathered, the "Draft" prepared by Muse, the "Approval" I review, "Publishing" where changes are applied automatically, and "Promotion." The only tools needed are a smartphone and chat.

## 1. Entry Point: Materials are gathered

Materials for the articles are gathered from several sources.

- "Likes": When you like a post you find on Instagram or Threads using a dedicated account, Muse picks it up (I wrote more about this in "[Likes Become the Site's Entry Point](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/iine-iriguchi)").
- Google Drive: Placing notes and drafts in Drive folders triggers site updates ("[You No Longer Have to Write on GitHub](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/drive-import)")
- Chat requests: I also often make requests directly from my smartphone, saying things like, "Turn this into an article."
- I've also verified the workflow for turning Facebook posts into articles, up to the experimental stage (integration into operations is yet to come).

My role is to find the materials and decide, "Make this into an article."

## 2. Draft: Provided by Muse

Once the materials are decided, Muse will prepare a draft.

The complete set includes not only the main text, but also drafts for the title and subtitle, a cover image specific to that article, and a summary. The text must be written with line breaks after every period and in plain language that is accessible to those not tech-savvy. It is also standard practice to keep established elements (track record) and undetermined elements (concepts) separate and not mixed together.

## 3. Approval: The Most Critical Hurdle

Drafts will not be published as-is. They must reach me first, and I will read them.

If there are any corrections needed, I'll point them out on the spot—whether it's replacing the title, toning down the phrasing, or fixing factual inaccuracies. Only after I hear the words "Publish it as is" do I move on to the next step. Because of this hurdle, I don't leave everything entirely to the AI.

I also documented the actual exchange in my production log.

- [3-Day Weekend Development Diary (on the blog)](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/weekend-3days-diary)

## 4. Publish: Once deployed, changes are applied automatically.

Approved articles are uploaded to GitHub as Markdown files. An automated build then runs, and they are reflected on the site within a few minutes. Since this isn't a system that runs programs on a server, there are no complex steps involved every time an update is made.

Publishing isn't the end of the process—you should actually open the page to verify that the title, images, and links are displaying correctly. If you want to change the appearance, either request it verbally or provide input via the DESIGN.md entry point ("[the DESIGN.md entry point](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/design-mo-markdown)").

## 5. Promotion: The Finishing Stage

Once an article is published, I post a notification on Threads and Facebook. Again, Muse prepares the draft, and I review it before posting. Just as with publishing, the rule is to "review before posting."

That concludes the workflow for a single article, including the promotion. My goal is to make this a single, seamless flow—including the promotion—leaving only the confirmation hurdle.

## The key to the process is how you place the hurdles.

Looking back, the key to this procedure isn't the names of the tools. It's how you draw the line between what runs automatically and what must always be verified by a human.

It's faster to leave material gathering and drafting to AI. But humans handle the decision on whether to publish and the verification of factual accuracy. I believe drawing that line is the core of this blog's update process.

tech:vuepress-hikaku.title: They Look Similar, but the Purpose Is Different
tech:vuepress-hikaku.subtitle: VuePress and My Markdown CMS
tech:vuepress-hikaku.summary: There is a solid precedent for the "write Markdown, get a static site" approach: VuePress. Comparing the two reveals that while the entry point is similar, their purposes differ.
tech:vuepress-hikaku.cover_alt: Beyond the fork in the road, on the left a developer's workbench with gears and blueprints, and on the right a folder of paper files and a small illustration of a sprout.
tech:vuepress-hikaku.markdown:
The other day, I came across an [introductory article on VuePress](https://qiita.com/sa-k0/items/4e0fca341b91c1fefe54) on Qiita. It was written in 2018 and covers version 0.10.2 at the time. VuePress works on the principle that "if you write in Markdown, you get a static site." Its underlying concept is quite similar to the Markdown CMS I built. While respecting it as a precedent, I decided to compare the two to see how they differ.

Additionally, let's take a look at the current state of VuePress. The original VuePress has entered a maintenance phase; from version 2 onward, the community has taken over, and it continues using Vue 3 and Vite as its tools. The official Vue.js team has released a successor called VitePress. This lineage persists today and remains a viable approach.

## Similarities

The similarities are clear. Both involve writing content in Markdown and converting (building) it into a static site. On the publishing side, no server-side program runs. This makes them fast and resilient. This very approach is something that VuePress has been demonstrating for a long time.

## Difference 1: Who uses it?

The biggest difference lies in the intended user. VuePress is a tool for developers. You set up the Node.js runtime, write a configuration file, and build the appearance using components from the Vue framework. Even an introductory article from 2018 cited the learning curve of Vue.js as a drawback. While it is a powerful tool for developers, it is not something for the average user to touch.

My Markdown CMS is designed from the inside out. The goal is for users not to be conscious of GitHub or Node.js. The entry point for writing is their familiar editor, a cloud folder, or a browser workspace. The underlying conversion and publishing tasks are handled by AI assistants and automated systems.

## Difference 2: What appears

VuePress outputs HTML for each page. A complete page is produced as-is.

The core of my system is data in JSON format, rather than HTML. The display side simply reads that JSON and renders it on the screen. This means you can create a portal that aggregates and displays JSON from other sites, or arrange sites with different characteristics—such as a tech blog and a gaming blog—using the same system. Rather than a "tool for building sites," it might be more accurate to call it a "system for connecting collections of sites."

## Difference 3: Dependency Heaviness

VuePress is built upon a large ecosystem of components: Vue, transformation tools, and Node.js. Consequently, it is affected by updates to the underlying infrastructure and major version transitions. Why Node.js updates can be a burden is closely tied to the discussion in the [supplementary material](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/php-nodejs-supplement).

As for me, I only use my own small conversion process—the core is simply a "plain text file." Even if the conversion process breaks, as long as the file remains, an AI can recreate it. This low dependency on tools directly translates into ease of maintenance.

## Where VuePress has the edge

To be honest, VuePress has certain advantages. Since you can embed Vue components within Markdown, you can create sophisticated, interactive pages that even utilize state management. In my setup, I've made a conscious trade-off there: whenever dynamic functionality is needed, I opt to leverage external tools. In terms of the richness of the pages you can build, developer-focused tools have the upper hand.

## The purposes are different.

Comparing the two, I realized it wasn't a matter of one being superior to the other, but rather a difference in purpose. VuePress is a toolkit for developers to build static sites. My Markdown CMS is a system for ordinary people to continue running a site alongside AI. While the entry point—Markdown—is the same, the vision we're aiming for at the finish line is different. Perhaps that's why comparing them is somewhat misplaced. Still, it served as a good opportunity to reaffirm where my own system stands.

I've summarized the comparisons with WordPress and EmDash in [this article](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/doko-de-ugokasu).

This article is also posted on [Qiita](https://qiita.com/oosawak@github/items/808124d1ac35e2a25eb4).

tech:weekend-3days-diary.title: Three-Day Weekend Development Log
tech:weekend-3days-diary.subtitle: From "Publish" to your article being live
tech:weekend-3days-diary.summary: Over the three-day period from October 24 to 26, 2026, I simultaneously set up a new site, published articles, uploaded videos, and gathered foodie information—all with just brief instructions to the AI assistant "Muse." Here is a record of that process.
tech:weekend-3days-diary.cover_alt: Smartphone and speech bubbles, site pages fanning out, small calendar illustration
tech:weekend-3days-diary.markdown:
I've listed the things I asked my AI assistant, "Muse," over the three-day period from October 24 to 26, 2026, in chronological order. It's like a production log. Looking at them side by side, I was a bit surprised myself—many of the requests were just short, single sentences.

## Day 1: The day I split up the locations

Saturday morning began with a system for archiving my Facebook posts. I created a dedicated discussion space (chat) and set up a workflow where, every Monday, I'd have the posts since the last update compiled and delivered to me.

In the morning, we also made progress on the promotional video for the novel site. We created separate chats for each stage of the video production and have completed the posts for Instagram, Threads, and Facebook. What we decided on that day was to separate the "production space" from the "discussion space." By organizing the chats by theme, we can keep the specific rules and preferences for each area from getting mixed up.

## Day 2: The day the foundation and the details both progressed on the same day

Sunday morning was design day. Starting with the question of whether Google Drive was the right choice for hosting articles, we worked through creating a draft of the specifications, actually linking the folders, and publishing a test article. That same morning, we also approved the design of the site itself. We created new Tech and Game blogs at oosawak.github.io and renamed the site to Lyre3 Games. Implementation began as soon as the decision was made, leading straight to publication. Along the way, we discovered an issue where the menu wouldn't appear on smartphones, but it was fixed and published that same day.

The afternoon was dedicated to the parts closest to the reader. "A line break after a period would be better." With just this one comment, I revised the writing style across all the articles on the blog and Qiita. On the Yamagata gourmet site, when I told them the cover art should be "softer, since it has a strong feel," 15 entries were remade with a soft, watercolor touch. I also started a personal list of restaurants I want to visit, and map directions were added below the articles. Every final detail was settled with a single exchange.

## Early morning of Day 3: The day the article was published overnight

On Sunday night, I put together a lengthy document, longer than those for WordPress or EmDash. I fed it into a tool called NotebookLM, converted it into 20 illustrated slides, and took it back with me, asking, "I want to publish this on a tech site." By midnight, an article combining text and illustrations was published on the tech blog and posted on Qiita, with links between the two. It took just a few hours in the middle of the night.

At one point, I did decline to approve a step. After receiving an explanation of what was being attempted and being convinced, I had them try again. Operations that go public—such as publishing or posting—were only approved after I had reviewed them. Internal prototypes and drafts could proceed freely. I think it was because of this clear line that it was safe to move forward with many things in parallel.

## What I noticed after comparing them side by side

Although it was three days, it was effectively just a series of short bursts of time over the weekend. I did all my work from my smartphone. I didn't spend a single moment sitting in front of a computer. The instructions were also mostly just short sentences: "Publish," "Sorry, go with Option B," "It's too heavy, make it softer." Even so, the number of sites grew, four articles were written, videos were posted, and gourmet information was gathered.

I think one of the reasons is that the core of this system is "just a file." The text is written in text files, and the settings in configuration files. That means the storage location, presentation, and deployment can all be changed later. GitHub and automated systems are merely conveniences built on top of that. Because the files are the core, I was able to break the work down into smaller tasks and proceed with them in parallel. This may be a practical manifestation of the "where to run it" discussion I wrote about in the [first article](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/homepage-wordpress-heavy).

Finally, just one thought regarding my vision. If I were to sell this system, I think it would be better to package it as "site folders and an operational framework" rather than as the program itself. This is still in the planning stage, and I intend to decide on the approach based on feedback.

And actually, this journal itself was born from my own request to "summarize a three-day request chronologically." I reread the notes I had compiled and turn them into articles. I believe this cycle is part of how I create things now.

This article is also posted on [Qiita](https://qiita.com/oosawak@github/items/efd9f23c2e52fbdbcb7e).

tech:wp-import.title: The Migration Tools Are Ready
tech:wp-import.subtitle: A converter and instructions for converting a WordPress site to Markdown files
tech:wp-import.summary: A tool for migrating WordPress sites to a Markdown CMS has been added to the commercial version (Cloudflare edition). The converter converts all posts and images to Markdown, while AI-powered instructions handle the procedures and decision-making. There are two entry points—the WordPress API and coded HTML—and both source files are stored in the Markdown site folder. The WordPress version has been proven on a single live site. Elements that cannot be made static, such as forms, are extracted along with replacement proposals.
tech:wp-import.cover_alt: An illustration of paper emerging from a large geared machine and transforming into a neat stack of documents on the right.
tech:wp-import.markdown:
I've created a tool to migrate WordPress sites directly to a Markdown CMS. This is an announcement that a "migration" feature has been added to the commercial version (Cloudflare edition) of the Markdown CMS. There are two entry points: the WordPress site and the coded HTML site. Both point to the same Markdown "site folder."

## Why migrate?

As I wrote in [“Is WordPress Too Heavy for a Website?”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/homepage-wordpress-heavy), my starting point is that for something like a website, there is no need for a system that keeps running a program on a server. That said, sites operated with WordPress over a long period still contain many articles and images. If it is possible to "migrate" rather than rebuild, that accumulated content can be transferred as-is into a format that doesn't run a program.

## The tools are the converter and the instructions.

What I've built this time is a combination of two things. One is a program I call a "converter," which handles the bulk of the work. The other is a set of instructions (in Markdown) to be passed to the AI, along with a checklist for the tasks. Since the procedures and decisions are written in the instructions, I've designed it so that even another Claude could read them and proceed with the migration using the same steps. This is a way of extending the approach I described in [“Passing Instructions in Markdown”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/shiji-markdown) to the migration process as well.

## What the converter does

The converter's job is to read and convert.

- Reads the target WordPress site via the public endpoint (REST API). No write operations are performed on the original site.
- Converts all posts and pages into Markdown files with frontmatter.
- Imports the images at their original size and rewrites the articles to reference them.
- Create a mapping table from the old URLs to the new ones.
- Provides a verification report showing the counts and whether the body text was transferred verbatim.

## There are two entrances.

We have provided two entry points for the conversion process, tailored to the structure of the original site. One involves importing via the WordPress interface (REST API) introduced in this article. The other is "HTML Import," designed for sites built with coded HTML and CSS. The HTML Import converter can import files from a local HTML folder or by navigating within the same host. This method also includes AI instructions, and the core conversion logic (the part that converts HTML to Markdown and performs the matching) is shared with the WordPress version. Since the output format is exactly the same—a "site folder"—the original files will both be a collection of Markdown files, regardless of the entry point.

## How the conversion process works

The entire process follows a set workflow. First, we perform an "inventory" to identify the number of articles and images, their file sizes, and the themes and embeds being used. Next, we convert the data and cross-reference the counts with the body text. We then recreate the look and behavior of the original theme to assemble it into a static site, and finally, we compare screenshots of the old and new versions to verify the results.

## Proven.

The WordPress version is already in production on a single live WordPress site. We have completed the migration of all articles and images, as well as the visual reproduction. I won't disclose the site name here, but this is a system we've verified by running it on a real site, rather than just "building a prototype." As for the HTML import, we have already verified the extraction, conversion, and verification from the prototype site's HTML (this is currently at v0.1).

## To be honest, things I can't do, too.

I'll be honest and identify the parts that cannot be converted to a static site. Elements that require a server-side mechanism for receiving data—such as contact forms—cannot be migrated as-is. I'll create a list of such parts, marking them as "cannot be migrated," and present them alongside proposed replacements so that I can discuss them with the site owner. The job of this tool ends with separating what can and cannot be migrated.

## Review and revisions, too—right from your smartphone.

The process for this migration itself remains the same. The AI handles the conversion and assembly. On my smartphone, I simply compare the screens before and after the migration and verbally point out the areas that differ from the original site. This comparison isn't limited to just text and photos; it also includes subtle behaviors—such as how the menu opens on the smartphone or how the header image is hidden during scrolling. For this migration as well, I compared every detail side-by-side with the original site and had the differences fixed. Both the verification and the requests for revisions can all be done from a smartphone. Specialized tasks are left to the AI, while humans focus on "looking" and "requesting." This tool is designed to support that workflow.

## As a feature of the commercial version

This migration was added as a feature of the commercial version, as detailed in [“Public and Commercial Versions of Markdown CMS”](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/markdown-cms-editions). It serves as a gateway for migrating small shop and business sites—previously hosted on WordPress—into a format that can be used reliably over the long term.

tech:yomukiku-cloudflare.title: The Novel Site "Yomukiku" Is Also Going to Cloudflare
tech:yomukiku-cloudflare.subtitle: Plan to publish alongside the current GitHub Pages version
tech:yomukiku-cloudflare.summary: I'll share my plan to create a Cloudflare version of the novel submission site "Yomukiku" alongside the current GitHub Pages version and publish them side-by-side. I'll break down what has already been decided from what remains to be determined.
tech:yomukiku-cloudflare.cover_alt: An illustration of two doors showing the same bookshelf. One side is a wooden library, the other is a sky with floating clouds.
tech:yomukiku-cloudflare.markdown:
The novel publishing site "Yomukiku" is a platform for publishing stories written in Markdown. When you upload a file, GitHub Actions updates the data and reflects it on the site. It is currently hosted via GitHub Pages.

Actually, "Yomukiku" also has a hidden feature. If you upload a ZIP file downloaded from Aozora Bunko, you can read the novel as-is. In fact, Eiji Yoshikawa's [“Records of the Three Kingdoms”](https://oosawak.github.io/MdYomuKiku/work-5LiJ5Zu95b-X.html) and Kotaro Takamura's [“The Journey”](https://oosawak.github.io/MdYomuKiku/work-6YGT56iL.html) are available to read in that format.

- [Visit the novel publishing site "Yomukiku"](https://oosawak.github.io/MdYomuKiku/)

## I'll create another distribution channel—the Cloudflare version.

A commercial version of Markdown CMS that uses Cloudflare is now available. Now, I'd like to try out how it works on my own novel site as well.

I plan to create a Cloudflare version of "Yomukiku" and publish it alongside the current GitHub Pages version. I outlined the differences between the public and commercial versions in my previous post.

- [Public and Commercial Versions of MarkdownCMS](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/post/tech/markdown-cms-editions)
- [Guide to the OSS Sample Site](https://oosawak.github.io/markdown-cms-oss/#/post/sample/oss-and-cloudflare)

## The goal of publishing them side-by-side

The same story will be available on both GitHub Pages and Cloudflare. The goal is to compare the differences in delivery and update methods using actual sites, rather than just samples.

Since "Yomukiku" is a novel site, its generation mechanism differs slightly from that of a Markdown CMS. Still, the core idea of hosting works in Markdown remains the same. We'll verify whether this approach works even when the delivery platform changes.

## Things yet to be decided

We'll decide on the configuration for the Cloudflare version moving forward. It's not yet clear whether we'll update via GitHub and serve from Cloudflare Pages, or update via R2 and serve from Workers. We also haven't decided on the release date yet.

This article covers only the plan to "create a Cloudflare version of Yomukiku." Once the details are finalized, we'll let you know.

game:gofudaicho-kaido.title: The Town That Followed Masamune
game:gofudaicho-kaido.subtitle: Gofudaicho and the Oshu Kaido in Wakabayashi
game:gofudaicho-kaido.summary: Gofudaicho — a town of merchants that relocated in its entirety from Yonezawa via Iwadeyama to Sendai. We walk through the koji shops, rice wholesalers, and lumber yards lining the Oshu Kaido in Wakabayashi, as well as the artisans in the backstreets. Beyond the highway lay Tamachi — a place that has vanished from addresses, remaining only in street names. A sequel to the first part, "Ashigaru Towns": the Townspeople and Artisans edition.
game:gofudaicho-kaido.cover_alt: An illustration of townhouses and lumber yards along the Oshu Kaido, dried dyed fabrics, and the silhouette of a castle visible on a distant hill.
game:gofudaicho-kaido.markdown:
In the first part, I walked through the ashigaru town of Wakabayashi—the town of "people" that had followed Masamune. This time, I want to talk about the "town" itself that had come along. Along the Oshu Kaido in Wakabayashi, towns of merchants and artisans line the way. At the forefront of these are the veterans who moved here along with the entire town.

![A schematic map of the Oshu Kaido in Wakabayashi. It shows the road leading from Kawaramachi to Minami-Zaimoku-cho, Kokumachi, Minami-Kaji-cho, Ara-machi, and Ta-machi, as well as the relative positions of the Wakabayashi castle ruins, the artisans' town in the backstreets, and the Shichigo-bori and Hirose River.](game/kaido-map-v2.webp)

A schematic diagram showing the relative positions of the towns along the highway looks like this. Since the boundaries and scale are not based on actual measurements, please treat them merely as a rough guide to the locations.

## The long-established Gofudaicho

There was a hierarchy among the merchant districts of Sendai. At the top were the Gofudaicho—six districts in total: Omachi, Sakanamachi, Minamimachi, Tachimachi, Yanagimachi, and Aramachi. Each was a district of merchants who had followed the Date clan from Yonezawa via Iwadeyama to Sendai, and they took great pride in their lineage.

Established merchants were granted privileges. Each district was granted a monopoly on specific trade goods: Omachi on cotton, secondhand clothing, and oil; Sakanamachi on fish; Minamimachi on produce and dry goods; Tachimachi on grains; Yanagimachi on tea; and Aramachi on koji. Every September, there was also the privilege of the "September Market," during which one of the Gofudaicho was designated as the trading hub for a major commodity. While the monopolies were temporarily abolished in Enpo 3 (1675), the status of the established merchants persisted thereafter in the form of the right to collect fees from the merchants of the castle town.

## Aramachi — The koji town that relocated in its entirety

That Aramachi is located in Wakabayashi. Originally, at the time of the founding of Sendai, Aramachi was situated around what is now Ichibancho (Hon-Aramachi). Following the construction of Masamune's Wakabayashi Castle, it was moved to its current location along the Oshu Kaido around Kan'ei 4–5 (1627–28). The entire merchant district was relocated.

Aramachi's specialty was koji. Miso, soy sauce, and sake—none of them could begin without koji. The koji makers of Aramachi held the keys to the culinary roots of Sendai. In the summer, when koji production came to a halt, the craft of making shibu-uchiwa (persimmon-bark fans) flourished as a side business, and it is said that it became a local specialty toward the end of the domain's rule.

The origin of the name is also intriguing. One theory suggests that in Yonezawa, the area was written as "Shinmachi" but read as "Aramachi," and that upon moving to Sendai, the characters became "荒町." Even today, Aramachi remains a shopping district where shops dealing in koji and miso persist, and the Edo-period layout—with its narrow storefronts and deep back alleys—is said to be still clearly visible.

## Beyond the Highway — Tamachi

Heading northwest along the highway from Aramachi, another town lies near a bend in the road. This is Tamachi. From here on, it is no longer Wakabayashi, but the castle town on the Sendai Castle side.

Tamachi was one of the twenty-four town districts and ranked 13th in hierarchy. At the time of the castle's founding, the southern entrance to the castle town followed a route from the Miyazawa ferry on the Hirose River, through Funacho, to Omachi; Tamachi served as the gateway to this area. It is said that, as a reward for their cooperation in the castle's construction, they were granted a monopoly on paper.

In 1873 (Meiji 6), it merged with Tashin-machi to become Tamachi, and was later absorbed into Gohashi under subsequent residential addressing systems, causing the name Tamachi to disappear as an address. Nevertheless, the name persists. The street is called "Tamachi-dori" and has been selected as one of Sendai City's roads utilizing historical town names; a street sign No. 29, "Tamachi/Shimizu-koji," also stands there. This is an example of the name of a vanished town continuing to live on as the name of a street.

## New towns along the highway

With the expansion of the Wakabayashi castle town, districts were demarcated along the Oshu Kaido from Aramachi to Kawaramachi. This was a district newly created specifically for Wakabayashi.

Minami-Kajimachi is an inverted L-shaped district located at the corner where the highway turns west. Blacksmithing was originally centered in Moto-Kajimachi (around present-day Kokubun-cho), but around the Kan'ei era, it split into north and south sections, and the blacksmiths brought by the Date clan since their time in Yonezawa moved here. It is a merchant district along the highway and is counted as one of the twenty-four town districts of the urban area.

Kokumachi was a district of rice wholesalers. Along with Tachimachi, Shin-denma-cho, and Futsuka-cho, it was known as the "Four Grain Towns" for its privilege in the trade of grains. At the boundary with Minami-Kajimachi, the masugata road—characteristic of castle towns—still remains today.

Minami-Zaimoku-cho originated as "Wakabayashi Zaimoku-cho," a district set aside for the construction of Wakabayashi Castle, and became Minami-Zaimoku-cho after the castle was abandoned. It held monopolies on timber and tobacco, with the Shichigo-bori moat running through the center of the town. Having escaped war damage, shops built in the dozo style still remain here and there.

The southern end of the highway was Kawaramachi. A town stretching along the banks of the Hirose River, it served as the southern gateway to the castle town. At the boundary stood a wooden gate called "Choginne," which opened at 6 a.m. and closed at 6 p.m. For generations, the Hariu family of Kawaramachi served as the gatekeepers in charge of the key. It is said that by the end of the Edo period, this family was even granted a monopoly on konnyaku and tori-mochi. In Kan'ei 17 (1640), a produce market was established; in addition to farmers bringing in their crops, nearby ashigaru also came to sell vegetables grown in their gardens, carrying them on shoulder poles. The side businesses of the samurai sustained the castle town's kitchen.

## Craftsmen of the Backstreets

Just a step off the highway lies a district of artisans.

Minami-Someshi-cho was a dyers' town along Nanago-bori. The dyers here were also retainers of the Date clan, having come from Yonezawa via Iwadeyama. They had originally lived in Koshiji (present-day Reiyashita), but in Kan'ei 13 (1636), they were relocated to this area for the construction of Zuihoden following the death of Masamune. Since dyeing required drying areas, the frontage of the residences was six-and-a-half ken—only half a ken wider than the usual six ken. It is said that items dyed with the water of Nanago-bori were of high quality. There was another dyers' town in Sendai, Kami (Kita)-Someshi-cho, located between Kitame-cho and Tamachi.

Tatami-ya-cho was a town of tatami craftsmen located north of Minami-Someshi-cho, and it had been formally established by the end of the Kan'ei era (around 1643). It bordered Rokujunin-cho to the east and Kokumachi to the west.

Minami-Ishikiri-cho was a town of stonemasons located behind the eastern side of Minami-Zaimoku-cho. In a map from Kanbun 4 (1664), it is marked as "Ishigaki-shu." The craftsmen were people invited from Omi Province (present-day Shiga Prefecture), and they worked on lanterns and torii gates for shrines and temples, as well as gravestones and stone monuments. The road connecting Minami-Zaimoku-cho and Minami-Ishikiri-cho was called Takeya-yokocho; since it is said that people who traded in bamboo lived there—literally—this means that behind the craftsmen's town lay another alley dedicated to a different trade.

Hakken-koji is a narrow alley south of Minami-Someshi-cho, named for the fact that there were once only eight houses in the vicinity. Even today, a narrow path befitting the alley's name remains. It must have been a quiet spot at the edge of the castle town.

There was another group of stone masons. Ishigaki-cho was a town along the slope descending from Bishamonten in Aramachi to Tsuchihi, where the residences of stone masons (ashigaru known as ishigaki-shu or gosakuji-kata) were located. It is believed to have been established around Kan'ei 5 (1628), when the castle town expanded during the construction of Wakabayashi Castle. The people who built the castle's stone walls lived near the castle.

## The town of Wakabayashi—there is more.

There are still other towns with names and descriptions. I will list them briefly.

Doba refers to the area along the banks of the Hirose River, named for the weirs that dammed the river to divert water into the Rokugo and Shichigo moats. It was a logistics hub housing the domain's timber and rice storehouses (Wakabayashi Go-zaimoku and Wakabayashi Go-komekura), and the bridge spanning the nearby Shichigo Moat still bears the name "Kuramaebashi." It is said that the place name first appeared on maps during the Meiji era.

Ishinasaka is a hillside town south of Yuminomachi and was counted as one of the "Seven Slopes of Sendai" during the domain administration period. As part of the town layout for the construction of Wakabayashi Castle, ashigaru residences were established there. The name is said to derive from "Ishina," a courtesan from this area who gained renown in Yoshiwara, though the details remain unknown. To the south lay the Miyazawa Ferry crossing the Hirose River, which served as one of the old routes into the castle town.

The Moto-chabatake is located on a sunny, east-south-facing slope south of Renbo-koji and west of Shibata-cho. From around Kanbun 11 (1671) to Genroku 8 (1695), it served as the domain's tea plantation, with the Magobei-bori moat flowing through the fields. After the tea plantation was abolished, the area became samurai residences, and the name "Moto"-chabatake remained. Today, most of the eastern half is the site of Sendai First High School.

Shin-Yumi-no-machi is a district bordering Minami-Zaimoku-cho to the east and Hachiken-koji to the north; it was established around Enpo 6 (1678). It was home to the Yumi-ashigaru-shu, who had been appointed after Fuse Izumi, a magistrate, petitioned the domain. It was a new Yumi-no-machi, distinct from Yumi-no-machi (the district of the Yumi-ashigaru-gumi mentioned in the first installment).

Higashi-Kubancho is one of the long, narrow streets, alongside Higashi-Nanabancho and Higashi-Hachibancho, with ashigaru residences lining the west side and temple residences along the east. The temples that still remain today are said to have carved out a 400-year history in this location.

Nikenjaya is located on the eastern edge of Shindera-koji; it derived its name from the fact that two teahouses—"Okubo" and "Kashima"—stood there during the late Edo period. Until 1889, it was a town on the outskirts of the castle town, belonging to Miname Village.

Gyoninzuka is said to derive its name from a mound enshrining a gyonin (yamabushi) who became a human sacrifice in an attempt to save people plagued by the flooding Hirose River. Today, the name no longer survives as a place name; Kojo Shrine stands in nearly the same location, and the name is said to be preserved only at the railroad crossing. Some town names have also vanished.

Tsuchitoi is a town extending east-west along the left bank of the Hirose River, established as one of the districts laid out after the construction of Wakabayashi Castle. It is said to have derived its name from the practice of channeling water flowing from Shimizu-koji through earthen troughs. In addition to samurai residences, many falconers and feeders (those responsible for procuring bird feed) lived here, and the ferry crossing to Seigan-ji Temple on the opposite bank was a strategic hub for transportation on the Hirose River. On the left bank near Atago Bridge, the residential groves of the samurai residences still remain today.

Shimizu-koji was one of the eight alleys of Sendai; during the domain period, the residences and estate forests of high-ranking samurai lined both sides of the street. Abundant spring water welled up here, flowing south through the center of the road and emptying into the Hirose River near the earthen troughs. A portion of this flow became the Magobei-bori and headed toward Aramachi. At the corner leading to Renbo-koji, the north-south and east-west moats intersected, and because five bridges spanned that point, the place name "Gobashi" is said to have arisen. Gobashi is a location where the name was derived directly from the number of bridges.

Goragi-dori is a street that extends eastward south of Kinoshita. In the past, there was a hollow at the base of a dead, large tree at the northeast corner, where Murasaki Myojin was enshrined. Because the hollow was called "gahora" in the local dialect, the area became known as "Gahoragi," and the phonetic characters for "Goragi" became the name of the street. Maps from the Genroku era show rows of samurai residences. The blacksmith district to the east of the street is said to be where Hongo Kunikane, a renowned swordsmith of the early Edo period, lived.

Nishi-Shincho and Higashi-Shincho are two neighborhoods flanking Hoshun-in to the east and west; both were established following the founding of Hoshun-in in Kan'ei 12 (1635). Nishi-Shincho was largely occupied by temple residences, while Higashi-Shincho contained both temple residences and the estates of the "go-ninjo-shu." Today, a freight line runs through Higashi-Shincho. Together with Hoshun-in-mae-cho, three neighborhoods that emerged after the temple's establishment stand side by side.

Renbo-koji is one of the Eight Alleys of Sendai, named for the path leading to the 24 monks' quarters of Mutsu Kokubun-ji. Established around Kan'ei 4–5 (1627–28), the area was lined with ashigaru residences throughout the domain period. The ashigaru here earned meager stipends; alongside side jobs selling vegetables grown in their gardens at the Kawaramachi produce market, they were also known for their brush-making. Almost every household in the neighborhood produced brushes, and it is said that during the Meiji era, a large brush wholesaler even opened a brush-making school, inviting craftsmen to serve as instructors. The brush shops that still remain today in areas such as Sanbyakunin-cho are said to have been founded by people from this neighborhood.

## Geological Strata of Town Names

Thus, when the town names of Wakabayashi are arranged chronologically, they begin to resemble geological strata.

The ashigaru towns and roadside towns date from the 1630s. Hoshun-in-mae-cho is newer than these, as it was established after Hoshun-in was founded in Kan'ei 12 (1635). The newest is Bunka-cho, created under the residential address system of Showa 42 (1967). To its east lay Minami-Koizumi Village until Showa 3—land that was part of the village rather than the castle town. Edo-period town names and Showa-period town names coexist within the same Wakabayashi Ward.

## Conclusion

The first wave of ashigaru, the merchants of the gofudai towns, and the artisans—blacksmiths and dyers—were all "people who had followed Masamune." When you consider that not only the people, but the towns themselves had journeyed together, the sequence of town names in Wakabayashi begins to look slightly different.

I am writing this piece as a blog for the game-in-progress *Ou Isshoroku*. The game can be found here: [Ou Isshoroku (Prototype)](https://oosawak.github.io/sengoku-life-sim/) Part 1, "Those Who Followed Masamune — Walking Through Sendai's Ashigaru Town": [Game Blog](https://oosawak.github.io/game/#/post/game/sendai-ashigaru-machi)

game:html-player.title: Ordinary HTML Becomes a Cartridge As It Is
game:html-player.subtitle: The HTML Player Is Ready
game:html-player.summary: I've prepared the "HTML Player"—a platform that you open in your browser and insert cartridges (games made with standard HTML) to play. There are two ways to distribute it: a system where the player holds the common components, and the 14 cartridges currently available, along with instructions on how to make them.
game:html-player.cover_alt: An illustration of a pixel square flowing from a smartphone game screen into a cartridge
game:html-player.markdown:
I've set up an [HTML Player](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/). It's a browser-based platform where you insert cartridges (games made with standard HTML) to play. It replicates the design of old game consoles, which separated the console from the cartridge, right within your browser.

## Why a single platform?

You can also publish games one by one, each on its own page. But with that approach, the play area and controls will vary from game to game.

If there's a single platform to support everything, things change. Players simply open the player and select a cartridge. Developers only need to focus on the game itself. We provided this player as a foundation to ensure "just open in the browser and play."

## The cartridge is standard HTML.

The cartridge isn't actually a special format—it's just a single, ordinary HTML file. No dedicated API or conversion is required.

The player loads and executes that HTML. The game is fundamentally designed to be playable even when opened standalone. Record saving is handled entirely within the browser (localStorage), ensuring that the game can be played without communicating with a server.

## There are two ways to distribute them.

There are two ways to distribute them.

One option is to include them in the player. You can link directly to included cartridges using a short URL (#g=). You can only specify those that have already been included.

Another option is URL embedding (#p=). This involves gzipping the game file and embedding it directly within the URL. This allows the game to be delivered via a single URL, even if you don't have a place to host it. As a guideline, the compressed size should be approximately 3KB, and the total URL length should be within 4,096 characters. This size is based on the specifications of Kitao-san's [Playload](https://github.com/kitao/playload), making it a size that can be pasted directly into an X post.

You can generate an embedded URL using the "Create Cartridge URL" tool on the player's page. Since compression is performed within the browser, the game's content is not sent to the server.

Note that the format for specifying and loading external URLs (the legacy ?game=) was removed in v0.26 as part of a security design review. Players only load included cartridges and embedded URLs.

## Common components are handled by the player.

This is the player’s most distinctive feature. Fonts, icons, and shared JavaScript are not included in the cartridge; instead, the player handles them and passes them to the game.

- 6 standard fonts (HP Serif/HP Sans/HP Round/HP Mono/HP Dot/HP Denki)
- Icon font "RPG Awesome" (monster and weapon icons)
- hp.js (input, game loop, sound effects, and UI components such as gauges and title screens)
- three.js (3D library, r128)

This allows the cartridge to be made smaller, as the amount of code on the console is reduced by the shared components. In exchange, games that use these shared components cannot be self-contained as standalone files; they are designed to run on the player. This trade-off is clearly stated on the player’s screen and in the documentation.

Take fonts, for example. Just the other day, I added the pixel font "Denki Chip" (created by patient-leader Hikku, SIL Open Font License) as the player's default font, "HP Denki." Once added to the player, any cartridge you want to use can display even kanji in bitmap form simply by specifying its name. The advantage of this approach is that you only need to add components in one place.

## Controls are via the on-screen controller.

The on-screen controller appears right below the game from the start. You can control it using the directional pad and the A/B buttons. You can also hide it by pressing the "Controller" button. On a keyboard, the directional pad corresponds to the arrow keys, A to Space, and B to the X key. On a smartphone, you can also play by tapping.

![Here's the HTML Player open on an actual smartphone. When you select a cartridge, the game's title screen appears right then and there.](game/ring-burst-jikki-v2.webp)

## Current cartridge

There are currently 14 cartridges available for players to choose from.

- Duel, Solitaire Mahjong, Shanghai, Monster Match, Monster Hunt
- [Star Breaker](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/star-breaker/) and [Ring Burst](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/ring-burst/) (two shooters)
- [LINE BOY](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/line-boy/) and [CubeBoy](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/cube-boy/) (the two common library versions)
- [Neon Maze](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/neon-maze/), [Neon Maze 3D](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/neon-maze-3d/), [Earth Defense](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/earth-defense/) (three WASM games)
- [LINE BOY (Pyxel)](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/line-boy-pyx/), [CubeBoy (Pyxel)](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/cube-boy-pyx/)

![Just opened "Duel — A Flash of a Moment." Two opponents facing off against the backdrop of the setting sun.](game/ikkiuchi-jikki-v1.webp)

![Just opened "Starbreaker." Enemies and planets are approaching from above.](game/star-breaker-jikki-v1.webp)

The player console and included cartridges are available under the MIT License.

## How to Make Cartridges

We have provided specifications for developers ([CARTRIDGE.md](https://github.com/oosawak/html-player/blob/main/CARTRIDGE.md)) and a template (TEMPLATE.md). To create the game, follow the template to write the game content, then provide it along with the specifications to the AI. You will receive a single HTML game; you can either place it in the player or use an embedded URL. The key is to concisely define "one game = one core experience."

## As long as there's a receiving end, you can keep adding more cartridges.

My ultimate dream is a "cartridge" system that lets you play a game immediately after downloading it from the web. I created the HTML Player as the HTML version of that platform. There is only one platform, and anyone can create a cartridge. I believe I've come somewhat closer to achieving that vision.

First, open the [HTML Player](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/) and try playing a game.

game:html-player-security.subtitle: Secure Design of the HTML Player
game:html-player-security.summary: Any mechanism that allows standard HTML to be distributed as-is must also account for potential misuse. As a follow-up to the previous HTML Player, I will introduce the design of the "cage" introduced in v0.18 (isolated execution, communication prohibition, and runaway detection).
game:html-player-security.cover_alt: An illustration of a game cartridge glowing safely inside a glass case and grid
game:html-player-security.markdown:
I've added a safety mechanism to the [HTML Player](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/) introduced in [the previous article](https://oosawak.github.io/game/#/post/game/html-player). It all started with a simple question: "I wonder if I could use this mechanism to create something like a virus?" After researching and rebuilding it, the answer I arrived at is the title of this article. You can't create a virus. But you can create scams. With that premise in mind, in v0.18, I added another layer of "cages" inside the tabs.

## Why can't you create viruses?

First, the outermost cage is the browser tab itself. Web pages can only operate within the tab. They have no access to the device's files or other apps. They cannot arbitrarily read or write pages from other sites. Once you close the tab, everything ends right there. Cartridges are also inhabitants of this cage. Therefore, a virus that infects and spreads across the device cannot be created using this mechanism. However, this doesn't mean that "anything is safe as long as it's inside a tab." There are still things you can do even within a tab. The danger lay right there.

## The danger took the form of "scams."

Cartridges can freely draw whatever they want on the screen. They can create a realistic-looking login screen and prompt you to enter an ID and password—that kind of "fake screen" can indeed be made. This is a form of phishing that leverages the trust of an open domain. This was a more real-world danger than viruses. I designed the countermeasures to fit this specific pattern.

The cartridge operates within the same tab as the player. If left unchecked, it could rewrite the player's page or use records from the same location as the player. To prevent this, I created an additional layer of enclosures inside the tab's cage. I added three such enclosures.

## Cage 1: Isolate and execute

Built-in cartridges and games with embedded URLs run within isolated frames. They cannot rewrite the player's page. They cannot read or write records (localStorage) from other sites. They cannot display warning dialogs or navigate the entire tab to a different site. Instead, the game's own records are also no longer preserved within the player. This is a form of execution based on the premise that "it could be HTML created by anyone."

## Cage 2: Prohibit Communication

The Communication Policy (CSP) blocks all external communication. Data transmission (via fetch or WebSocket), loading external images, and form submissions are all disabled. Even if a user is prompted to enter information on a fake screen, there is no destination for that data. Additionally, the specifications for developers ([CARTRIDGE.md](https://github.com/oosawak/html-player/blob/main/CARTRIDGE.md)) prohibit forms and input elements themselves. The line is drawn such that while HTML elements for display are permitted, input fields are not.

## Cage 3: Detecting Rampage

I've also implemented countermeasures to prevent cartridges from freezing due to infinite loops and other issues. Games using the common library (hp.js) send a survival signal to the player every 0.5 seconds. If the signal is lost, the player automatically stops the cartridge. Once stopped, the player can resume from the same tab by reloading. If loading does not start immediately after stopping, the player will automatically reload it again. This can also be turned off using the player's "Runaway Detection" button.

## I've removed anything that was out of scope.

When it was first released, major external titles loaded via URL (such as Cube Core Dungeon and DUNGEON//LOAD) were exempt from this isolation. I made it clear in the article that this was the boundary. Afterward, I reconsidered the very notion of having exceptions and stopped URL-based loading altogether (v0.26). Now, players only load included cartridges and games with embedded URLs (#p=). Included cartridges can also be linked directly via short URLs (#g=). Only pre-included titles can be specified. All titles are now subject to this confinement.

## I've verified this.

I created an attack test cartridge to test reading and writing records, interference with the parent page, communication, external images, form submissions, and dialogs, and confirmed that everything stopped. The infinite-loop cartridge was halted by runaway detection. In normal games (Ring Burst, Monster Match), there were no malfunctions, and fonts and icons are displayed as usual. Additionally, to ensure compatibility with the isolation, I restructured the font delivery method so that "the cartridge loads the CSS file."

Anyone can now try this verification. A cartridge titled "[Security Check Sample](https://oosawak.github.io/html-player/#g=games/security-check/)" is included in the player. Once selected, the check begins automatically and displays a list of how record saving, cookies, access to the parent page, external communication, and loading external images are all blocked. Opening a separate window, full-screen transitions, form submissions, dialogs, and infinite loops can be tested one by one via buttons. With the infinite loop button, you can see the process run until the runaway detection kicks in and stops it.

## The original Playload is in a cage from the start.

The original approach—"distributing games via URL"—is Kitao-san's [Playload](https://github.com/kitao/playload), which is designed to isolate and execute games within a dedicated runtime environment and verify the returned data one by one. Time limits for startup and per-frame execution are also built-in from the start. Our player chose the freedom of "running plain HTML as-is," so the "cage" was added as an afterthought. Different forms of freedom require different approaches to security.

## Because there's a cage, it can be distributed.

Anyone can create one and distribute it via a single URL. To protect that freedom, we need an execution model where "no matter what's inside, there's no risk of harm." The cage isn't just for protecting the players—it's two sides of the same coin with allowing creators to distribute with peace of mind. For a detailed explanation of the reasoning, see [the "Security Approach" section of the README](https://github.com/oosawak/html-player).

game:saburo-to-tendo.title: A Sengoku Warlord Who Lived in My Neighborhood
game:saburo-to-tendo.subtitle: Saburo and Kitaro Inari Shrine
game:saburo-to-tendo.summary: I chose Tendo as the first town on my gourmet map. The reason traces back to Saburo—Yorozumi Tendo—from my own SRPG, *Okitama Snowball Fight*. Kitaro Inari Shrine, said to have illuminated the night of the castle's fall; the house inherited by Masakage's son; and the landscapes of Tagajo and Rifu. These are stories of the Sengoku-period warlords who lived nearby.
game:saburo-to-tendo.cover_alt: An illustration of the three characters from "Okitama Snowball Fight" and Muse walking hand-in-hand through the snow
game:saburo-to-tendo.markdown:
This morning, I was deciding on the first town for a project to showcase gourmet information on a map. The candidates were Higashine, Tendo, and Takahata. I was about to go with Higashine, as it has many great restaurants, but in the end, I chose Tendo because "I like Tendo."

The root of that "liking" lies in the SRPG I created, [“Okitama Snowball Fight”](https://oosawak.github.io/srpg/play/okitama/). The model for Saburo in the story is a man named Yorozumi Tendo. His common name happened to be Saburo. As the 10th head of the Tendo family and the same age as Bontenmaru (later Masamune Date), I placed the three of them side by side. Of the three, my favorite is Tokimunemaru — the childhood name of Shigezane Date. Shigezane was a man who wore a caterpillar-shaped crest on his helmet, meaning "never retreat." This perfectly mirrors Tokimunemaru's personality as he charges headlong into the headwind. Conversely, I've set Masamune up as short, incompetent, and a bit of a jerk. The story is primarily driven by Tokimunemaru and Saburo.

## Someone who lived nearby

Yorozumi's life was quite tumultuous. In 1584, Tendo Castle fell to an attack by Yoshimitsu Mogami, and he crossed the Sekiyama Pass to become a retainer of the Date clan. It is said that he later lived in the Miyagi area—the land that is now Tagajo City (at the time, Hachiman in Rifu Village). For me, living in Sendai, it is just a stone's throw away. While Sengoku warlords may seem like figures from a distant world, this man lived right in my neighborhood.

There is also a story that while clearing land, he found a stone monument and realized it was the site of the ancient Taga Castle. While this is a matter of tradition, the image of a later warlord tilling the soil on the land where the Taga Castle monument remains is not bad. Shortly after Saburo moved there, the 1611 Keicho Sanriku earthquake also struck.

What was interesting this morning was the matter of the brothers. Among Yorozumi's brothers was Higashine Yorikage. Higashine and Tendo, who had been lost during the morning, were connected as brothers even within this person's house from 400 years ago.

## Kitaro Inari Shrine

In Hachiman, Tagajo City, the tutelary deity of the Tendo clan remains. It is Kitaro Inari Shrine, also known as Tendo Shrine. The deity enshrined there is Kitsurazaki Kitaro, a retainer of the Tendo clan. It is said that it all began when Kitaro visited Fushimi Inari, attained divine power, and was enshrined as the guardian deity of the Tendo castle town.

A tale of the night the castle fell is preserved in the written history of the shrine grounds. It is said that while Yorozumi was struggling in the darkness after crossing Sekiyama Pass, Kitaro appeared, lit a lamp, and guided him to Ayashi. He was enshrined as the savior of his life. I will leave this, too, as a matter of tradition.

When the Tendo clan was granted a residence in Hachiman, this shrine was also moved with them. It is said to be that there were four identical Kitaro Inari shrines in their original home in Tendo City, three of which still remain around Mount Maizuru today. The remaining one is reportedly the one that was moved to Hachiman. The friendship between Tagajo City and Tendo City is said to be rooted in this connection of the Tendo clan. A town in Yamagata and a nearby town in Sendai were linked by a single shrine.

## The house inherited by Masakage's son

Yorozumi had no children, and the family line continued through adoption. The second son of Rusu Masakage was adopted and became Tendo Shigeyori, succeeding the family in 1611. Masakage was the man who led the Date army in the Battle of Yamagata in 1600. The connection that his son succeeded Saburo's house is also quite interesting. The Tendo family ruled Hachiman until the end of the Edo period. Hachiman, where the residence was located, sits at the junction of the highways coming from the north, between Sendai and Shiogama.

## Lowlands near the sea

The place where they settled was a lowland area near the sea—the polar opposite of the mountainous region of Dewa. There is a story concerning the Tendo family associated with Kasenuma in Rifu. The embankment of that reservoir is the subject of an ongoing debate: one theory suggests it was expanded by Tendo Yorishige, who was in Rifu during the Tensho era, while another claims it was converted into a reservoir in the early Edo period. Regardless of who built it, the water from the marsh has nourished the surrounding rice fields.

Just by the sea lies Uma-no-se in Rifu. It is a cape stretching long and narrow into Matsushima Bay, a mere stone's throw from the local Hachiman shrine. Both Shiogama and Matsushima lay as an extension of this estate.

Finally, I created an illustration of the three characters from the story holding hands as they walk through the snow. With the four of them lined up, it turned out to be quite a nice picture. The cover of this article is that image.

## Muse's winter coat

Looking closely, only Muse's face had fluffy fur. After some discussion, we decided to call this "winter fur," a version tailored for the snow country. Muse has both winter and summer fur, and in winter, even her face becomes fluffy. We adopted this as official lore.

The first town on the map is Tendo. Tracing the reason back led us to a Sengoku-period warlord who lived nearby.

## Reference

- [Yorozumi Tendo (Wikipedia)](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A9%E7%AB%A5%E9%A0%BC%E6%BE%84)
- [Kitaro Inari Shrine (Tagajo City "Winds of History: Shrines Edition")](https://www.city.tagajo.miyagi.jp/bunkazai/shiseki/bunkazai/salon/jinja.html)
- ["Okitama Snowball Fight" (SRPG)](https://oosawak.github.io/srpg/play/okitama/)

game:sendai-ashigaru-machi.title: The People Who Followed Masamune
game:sendai-ashigaru-machi.subtitle: Walking Through Sendai's Ashigaru Town
game:sendai-ashigaru-machi.summary: Gojyunin-machi in Sendai, where I once lived, is a town of only 50 people, yet it looks larger than towns of 300. Driven by this curiosity, I delved into Sendai City records and uncovered shrines transferred from Yonezawa, former retainers left behind in Date District, and ashigaru entrusted with banners. This is a story of Wakabayashi Castle and two castle towns.
game:sendai-ashigaru-machi.cover_alt: An illustration of the streets and shrines of an ashigaru town, with the castle and Hirose River in the distance and Muse walking in the foreground.
game:sendai-ashigaru-machi.markdown:
## Lived in Gojyunin-machi

In Wakabayashi Ward, Sendai City, there is a neighborhood called Gojyunin-machi. I used to live in this neighborhood.

The town's guardian shrine was Date Hachiman Shrine; from what I've heard, it was a neighborhood of fifty ashigaru—a settlement of people who had come from Yonezawa. The current Date Hachiman Shrine is very small. However, I find it hard to believe that the shrine enshrining the guardian deity of Masamune's father, Harumune, brought from Yonezawa, could have been that small. It must originally have been about the same size as Hoshun-in, where the memorial tablet of his mother, Yoshihime, is enshrined. If that were the case, the shrine's grounds would have occupied a considerable portion of the town's area.

Comparing the nearby towns on a modern map, I notice something a bit odd. Gojyunin-machi appears larger than Sanbyakunin-machi, and Rokujunin-machi is quite small. Looking at the numbers alone, a town of 50 people being larger than one of 300 is the opposite of what you'd expect.

Prompted by this question, I looked through materials on Sendai City.

![Schematic map of the ashigaru towns of Wakabayashi. It shows the spatial relationship between the 300-person, 50-person, 60-person, Shibata, Narita, Minami-kaji, Yumino, Higashi-hachibancho, and Funacho towns, as well as the site of Wakabayashi Castle and the Hirose River.](game/ashigaru-map-v6.webp)

A schematic diagram showing the relative positions of the towns looks like this. Since the boundaries and areas are not based on actual measurements, please treat them merely as a rough guide to the locations.

## The town of Sendai is riddled with traces of "relocation."

To begin with, the castle town of Sendai is one where the traces of people's movements are preserved in the town names.

Before Masamune built Sendai Castle, during the campaign against the Uesugi in 1600, he used Kitame Castle in Koriyama, Taihaku Ward, as his base. Originally the castle of Awano Daizen, Masamune is said to have stayed there for about two years. Once the Sendai castle town was established, the people there were relocated, and it became "Kitame-cho." Kokubun-cho, whose name came with its people from Kokubun, and "Gofudaicho" (such as Ara-cho)—townspeople who had followed for generations from Yonezawa and Iwadeyama—follow the same pattern. It was not that the towns moved; rather, the people moved, and the names followed.

Iwadeyama is no different. Originally Iwatezawa Castle. In 1591, Tokugawa Ieyasu, who had come down during the Oshu Shioki, stayed there for about 40 days to repair the castle; when it was handed over to Masamune, it was renamed "Iwadeyama." It is said that Ieyasu himself named it. Even the names of the land move along with the people.

## Gojyunin-machi and a shrine from Yonezawa

Gojyunin-machi is a district nestled between Sanbyakunin-cho and Rokujunin-cho, named for the fifty ashigaru who lived there. It is said to have been laid out around 1630 (Kan'ei 7). While residential areas still line both sides today, the town layout of the ashigaru residences—with narrow frontages and deep interiors—has been preserved.

Gojyunin-machi is also a long street. To the west, it extends as far as the Oshu Kaido. When I lived there, the town was divided into Upper, Middle, and Lower districts. It stretched out so narrowly and long that it had to be split into three parts just to function.

Date Hachiman Shrine is said to have been transferred from Yonezawa in Keicho 5 (1600) to serve as the town's guardian deity. It is said to enshrine the guardian deity of Date Harumune. The legend that it is a "town of people who came from Yonezawa" at least aligns with the shrine's origins.

According to city records, Gojyunin-machi is referred to only as the "Fifty Ashigaru Group," while it is the adjacent Sanbyakunin-cho that explicitly mentions musketeer ashigaru.

## Sanbyakunin-cho — Those Left Behind

The ashigaru of Sanbyakunin-cho were former retainers of the Date clan who had remained in Date District, Fukushima. They were those left behind in that region when the Date clan lost Date District.

In Keicho 5 (1600), when Masamune attacked Shiroishi Castle, they took part in the fighting, returned to the service of the Date clan, and settled in Sendai. The Shinobu Shrine in the town is said to have been established in Keicho 15 (1610) by inviting the deity of a shrine in Shinobu District, the ashigaru's place of origin.

He welcomed back former retainers who had been left behind for nearly a decade—along with their entire community—and even had them enshrined at the shrine in their hometown. I suspect that for Masamune, "those who had stayed by his side since long ago" were indeed special.

## Hometown, specialty town

There is another type of ashigaru town—one where people moved in en masse, grouped by their place of origin.

Shibata Town consisted of 169 ashigaru from Shibata District (around 1633). They enshrined the Otakayama Shrine from their hometown, which later became known as Shiratori Shrine. Shiratori Shrine still stands in Omote-Shibata Town. Narita Town consisted of 60 ashigaru from Narita Village in Momoki District (present-day Kahoku, Ishinomaki City); they were said to have belonged to the O-ban-gumi and were tasked with guarding the group's banners. Guarding the banners was a duty entrusted only to those deemed trustworthy. Hakoishi Shrine, enshrined from their hometown, remains within the town.

Rokujunin-cho also has its own tutelary shrine. It is Shirotori Shrine, enshrined on the boundary between the castle town and Minami-Koizumi Village; it is said to have been named as such because a rope used in the town layout of Sendai Castle in 1626 (Kan'ei 3) was buried there. Another shrine with a name very similar to that of Shiratori Shrine in Shibata Town stands side by side in the same vicinity.

There were also specialized districts. Yumino-cho was the town of the bow ashigaru unit (around 1633). Higashi-hachiban-cho was home to musket ashigaru from Ogawara Village and was also called "Ogawara-cho." Funacho was the town of the boatmen who handled water transport on the Hirose River. Muskets, bows, boats. Towns organized by equipment and skill lined the southeast of the castle town.

Along the highway, there are also artisan districts. Minami-kaji-cho is a town along the Oshu Kaido, situated between Ara-cho and Koku-cho. Blacksmithing was originally based in Moto-kaji-cho (around present-day Kokubun-cho), but around the Kan'ei era, it was divided into north and south sections; it is said that the blacksmiths brought by the Date clan since their time in Yonezawa moved here. The shape of the remaining town is interesting—it is an inverted L-shape. According to Sendai City records, the Oshu Kaido bends from the south toward the west around this area. The town curves along that bend. This means the Oshu Kaido, which the western end of Gojyunin-machi reaches, turns right here.

## Songs of Poverty and Trust

Around Renbo-koji, playful songs remain that poke fun at the poverty of the ashigaru town.

"Renboya, with katafusa hanging—Shibata-cho, Narita: three hundred, fifty, sixty."

The ashigaru reportedly earned meager stipends, growing vegetables in their gardens to sell at the Kawaramachi market or taking on side jobs making brushes. Those who had been trusted in times of war—entrusted with flags and permitted to tend to the shrines of their hometowns—had to settle for paltry wages in an era of peace. Both of these sides likely represent the true nature of these towns.

## Two Castle Towns

The towns mentioned today are not, in fact, the castle town of Sendai Castle. They are the towns of Wakabayashi Castle, built by Masamune in Kan'ei 5 (1628), and its castle town.

Wakabayashi Castle was Masamune's residence in his later years. During the era of the "One Castle per Province" edict, it was nominally built as a residence, but in practice, it served as a second stronghold equipped with stone walls and moats. In Kan'ei 13 (1636), Masamune passed away at his outer Sakurada upper residence in Edo, where he had gone for sankin-kotai; his body was returned to Sendai and buried at Kyogamine. After Masamune's death, Wakabayashi Castle was demolished, but the town remained. The diagonal grid layout of the town on the Wakabayashi Ward side of Sendai City—which differs in angle from that of the Aoba Ward side—is a remnant of this second castle town.

Those who accompanied him were stationed around Masamune's final castle. Viewed this way, one could say that the townscape of this area is a literal reflection of the lord-vassal relationship on the ground.

## The star-shaped prison at the castle site

The site of Wakabayashi Castle is now Miyagi Prison.

In 1879, the Miyagi Correctional Institution was built on the site. It was a panopticon-style prison known as the "Yukigata Rokushu-no-Kamae," featuring a four-story hexagonal tower at the center with six two-story barracks radiating outward; when viewed from above, it resembled a snowflake. It is said to have been a facility for detaining prisoners captured during the Satsuma Rebellion. While the current building has been rebuilt, the earthen ramparts and moats of Wakabayashi Castle remain, surrounded by a wall.

## Turning the lives of the people of these towns into a game

Currently, I am prototyping a game where players live out the lives of people from this era. Players reincarnate as real-life figures from the Sengoku period; time passes automatically as they encounter historical events and choices, and at the end, they reread their life story in a "Biographies" section. It is a Tohoku version covering Sendai, Yamagata, and Fukushima.

- Prototype "Ou Isshoroku": [oosawak.github.io/sengoku-life-sim](https://oosawak.github.io/sengoku-life-sim/)
- Prototype guide for castles and figures: [oosawak.github.io/sengoku-guide](https://oosawak.github.io/sengoku-guide/)

The characters, the castles, and the reading material itself are all managed in Markdown files. The systems for creating game data and writing articles are built on the same Markdown CMS. Exploring the town, creating data, and writing articles all form a single workflow.

The reason why Gojyunin-machi is larger than Sanbyakunin-cho remains, in the end, unknown. However, when measuring the current areas later using official boundary data, Gojyunin-machi was approximately 8.26 hectares and Sanbyakunin-cho approximately 8.49 hectares—nearly the same. Rokujunin-cho is approximately 5.47 hectares. It wasn't an optical illusion that it looked larger. Of course, these are figures based on current boundaries, not the actual extent of the Edo period. The current shape of the towns is also the result of railways, schools, and land readjustment. Even so, it has become clear that these figures represent population, not area. Such investigations can only begin when the people who lived there feel that something is "off."

- Sendai City "[Shrine Tour: 'Minamizai Area'](https://www.city.sendai.jp/waka-katsudo/wakabayashiku/machizukuri/miryoku/terameguri/minami.html)" (Date Hachiman Shrine, Shiratori Shrine)
- Sendai City "[Shrine Tour: Renbo Area](https://www.city.sendai.jp/waka-katsudo/wakabayashiku/machizukuri/miryoku/terameguri/renbo.html)" (Shiratori Shrine)
- Sendai City "[Wakabayashi Castle: Past and Present](https://www.city.sendai.jp/waka-katsudo/wakabayashiku/machizukuri/miryoku/wakabayashijo.html)"
- Sendai City "[Walking the Oshu Kaido](https://www.city.sendai.jp/waka-katsudo/wakabayashiku/machizukuri/miryoku/oshu.html)" (Minami-Kajimachi, bend of the highway)
- Miyasen "[Modern Miyagi Gazetteer #42: Wakabayashi Castle](https://note.com/miya_sen_mame/n/nb6e95ab1699a)" (Inverted L-shape in Minami-Kajicho)
- Osaki City "[Iwadeyama Castle Ruins (Shiroyama Park)](https://www.city.osaki.miyagi.jp/kanko/sizen/kouen/4294.html)"
- For Miyagi Prison and Wakabayashi Castle, refer to the entries for "Miyagi Prison" and "Wakabayashi Castle" on Wikipedia.
